"The Deep Fake."
This is how you can detect the fabrication of sound and image.
In the era of what is known as deep fakes, it has become difficult to tell whether a video is real or not with the naked eye.
But we shouldn't worry, there are ways to find out.
DW has some advice to find out.
Combining the dance, voice and image of American singer Bruno Mars I would advise an example of employing the technique of "deep fakes"
Imagine dancing and singing with the same dexterity, agility and sound power as Bruno Mars!
Many people may think that the technology used to enable anyone to do or say things they have never done is complex, and it can be easily owned, as it only takes footage and video to start creating an “alternative reality. ”
This technique of manipulating both visual and audio content using artificial intelligence is called deepfakes.
This example dates back to 2018 and is still impressive, but now thanks to the “deep fakes ” technique it can be very realistic and convincing.
What is "deep fakes"?
The term "deep fakes" accurately describes the process of collecting audio and video files by artificial intelligence or machine learning.
All areas of "deep fakes" are possible, starting from changing faces, meaning replacing one person's face with another, or synchronizing the movement of the lips, where the speaker's mouth can be set to an audio file different from the original sound or the reproduction of the sound, where a copy of the sound is reproduced for use to say other things.
It is not only at this level, but also completely artificial faces and bodies can be created, for example, a digital avatar.
What ’ s more, “deep fakes ” can be used to evoke the dead, as the Dali Museum in Florida did with Salvador Dali, where the American Museum used this technique to allow visitors to take a live photo with Dali — who died in 1989 — and take selfies himself.
The process of using artificial intelligence to manipulate a video is based on a technique known as the "generative adversarial network", which is a model of machine learning, where two neural networks compete against each other for more accurate results, as this technology aims to improve results.
We may find it difficult to understand what is meant by the competition of two networks, but we will explain how the process works: one computer will inform the other computer if the digital reproduction, whether visual or auditory, that it has made for anyone is convincing and substantially identical to that person ’ s original; that is, whether the lip movement in the cloned copy is identical to the original, and whether facial expressions are identical.
Using the "generative adversarial network", the system as a whole is optimized until a convincing result is reached.
Although this technology is constantly being developed and improved, anyone can detect manipulation whether visual or audio in other words catch “deep fakes ” if the thing we ’ re looking for is identified.
Methods of Detecting "Deep Counterfeiting"
Capturing clips that have been subjected to "deep fakes" does not require one to be an expert in this complex technique in order to distinguish what is real from what is fake.
In that, DW offers some tips to help investigate “deep fakes. ”
First watch the clip carefully and do not rush to publish it, and ask yourself the question: is this clip real?
Couldn't it have been fabricated?
If you are in doubt, do not post it or send it to anyone.
In case of doubt, you should do a search for the same story or clip from different but trustworthy sources on the Internet, as finding a similar story will help you grab the edge of the thread to get to the real story.
If you suspect an audio, image, or video clip, enter that part into Google or DuckDuckGo and look for a similar version.
The two versions can then be compared.
Detecting and detecting some of the effects of manipulation is the biggest challenge, but there are some aspects that may help, such as the presence of inconsistent footage or change in tone or quality of sound and others, no matter how small, may be useful and you have to trust your visual and auditory senses and always ask yourself: Does it make sense?
You should remember that it only takes a lot of focus and you may need to seek help from someone else to help you identify where the manipulations might be simple things like nose, ear, teeth, whiteness or even hairstyle and whether it looks the same.
It may be necessary to view the clip at a scene rate to detect inconsistencies, for example the VL Media Player.
See also watchframebyframe.com.
Also, zoom in on the movements of the mouth and lips and compare them to the original version to discover the synchronization of the movement of the lips, and whether it makes sense.
Enhance your audio-visual skills
It is clear from all the above that it is all about the human senses, especially the auditory and visual skills, and fortunately you can enhance these abilities, through this training you can improve your hearing and vision skills to detect any manipulation of the image or sound.
High risk of "deep fakes" technique
The technique of "deep fakes" can be used in the field of pornography that comes within the framework of what is known as "revenge porn", in which fake pornographic images or clips are posted in order to blackmail or even damage the reputation of the victim.
“Revenge porn ” is defined as posting mostly pornographic images or videos online with the aim of taking revenge and harming people.
As for societies in general, the dangers of deepfakes depend on how we consume the Internet: people see too much when browsing the web and social media and are not always sure what they are posting or sharing, whether it is real or fabricated.
How to Detect Misinformation and Detect Deep Counterfeiting?
In polarized societies, deep fakes are a great opportunity to trick people into believing certain things.
It is not about the quality of the fake video, it may be what you saw, even if it is not true, for example a video of former England star David Beckham speaking nine languages.
In April 2019, Beckham launched a campaign to eradicate malaria by sending a message through a video clip in nine languages.
He began the letter in English and then spoke in eight other languages, but the other eight languages were not in his own voice but in the voices of malaria survivors and doctors.
At the time, the British organisation that produced the video said it had used video technology to make Beckham appear to speak these eight languages.
Politically, a fake “deepfakes ” video was produced by De Correspondent showing Dutch Prime Minister Mark Rutte talking about a major policy change, saying he would fully support long-term climate action.
Some politicians may benefit from a media climate filled with misinformation, but the presence of technology such as "deep fakes" allows them to claim that what they have said is untrue and false and it will be difficult to prove otherwise.
Perhaps the most striking example of this is former US President Donald Trump ’ s claim in 2016 that a 2005 video in which he spoke profanely about women was fabricated, although he later apologized for those words.
Salvador Dali Museum in Florida used artificial intelligence to bring back international painter Salvador Dali "from the dead"
Lesson learned
The bottom line is that spreading misinformation can be for the most prominent reasons of arousing suspicion and controversy or supporting certain beliefs in a deceptive way, but it does make the desired noise.
It may be difficult to verify manipulated videos or audio, but one can be trained to learn how to spot “deep fakes. ”
Above all, it is necessary to stop posting or sharing anything that has not been verified as authentic.

Intermittent fasting: What do you know about its health benefits for weight loss?
• William Park
• BBC
Intermittent fasting makes changing meal times, not meals themselves, helpful, but what to do and what not to do in terms of cutting back on food?
Celebrities and CEOs support intermittent fasting because of its health benefits and weight loss aid.
Although there is promising evidence that fasting can help our bodies in terms of health and possibly prolong our lives, it may not be the best way to lose weight.
Nutritionists urge caution before fasting in order to lose weight.
Intermittent fasting is a type of time-restricted diet, as fasting people leave a long period of time between the last meal of the day and the first meal of the next day, which leads to the compression of their meals in a shorter period during the day.
Typically, fasting people try to leave a gap of up to 16 hours without food, while eating during the remaining eight hours of the day.
Intermittent fasting is not the only type of time-restricted diet; another is called the "5: 2 diet" (a person eats a normal amount of food over five days and then, during the remaining two days of the week, eats only 25 percent of their usual calories).
This system focuses more on the amount of food consumed, rather than the time between meals.
Rachel Clarkson, founder of London-based consultancy DNA Nutrition, said: “Time-restricted nutrition is used as a weight loss tool, but it ’ s not my style.
“You ’ re cutting calories, but you ’ re not learning to change basic behavior about what you put in your body. ”
Clarkson points out that without knowing what a healthy diet looks like, people gain weight again when they stop fasting: “If it means you feel hungry and food restrictions, it could lead to you overeating the next day. ”
Therefore, intermittent fasting may not be the right way for people seeking to lose weight, but there may be other reasons to change your eating patterns.
Fasting is linked to a process called autophagy, which attracts a lot of attention for its potential health benefits.

Autophagy is the process by which the body begins to recycle structures within its cells, including the nucleus, where DNA is stored, mitochondria, which makes the chemical our cells use for energy, and lysosomes, which remove waste from our cells.
In doing so, the cell can remove obsolete structures, freeing up new raw materials from which new cell structures can be built.
Some new raw materials can be used to make cell protective proteins that extend the life of cells.
There is interest in whether “autophagy ” can extend the lifespan of entire organisms as well – although so far this has only happened with animals, such as 1-mm nematodes and mice, not humans (research has linked autophagy inhibition to the early onset of aging).
Until there are more studies of intermittent human fasting, it is too early to say it will extend our lifespan.
But animal studies have linked autophagy to improvements in immune system memory.
In addition, the fact that autophagy is necessary to maintain cell health has also generated interest in its role in fighting cancer.
There may be more reasons than increasing the shelf life of attention to autophagy.
For most humans, autophagy occurs during sleep, but it also occurs when exercise and hunger occur.
Can regular fasting help stimulate this autophagy?
Unlike calorie-restricted diets (which studies have also linked to longevity), the purpose of intermittent fasting is to increase the time between the last meal of the day and the first meal of the next day.
(Theoretically, a person who fasts can get the same amount of calories as usual, although Clarkson says that in practice this results in most people reducing the amount of food they eat.)
Clarkson says, “When you stop eating at 7 p.m., you ’ ll stay in the ‘ feeding state ’ until 10 p.m. because you ’ ll continue to digest nutrients.
Any carbohydrates in your diet will give you a good supply of glucose, our excellent source of fuel, for a few hours. ”
“Nutrition status ” refers to the period when the body uses glucose in the blood as an energy source.
Once this energy source is used, the body turns into a state of catabolism or catabolism – usually about three hours after eating.
At this stage, glycogen stored in the liver and muscles breaks down into glucose.
When glycogen stores are depleted, the body switches from glucose to ketones, which are made in the liver from fatty acids.
At this stage, a stage called the "ketogenic state" begins, which provokes "autophagy".
Clarkson says, “We don ’ t know exactly when to switch from glucose to ketones.
It depends on many things; genes, health status and lifestyle.
“The amount of glycogen you have will depend on how much you ’ ve eaten and how much energy you ’ ve burned. ”
A person on a high-carb diet may never move beyond a state of catabolism or catabolism, since they will always have a reserve of glycogen.
However, a person who follows a low-carb diet and exercises regularly may transition from this condition very quickly (the "keto diet", in which you move away from almost all carbohydrates to keep blood sugar levels and glycogen stores low, works in the same way).
Clarkson said, “To fast, you have to reduce the feeling of hunger. ”
We get hungry when ghrelin, a hormone secreted from our stomach, produces two other hormones, NPY and AGPR, in the pituitary region.
While these three hormones generate hunger, there are a plethora of other hormones that suppress the process of feeling hungry, sometimes called “satiety hormones, ” the most important of which is leptin, which is released from fat cells to suppress the production of ghrelin — essentially telling the body“ there ’ s fat here that you can burn. ”
Ghrelin is sometimes called a "short-term hunger response" because it is released when the stomach is empty and the pressure is less on the stomach wall.
It can be overcome to some extent by drinking water.
In the meantime, the leptin works in the long run.
Clarkson says, “Our hunger hormones are regulated by many things, and genetics is one of them.
But thinking about the nerves connected to our stomach and digestive system means that if your stomach isn ’ t swollen, your body will think it ’ s hungry. ”
Keeping your body hydrated can help you feel hungry early so your body adapts.
“It ’ s going to be tough in the first two weeks, but you ’ ll get used to it. ”
With a careful approach, intermittent fasting may help your body recover.
“Autophagy ” seems to decline with age, so it may be helpful to give yourself a boost by fasting in that period.
But be aware that fasting may not be the right weight loss strategy, and there is no alternative to a balanced diet.

Selenium
When experiments were conducted to find out the protective action of dietary supplements for cancer, the trials had to be stopped because the original act of supplementation was contrary to what was expected, as studies in men were published exclusively in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute, and showed that overdoses of selenium could lead to increased chances of developing high-grade cancers, not in people lacking selenium, but in people with adequate levels of selenium. Vitamin E
Selenium regulates thyroid hormones and works together with vitamin E to reduce free radicals generated in the cell, free radicals are inherently carcinogenic, so both vitamins are mostly associated with anti-cancer properties, however, studies have shown that when people with already high levels of selenium consume vitamin E supplements, the risk of prostate cancer was found to increase by 69%.

7 Weirdest Robots That Science Has Reached “You ’ ll Never Imagine ”
© Photo / pixabay / mariananbuA bee-shaped robot with a fan
Follow us via
Scientific robotics companies are competing to create sophisticated models that can meet many different needs, especially in medicine and other fields.
The large and massive development in the field of artificial intelligence, chips and complex mechanics supported by advanced technology contributes to increasing the speed of development of robots and the multiplicity of their varieties and sizes, which has produced a series of very strange robots, the most prominent of which are:
1- Metabird Robot
The MetaBird robot is a drone, almost indistinguishable from real birds, and is based on the principle of biomimicry from Bionic Bird.
The principle of biomimicry is the successful and accurate replication of the properties or mechanisms of action of things that already exist in nature.
The bird-shaped aircraft weighs less than 10 grams and has no propellers, making it safe to maneuver. It is also equipped with flexible wings made of carbon fiber and liquid crystal polymers. The body itself is made of durable foam, so it is not affected by water and shocks. It is equipped with a battery to help it fly for 10 minutes and is controlled by a mobile device.
Robot (Bat Bot).
Researchers at the California Institute of Technology and the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign have recreated key bat flight mechanisms and embedded them into the Batbot.
The robot weighs about 93 grams and flies with wings made of an easily stretchable silicone membrane.
The robot can simply change the shape of the wings, bend and disassemble them, and can fold the shoulders, elbows, wrists and legs.
The computer and sensors are embedded in the Batbot head, and there are five precision motors along the spine.
It provides him with the ability to mimic flying mammals well by controlling him with a special device.
Researchers suggest that thanks to flexible wings, robotic bats are more energy efficient than other flying robots.
Lightweight and agile, these robots are useful as traditional quadcopters can collide with objects or people causing damage or injury, such as on construction sites.
3. Salamander Robot "BlueRobot"
The "Pleurobot" robot, created by researchers at the Federal Polytechnic School of Lausanne (EPFL), can walk on the ground, swim underwater and navigate between the two with similar success to the amphibian salamander.
To develop the robot, scientists used salamander X-rays and studied how its skeleton worked during movement.
The low center of gravity, which allows the robot to move on rough terrain without losing balance, also provides the ability to swim and can make it a useful tool for search and rescue operations.
The researchers also plan to study the interaction between the spinal cord, the body and the environment.
According to the project leader, Olek Eisbert, understanding the basis of this interaction will help develop neuroprosthetic therapies and devices for those with hemiplegia and amputation.
4. The water snake robot "Elum"
The snake-like body allows the robot to move effectively not only on the ground, but also in the water.
The Norwegian robotics company has borrowed the nickname "Eelume" to design an autonomous autonomous robot.
His slim, flexible body gave him the ability to work in confined spaces where conventional underwater vehicles could not get in.
Eelume is suitable for inspections and light repairs of underwater structures such as offshore wind farms, fish farms, oil and gas installations and pipelines.
The device consists of modules that can be interconnected in different groups depending on the task.
The robot is shipped from the docking station on the seabed so that it can stay underwater continuously and not depend on weather conditions.
The cockroach robot "CRAM"
Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have developed a prototype of a roach-like CRAM robot.
The design of the robot was inspired by the unique way insects move and are immune to damage.
The robot has an exoskeleton made up of strong panels and a soft cover that allows it to change shape and adapt to very narrow gaps.
Such a robot could help search for and rescue people under rubble formed as a result of hurricanes, earthquakes and explosions.
6. Pet Robots
These robots work on the principle of interactive communication between humans and robots with the aim of improving the quality of life of the elderly, such as the robot "AIBO" from Sony.
An example of this is also the robot dog produced by the company "Tombot".
This robot is almost like a real Labrador puppy and, according to the developers, should solve the problem of elderly people who need a friend, but are unable to care for a living dog.
The company ’ s founder was inspired by his mother, who suffered from Alzheimer ’ s disease and was no longer able to care for her dog, with whom she was so attached.
The dog became aggressive towards its mother, exacerbating the woman's depression and loneliness.
Accompanying robots could solve loneliness and social isolation in older adults and people with cognitive disabilities, as part of a study funded by the American insurance company.
7- The therapeutic robot "PARO"
PARO is one of the most important humanoid therapeutic robots developed by Dr. Takanori Shibata, of Japan ’ s National Institute of Industrial Science and Advanced Technology.
The robot is similar to a children's toy, except that it has sound, light, temperature, position, sensors and touch sensors.
PARO can move its tail and fins, open its eyes when caressed, and imitate the sounds of a real seal.
It reacts to words that its owner frequently uses and can express emotions such as surprise, happiness and anger.
Communication with the robot "PARO" has the same effect as the treatment provided by real animals.
Patients showed improvement in psychological and physiological factors, as well as social activity.

An announcement to hire 30 female train drivers in Saudi Arabia has attracted nearly 28,000 applications from women, highlighting how much women want to join the labor market as the conservative kingdom creates more opportunities for women.
Spanish railway company Renfe said on Wednesday an online assessment of academic degrees and English language skills had helped it cut the number of female candidates by half and would clear the rest by mid-March.
Those selected will drive fast trains between the cities of Mecca and Medina after a year of paid training.

Women were not allowed to drive in the kingdom until 2018.
Female labor market participation has doubled in the past five years to 33 percent amid a campaign by the crown prince to pull Saudi society out of the cocoon and diversify the economy, and women are now starting to get jobs that were previously restricted to men and migrant workers.
But the proportion of women working in the kingdom still hovers around half the proportion of men in the third quarter of last year at 34.1 percent, and female unemployment is three times higher than that of men at 21.9 percent.
Saudi Arabia is highlighting its progress on women ’ s issues at a time when it faces Western scrutiny over its human rights record, including its crackdown on dissent that has led to the arrest of dozens of women ’ s rights activists and the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi in 2018.

Airbus earns the highest profit in its history with 4.2 billion euros
Airbus will distribute dividends to shareholders with plans to offer a €1.5 share per share.
Airbus returned to growth in 2021 with the biggest profit in its history, unaffected by the historic air transport crisis in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic.
After posting losses for two consecutive years, the European planemaker reported a net profit of 4.2 billion euros in 2021, surpassing the 2018 record level of 3.1 billion euros at a time when it was manufacturing nearly a quarter more aircraft than the current number.
Guillaume Fawry, the group ’ s chief executive, said in a statement that “our focus has shifted from managing the epidemic to recovery and growth. ”
Fawry attributed these "remarkable" results to the increase in the number of commercial aircraft delivered, which amounted to 611 aircraft in 2021, an increase of 8 percent over 2020, to the "good performance" of space and defense activities, as well as to the helicopter division "and" the focus on cost reduction and competitiveness ".
The volume of deliveries is a reliable indicator of profitability in the aircraft industry, with customers paying the bulk of the bill when they receive the aircraft.
In its 2022 guidance, Airbus said it “does not expect further disruption to the global economy, air traffic, the company ’ s internal operations and its ability to deliver products and services. ”
Airbus will distribute dividends to shareholders with plans to offer a stake of 1.5 euros per share, after cancelling it in the past two years.
But U.S. rival Boeing did not make a profit, posting a loss for a third year in a row in 2021 as the cost of delayed deliveries of the 787 and more expensive production runs higher.
Aviation collapsed in 2020 as the COVID-19 pandemic forced countries to close their borders.
Since the start of the health crisis, Airbus has cut production significantly and announced the abolition of 15,000 jobs before finally reducing that number to 10,000.
The group, which had 126,000 employees at the end of 2021, plans to employ at least 6,000 people this year.
Airbus, whose production has fallen by a third to 40 A320 single-aisle aircraft (A319, A320 and A321) per month since April 2020, was producing about 45 aircraft per month at the end of 2021.
It plans to increase its production to 65 A320 aircraft per month in 2023, an unprecedented number.
Revenue increased 4 percent to 52.1 billion euros last year thanks to the number of commercial aircraft delivered.
Its operating profit was €477 million at the time the company abandoned its A380 Jumbo program.
It received 507 new orders, more than twice as many as in 2020, including the first orders for the new E-350 cargo plane.
While the frequency of air travel remained low last year, and will return to pre-COVID-19 levels only in 2023 for domestic travel and in 2025 for long-distance flights, "it has become clear that people want to fly again and will do so as soon as travel restrictions are lifted," Fawry told a news conference.
The pace of global travel is expected to double, compared to pre-epidemic levels, by 2050.
Airlines struggled with travel restrictions last year, especially in Asia, where China imposes strict border measures.
Air France-KLM reported net losses again in 2021, though less than half of what they were in 2020, at 3.3 billion euros.

January and February are the coldest months of the year and the most dangerous for the immune system, as the presence of cold and flu viruses is very high at this time.

But, according to health experts, hot showers, despite their short-term and long-term benefits, may be less beneficial than cold showers.
The idea of bathing in cold water in the morning may seem crazy in the middle of winter, but some studies have found that the practice can strengthen the immune system.
Studies have also found that it can improve brain function and improve symptoms of depression.
The results come from two studies, one from the Netherlands and the other from the Czech Republic.
The study, conducted in the Netherlands on more than 3,000 people, found that routine cold showers led to a statistical reduction of self-reported disease in adults without severe comorbidities.

However, while the results of the studies were positive, a number of experts warned that "the biological significance of the observed changes remains to be clarified."
Other benefits of plunging into cold water or bathing in cold water include activation of the sympathetic nervous system.
This part of the nervous system controls the body ’ s fight-or-flight response, producing a hormone known as noradrenaline or norepinephrine, which classifies its functional role as hormones and neurotransmitters in the brain and body.
Shower in the morning or evening.

A previous study in 2000 found that participants exposed to cold water experienced a 350% increase in metabolism.
This, in turn, means that long periods of cold showers can help people lose weight.
In addition to providing physical benefits, cold showers and soaking in cold water are thought to have mental health benefits as well, and this includes treating depression.
Shevchuk suggested that during cold showers, a huge number of electrical signals are sent to the brain due to the large number of cold receptors in the skin suggesting that this leads to an antidepressant effect.

Many may not have tried avocado fruit, but knowing its great benefits may prompt them to change their mind and rush to the nearest place to buy it.

Scientists have found that eating avocado has a positive effect on the health of the digestive system and stomach.
Adding avocados to one meal a day significantly improves the bacterial diversity of gut bacteria that helps in the proper and healthy functioning of the digestive system.
A study examined 163 participants aged 25-45, who were overweight or obese.
For each of the participants, the researchers replaced one of the day ’ s meals with the one they made up.
The experimental group received a meal containing avocado, while the control group received the same menu – but no avocado was eaten.
The results showed that although avocados were a high-fat food and the participants in the experimental group consumed more calories per day than the control group, they also burned more fat than they did.
Burning fat at a higher rate means that participants who ate avocado accumulated less fat in their body cells than the food they ate.
The researchers added that avocado contains a lot of dietary fiber and monounsaturated fats, two components that contribute to heart health, and eating avocado prompted participants to develop a more diverse group of intestinal bacteria, which simplifies the process of breaking down dietary fiber in digestion.

2.

Incorporating avocado into your daily diet can help reduce cholesterol levels, thereby reducing cardiovascular disease.
Harmful cholesterol builds up inside the arteries, causing them to narrow and obstruct blood flow through them.

The participants were divided into 3 groups, each of which was given a different menu for 5 weeks: a low-fat diet, a moderate-fat diet, a moderate-fat diet + one avocado per day.

6 Pros and Cons of Intermittent Fasting
Published 04 March 2022 - 09: 00
Pros and Cons of Intermittent Fasting
Intermittent fasting is one of the most common health trends of the past decade, with some people finding it helps manage their appetite and weight and supports optimal health.
However, intermittent fasting may not be suitable for everyone, either for medical reasons or because it doesn ’ t match some people ’ s perception of a nutritious and sustainable diet, and through this article we ’ ll look at some of the most common ways to do intermittent fasting, as well as some of the pros and cons.
What is Intermittent Fasting?
Intermittent fasting is an eating pattern in which you refrain from eating any calories for a long period of time, this period usually lasts between 12 and 40 hours, water, coffee and other calorie-free drinks are allowed during fasting, but solid foods or calorie-containing drinks are not allowed.
For example, if you finish dinner at 7pm, you don ’ t eat again until 7pm for the next day, and so you have completed a 24-hour fast, some people also choose to fast from breakfast to breakfast or lunch to lunch, but the time frame that works best depends on the individual.
Full 24-hour fasting every other day may seem extreme and may be difficult for many people to maintain, so it ’ s not usually recommended for beginners.
Advantages of Intermittent Fasting
Researchers have already linked several health benefits to intermittent fasting and continue to examine them, in addition, for some people, intermittent fasting fits well into their model of a healthy, sustainable, long-term diet.
And if you ’ re wondering if intermittent fasting is right for you, here are some benefits you might be interested in, which include:
• Supports weight loss and improves metabolic health
Two main reasons people try intermittent fasting are to manage their weight and metabolic health, as metabolic health is a sign of how well the body processes or metabolizes energy, and is often measured by blood pressure, blood sugar and blood lipid levels.
In fact, fasting or abstaining from food can lead to calorie deficiencies, which means your body has fewer calories than it needs to maintain its current weight, which is why calorie-restricted diets, such as fasting, are the hallmark of most weight loss diets.
Research shows that some types of intermittent fasting can be effective for weight loss, though not necessarily more effective, like other diets that also rely on limiting daily calorie intake.
• It can be a sustainable lifestyle change
Intermittent fasting may seem complicated and scary, but it can sometimes be simple.
In fact, you may find that fasting helps streamline your day because you need to plan fewer meals.
Moreover, it usually doesn ’ t require counting calories, eating certain foods you may not be used to, or eliminating certain foods you otherwise enjoy.
For example, having an early dinner followed by a late breakfast the next day is one way to fast intermittently, and if you finish your last meal at 8 p.m., and don ’ t eat until noon the next day, you ’ ve technically been silent for 16 hours.
For people who are hungry in the morning and love breakfast, or for those who can ’ t eat until later in the evening due to work schedules and other commitments, it can be difficult to get used to this method.
• Works well with a nutritious whole foods diet
Because intermittent fasting focuses more on when rather than what you eat, it ’ s generally easy to implement along with your current diet, as you won ’ t necessarily need to buy any special foods or much different from what you normally eat.
And if you ’ re already satisfied with the state of your current diet but are looking for other ways to continue boosting your overall health, fasting may be something you want to explore.
For example, intermittent fasting may work particularly well for someone who wants to pair it with a resistance training program and a high-protein diet, however, that doesn ’ t mean that what you eat doesn ’ t matter, as there ’ s no doubt that you ’ ll reap the greatest benefits from intermittent fasting by eating a variety of nutritious foods and limiting ultra-processed foods.
Cons of Intermittent Fasting
Intermittent fasting is one way to regulate calorie intake and work to improve your metabolic health, but while an eating pattern can certainly be part of a healthy diet, it will likely require some adaptation to it initially.
Here are some of the downsides you can experience when trying intermittent fasting for the first time, which include:
It may conflict with your intuition.
Intermittent fasting requires discipline, self-control, and planning for the future, and for some people, using these tactics to keep calorie intake within a set time frame is not a problem, but for others, it may seem unnatural at first, and this may be especially true if you are used to relying on your intuition to decide when to eat.
Moreover, if you prefer not to follow a strict schedule, you may find intermittent fasting frustrating, and also if your schedule tends to vary from day to day due to work, family, or other commitments, keeping your calorie intake within a set time frame can be difficult.
You are likely to feel hungry.
Even fasting for 8 or 12 hours may seem like a long time when you are not used to fasting, you may go to bed hungry several times a week, and this may naturally seem unpleasant and unsustainable in the long run, in addition, sometimes it may be necessary to bypass the natural signals of hunger and fullness so as not to break your fast earlier than planned.
Once you adapt to intermittent fasting, you may find that it makes you feel less hungry, and in fact many people adapt to the routine, and some find that they enjoy it after a few months, but nevertheless, hunger and frustration are certainly things to be expected and realized at the beginning.
• Side effects can affect your mood
When you try intermittent fasting for the first time, one of the first things you might notice is the ups and downs in your mood, which is understandable.
Besides initially increasing hunger levels, fasting can have side effects, including headaches, constipation, fatigue, sleep disturbances, and more.
Moreover, irritability and anxiety are classic symptoms of low blood sugar levels, this is a common physical response to fasting or calorie restriction, however, like hunger, your emotional well-being may be another side effect of intermittent fasting that will improve with time and practice.

Um Osama continues: “The days passed, and the circumstances changed, and our conditions worsened, so we moved to Turkey, where my husband suffered several heart attacks, and as a result, I was forced to work, and because I did not have any scientific degree, and I did not master any interest or craft, and the biggest obstacle to me was the language, all that forced me to work in cleaning dishes. At a restaurant in Urfa.
This shift in the culture of society is behind the reality of war, where work is no longer a culture, development and right, but a duty imposed by the difficult living conditions of the Syrian family. to work in harsh conditions.
Um Mohammed Shalgham was not older than the end of the fourth decade when her husband abandoned her and his second wife influenced her, and abandoned her with her two children, so she was forced to work in agriculture, and several other professions, the last of which was in a cotton mill at the beginning of the winter season, because agricultural work stopped in this season.
The years of war in Syria have put women and girls in front of the reality of work, to bridge the gap resulting from burdensome economic conditions, and sometimes they were the only breadwinners in the absence of a forced man, between arrest, death, migration or involvement in war with one of the parties to the conflict, which gradually formed social acceptance of women ’ s work due to exceptional social conditions, after Syrian families rejected it for years.
A study carried out by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) showed that about 145,000 Syrian families, in which women play the role of breadwinner, and are solely responsible for providing all their necessities with the absence of men.
Challenges facing women in the labour market
Women face significant challenges in the employment sector, such as limited employment opportunities or limited options, especially for holders of degrees.
A study by Orange Foundation, covering women ’ s access to the labor market in Syria, identified potential challenges for Syrian women to work in organizations or companies, most notably logistics. 82% of participants faced the challenges of having facilities for children, 55% faced problems related to having children, while 43% faced challenges related to working conditions, family obligations (39%), and social and cultural customs (30%).
There are major challenges facing women in the labor market, including obtaining work permits, “sikorta ” (health insurance), language, the perception of some host countries that refugees are depriving them of their opportunities to work, because they accept less than the minimum wage, in addition to some social customs and traditions, and the male perception of some communities and families about women ’ s work.
Umm Mohammed did not realize that her work and social life would stop in the cotton gin. One day, while cleaning around one of the machines, she suddenly fell and the machine pulled Umm Mohammed ’ s foot inside, but her large weight helped her foot stop at the first machine, but after it was too late, the blades hit her foot badly. The owner of the lab took her to the hospital and after the police came to take her statement. In the Turkish language, they asked her to testify, that Umm Mohammed fell from the car, so that the owner of the factory does not have any responsibility, and pays large sums of money, because the Syrian workers work without a sikorta, any health insurance, and have no official records or restrictions, and the investigation ended.
Umm Mohammed, who was under the influence of the operation and the excruciating pain eating her foot, did not know what happened, and what was written in the investigation, and at the end of the day gave the Batroun to Umm Mohammed equivalent of 1500 Turkish liras, and he came out, and Umm Mohammed still to this day retreat the hospital, and operations are conducted one after another has become almost helpless and use crutches to do some things, and have no one.
In the countries of asylum
For example, Jordan has allowed Syrian refugees to work in the agricultural, construction and manufacturing sectors only, and to obtain employment in these limited fields requires a work permit, not to mention the cultural challenge for refugee women to integrate and learn the language before seeking employment.
Um Osama adds: “The working hours are very long, and sometimes forced to switch shifts, to become from 3 pm to 11 pm, in addition to the double pay, which does not reach 80 Turkish lira, and this wage that Umm Osama receives, does not reach the minimum wage of workers in Turkey, but Umm Osama insists that employers control us, because of poor living conditions, that force us to accept any work. ” No matter what you say, pay and pay.
Om Osama explains: Employers evade getting a work permit, or “Sikorta, ” in order to evade paying taxes to the state, and not to give us our full wages.
The role of organizations and civil society in the empowerment of women
The Syrian Women ’ s Committee is an organization registered with the Turkish government and is a non-profit organization to support and empower Syrian women in Turkey.
The organization includes about 1200 women of different ages and geographical areas in Syria who sought refuge in Turkey / Reyhanli.
The aim of the organization is to empower Syrian women in all fields through economic and awareness projects that enable them to overcome the challenges they face in the country of asylum. There are several projects that the Women ’ s Committee in Reyhanli is interested in, such as the domestic food supply project, the rattan industry project, the Sufi works and dolls project, the women ’ s haircut project, and the crochet project.
There are many obstacles facing the activities of the Women's Committee, the most important of which is the lack of funding or financial support, or the marketing body for women's products in the Committee, as well as the lack of experience in electronic and physical marketing, so many difficulties, and the Women's Committee tries to overcome and reach its goals with success, even at a small level initially to reach the biggest successes later.
Another obstacle is the language factor, which hinders the development of the committee ’ s projects and their spread in the surrounding society.
As for the quality of projects that achieve economic benefit, it depends on handicrafts and the manufacture of sweets and Syrian foods, in addition to the preservation of mortars and drying of food, works of wool and art, accessories and wall paintings, which in its entirety does not require muscle effort as much as it needs creativity and training and mastery and art.
Economic Empowerment:
Economic empowerment provides women with the ability to control family resources and sources of income, in addition to many economic matters; access to markets and provide them with equal employment opportunities with men in access to important economic positions, participation in economic decision-making, and enhancing their ability to financial independence through earning money, and participation in the workforce.
Research suggests that women could contribute as much as $28 trillion to global GDP by 2025 if they can participate fully in the global economy.
Women ’ s empowerment opens the door to economic potential at all levels of society, from the state, through private companies and government institutions, to individual women, their families and their communities.
Seventy years ago, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was published: “All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. ”
These words, which are very simple in nature, are also very profound, if we devote a moment to think about them.
We are all equally valuable.
Our right to freedom is inherent in each of us, our right to freedom from fear and want, and to freedom of choice in its simplest form, including the freedom to make decisions about our personal lives.
Women ’ s autonomy, choices, and rights lead to greater economic growth: it ’ s self-evident that women make up half the world ’ s population.
It is also more sustainable, since its pillars are broader and its benefits more rooted.
But the empowerment of women is also important, because women are important and their choices are important, and we must never forget to focus on this aspect, and we can only empower women and girls if we respect, protect and achieve women ’ s human rights.
Women ’ s economic empowerment – their ability to succeed and advance economically and their power to make and act on economic decisions – is a fundamental human right, and all countries in the region have ratified the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW).
However, seven countries registered reservations to article 15 (on the equal rights of women to conclude contracts and administer property) and 11 to article 16 (on the right of married women to own, administer and dispose of property on an equal basis with men).
This has a negative impact on women ’ s economic empowerment in the region, as it affects women ’ s equal access to resources.
Expanding economic opportunities for women is important because it is a critical factor in women ’ s empowerment, and UN Women ’ s efforts on economic empowerment are being implemented in the context of women ’ s rights and work, social justice, and inclusive sustainable development that includes social, economic and environmental dimensions in line with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
It promotes Women Empowerment Principles (WEPs), engaging with the private sector to improve women ’ s position in the economy, for inclusive and sustainable growth; challenging gender stereotypes; and raising awareness and support to address gender-based discrimination at the individual and family levels that hinders women and perpetuates gender inequality in society.
In all of our economic empowerment programs, UN Women works to reach the women most in need, often through engagement with grassroots and civil society organizations. In this context, marginalized groups include rural women, domestic workers, some migrant women, and low-skilled women.
By adopting a comprehensive programme approach, UN-Women aims to contribute to higher levels of income, improved access to and control over resources, and increased security for all women, including protection from violence.
Why women need to be empowered?
In their definition of women ’ s empowerment, feminist studies have pointed to several prominent reasons for women ’ s empowerment, including:
• Reduce the increasing and continuing burdens of poverty and ignorance placed on women.
Inequality and inequality in health care and economic, social and political rights.
• Inadequate and effective mechanisms for the advancement of women at all levels.
Women ’ s empowerment (also: Women ’ s empowerment) is defined as the process by which women, individually and collectively, become aware of the way power relations affect their lives, gaining self-confidence and the ability to address inequality between them and men.
The most important international conferences dealing with women ’ s rights:
In the 1970s, motivated by inequalities in many areas of daily life, as well as women's poverty and discrimination against young girls, the United Nations decided to launch the United Nations Decade for Women: Equality, Development and Peace, 1976-1985. The Commission on the Status of Women organized four major world conferences aimed at mainstreaming women's rights: Mexico, 1975-Copenhagen, 1980-Nairobi, 1985.
This decade culminated in the adoption of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (CEDAW).
This document is the most important human rights instrument for the protection and promotion of women's rights, as it recognizes, for the first time, women as full human beings. The Convention covers civil and political rights, as well as economic, social and cultural rights.
One of the main goals for which he created microfinance is the empowerment of women, where low-interest loans are given to women in developing communities, so that they can start small businesses that help them support their families.

Major industries typically take over the helm of the economy and create jobs in society.
The growth of the world economy in the past decade has been boosted by developments in various industries, in particular technology, science, health and manufacturing.
As the pace of spending and wealth increases around the world, existing industries grow and others disappear from the scene amid the rising development of human society.
It is the responsibility of large industries to provide essential products and services that improve the lives of billions of people around the world.
The aviation industry is among the industries most affected by the COVID-19 virus, with Boeing, for example, suffering losses of about $11.9 billion in 2020.
This industry includes a number of companies that are involved in the development and manufacture of aircraft for purposes including commercial, passenger, military, cargo, government, surveillance and refueling of other aircraft in the air.
It also includes sales by private companies of equipment used for space flights and missions.
The value of the global aviation sector declined to $359.3 billion in 2020, from $818.3 billion in 2019, as a result of the Coronavirus epidemic, with expectations of $471.8 billion this year.
The aviation industry encompasses almost all aspects of air travel and related activities.
This means that it includes the entire aviation sector, the aircraft industry, research companies, military aviation, and others.
The term aviation is usually used to describe mechanical air transport that is carried out through the use of aircraft.
The sector consists of two types of aircraft, regular and helicopter, as well as the new type of drones.
The aviation industry has two types of activity, the first related to passenger and cargo transport, while the second includes aircraft manufacturing, research operations, safety and military aviation, as well as companies specialized in the production, design and use of drones.
The importance of the aviation industry lies in connecting different continents, countries and cultures, as well as facilitating long-distance travel.
It also contributes significantly to the global economy, trade between countries and the creation of millions of jobs around the world.
Among the largest aircraft manufacturers are Boeing, Airbus and Lockheed Martin.
The European Airbus, which has industrial facilities in Germany, France and the Netherlands, is the largest in the world.
The Airbus A380 is also the largest aircraft in the world.
American Boeing, based in Chicago, comes in second place.
In addition to producing military aircraft, the company is also known for manufacturing spaceships.
Lockheed Martin is the world's largest manufacturer of warplanes, including the F-16, F-35 and others.
Aircraft manufacturers are planning to reduce the rate of production of large aircraft and focus on smaller ones, a trend that began just before the outbreak of the pandemic.
These companies are working to convince airlines to buy this type of aircraft because of its fuel efficiency of 15%.
Among the largest suppliers in the aviation industry are United Technologies, General Electric Aviation, Safran, Rolls-Royce Holdings, Honeywell Aerospace and others.
The activities of manufacturers vary from the design, construction, testing, sale, maintenance and production of spare parts, spaceships and others.
The value of aircraft production in 2015 was about $180.3 billion, of which 61 percent was for airlines, 14 percent for business and general aviation, 12 percent for military helicopters and about 3 percent for civilian helicopters.
The value of maintenance, repairs and refurbishment of the aircraft is estimated at $135.1 billion, bringing the total volume of production to $315.4 billion.
Boosting demand activity is the growing affluence of the middle class in emerging markets.
Air traffic is expected to rebound significantly in Latin America and Africa, although these regions are expected to suffer even more from the spread of COVID-19.
While the proportion of aircraft grounded is usually estimated at 10%, it rose to 60% during the epidemic for 13,350 aircraft.
According to data from Asnad Aviation Consultancy, 902 new aircraft were ordered from Boeing and Airbus this year, excluding cancelled orders and orders from non-profit customers, compared to 672 in 2020.
In this climate of awakening, airlines are planning to renew their fleets, driven by a rebound in summer travel, even in Europe, despite the slower pace of recovery from the epidemic than in the United States.

The Map of Doctrines and the Consolidation of Pluralism in Saudi Arabia
What is the map of sectarian diversity in Saudi Arabia, and how the Kingdom ’ s Vision 2030 works to build a society that respects pluralism and preserves coexistence and civil peace?
A special report for the website "Araby.net"
Posted in: Last Updated:
“Saudi Arabia has Sunni and Shiite sects, and in the Sunni sect there are four sects, and Shiites have different sects as well, and they are represented in a number of legitimate bodies, and no one can promote one of these doctrines to make it the only way to see religion in Saudi Arabia, ” Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud said in an interview with The Atlantic magazine....
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman
The frankness that characterized the speech of Prince Mohammed bin Salman, aims to consolidate sectarian pluralism in Saudi Arabia, and present the Kingdom as a homeland for its various social components, and that "citizenship" is the building block of the state, and various citizens have the right to choose the Islamic doctrine to which they belong, without discrimination or preference for one person or sect over another.
When King Abdul Aziz bin Abdul Rahman Al Saud announced the establishment of the third Saudi state in 1932 and the unification of the Arabian Peninsula, he knew that his state embraces multiple cultures, tribes and sects, and that one of the elements of the strength of the state, to maintain peaceful coexistence among all these components, and make them cooperate with each other.
As the leader of the people, he represented the symbol of their unity, and therefore the building block was the act of "political" rather than "religious", where the state was based on a political vision aimed at development, security and stability.
King Abdulaziz Bin Abdulrahman
The existing plurality!
In 2015, Al-Mesbar Center for Research and Studies published its monthly book No. 107: “Pluralism in the Gulf and its Neighbourhood: Reality and Prospects, ” in which I participated in a study on sectarian diversity in Saudi Arabia, titled“ Pluralism that is not wanted to be seen, ” in which I referred to “the resistance of a large segment of radical clerics, who sought to highlight the kingdom in the image of the Salafi state. ” Salafism is any other doctrinal or doctrinal vision, in which these clerics find a kind of violation of the Sharia and the heresy and a departure from religion," which "perpetuated the stereotype in a more negative way, striking a curtain that prevents seeing any diversity within a society that has not been one throughout its history." Saudi Vision 2030 views it as a factor of strength and wealth, and wants to turn this pluralism into an attractive element, as Saudi Arabia is a major Arab Islamic state, open to different religions, sects and cultures, and thus carries a project that rejects sectarian discourses and ideas of extremism and terrorism.
Religious diversity!
The map of the various Islamic sects in Saudi Arabia, dealt with in detail in the study referred to above, which can be summarized as follows:
The central region, where the capital Riyadh, and major cities such as Buraydah, Anaizah, Qassim, Zulfi and others, is dominated by the Hanbali school, belonging to Imam Ahmed bin Hanbal school, specifically in its version developed by Sheikh Islam Taqi al-Din Ahmed bin Taymiyah, and subsequently Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Wahab.
The area contains a scientific barren weight.
Where many influential scientific figures, such as Sheikh Mohammed bin Ibrahim Al Sheikh, Sheikh Abdul Aziz bin Baz, Sheikh Mohammed bin Saleh bin Othaimeen and others.
Shaykh Abdul Aziz Bin Baz
Historically, the central region has also been home to many “Shia ” families, some of whose homes have so far remained in Riyadh, others have converted to Sunni Islam, while a number of them have intertwined their sectarian identity with practices of doctrines and rituals from both Sunni and Shia cultures.
The western region, which is historically known as "Hijaz", includes the two Holy Mosques in Mecca and Medina, in addition to cities such as Jeddah and Yanbu.
The population follows several doctrines, but the most prominent of which are the Maliki and Shafi ’ i doctrines, in addition to many Sufi methods, which had their seasons and angles spread in the beginning of the last century, before these takaya were removed, and are limited to limited celebrations and births.
Twelver Shi'ism is also present in Hejaz, specifically in Medina, as in Jeddah, albeit in a limited way.
Among the most prominent Maliki scholars in the Hijaz, Sheikhan Alawi Abbas al-Maliki and Muhammad Alawi al-Maliki.
As for Shafi ’ i, one of the most famous houses: Zawawi, Babsil, Yamani, and Messrs. Maraghna.
Among them were Shaikhs Muhammad Said Yamani, Muhammad Hassan Yamani, and Sheikh Yasin Faden, the latter famous for being a modernizer, rather than a jurist.
Contemporary Shafi ’ i figures include the late Saudi Oil Minister Ahmed Zaki Yamani, Dr. Omar Kamel, and Sheikh Abdullah Farraj al-Sharif.
Mr. Alawi Al Malki
Sheikh Mohammed Ali al-Omari is considered the most prominent Shiite name in Medina, before he passed away in 2011.
Al-Ahnaf, in turn, had a historical presence in the Hijaz, specifically in Mecca.
Sheikh Abdullah bin Abdul Rahman Siraj, as one of the scientific names of the Hanafi school, where he was the mufti of Al-Ahnaf and judge of the judges of Mecca, and reference in jurisprudence, before he died in 1848.
Eastern Region, which includes Al-Ahsa, Qatif, Dammam, Dhahran, Khobar, and others.
Twelver Shiism is present as a dominant doctrine in the cities of Qatif, Awamiya, Sihat, Safwa and the rest of the villages of Qatif province, in addition to a large part of the province of Al-Ahsa, without losing sight of the presence of Sunni Saudi citizens in the province of Qatif, specifically in: Anak, Al-Zour, Darin, Al-Nabiya.
Al-Ahsa can be considered an example of sectarian diversity and peaceful coexistence among the various Saudi components, as it includes Shia and Sunni citizens.
Shaikh Abdul Hameed Al-Katebi
Many of the Shiite scientific names in the eastern region had their presence idiosyncratic and popular influential followers, such as: Sheikh Ali Abu Abdul Karim al-Khunaizi, Sheikh Abdul Hamid al-Kotaibi, Sheikh Abdul Hadi al-Fadhli, Mr. Majid al-Awami, Sheikh Mohammed al-Hijri, Sheikh Hussein al-Omran, Mr. Ali al-Salman and others.
For its part, the family of "Al-Mubarak" in Al-Ahsa included many symbols of Maliki scholars, including Sheikhs: Abdul Hamid Al-Mubarak, and Qais Al-Mubarak.
Sheikh Qais Al Sheikh Mubarak
Shafi ’ i had their presence in Ahsa among a number of famous houses, where most of them are located in the cities of Hofuf and Mubarraz.
Sheikh Ahmed bin Abdullah al-Dugan, who died in October 2013, is one of the most prominent Shafi ’ i religious leaders.
The family "Mulla" of the Ahsa houses, which historically belong many members of the Hanafi school, and their personalities Sheikh Abu Bakr bin Omar Mulla, and his son Abdullah.
The southern region, which includes Najran, Jizan, Asir, and other cities and villages scattered.
In this region, the doctrine is mixed with the tribe, where the latter is present as a major and active component, exceeding in importance the doctrine and advancing it.
The chief of the tribe still has his voice heard and respected.
Najran is inhabited by the Yam tribe, many of whose members follow the Ismaili Shia sect and are known as the Makarma.
Sheikh Abdullah bin Mohammed al-Makrami, who died in April 2015, is one of the most prominent tribal and sectarian leaders of Ismailism in the kingdom.
Sheikh Ahmad Al - Jamali Al - Mukarami took over the management of the affairs of the community.
The Zaidi Shiites who make up Yemen, and specifically the capital Sanaa, a center of human and scientific gravity for them, have a small and limited presence in the south of the Kingdom.
However, most Zaidis have either moved to Yemen, or have melted into the general Sunni Muslim fabric.
It is historically difficult for its inhabitants to adopt the Shafi'i doctrine.
However, the lack of scientific figures confronting the fatwa in the region, and the preoccupation of its inhabitants with work, agriculture and the field, and the nature of simple and innate religiosity, led to the transformation of many Shafi'i to Hanbali, especially after the entry of "scientific institutes" and the delegations of clerics for the call.
The Saudi Wealth!
The previous geo-sectarian distribution shows the overlap between multiple cultures and sects, and that the imagined borders in the minds, and the sectarian and political divisions, are the result of the perpetuation of a radical discourse, using religion to achieve specific political and partisan goals, and also because of a stereotypical reading of religion by some currents, who wanted to generalize a unilateral image that they see as the absolute right, an approach that contradicts human nature. For centuries.
Hence, the "Vision 2030" came to restore and preserve diversity under the roof of the state and protect it with the force of law.
The doctrines have converged over the past hundreds of years, although this juxtaposition has some tension, which is normal for any society, and occurs within the sectarian component one, but the origin is the good relationship and coexistence between people, commercial dealing, and solidarity in the event of crises and adversities to overcome.
This great positive legacy, the “hardliners ” do not want it to be told or seen, because they want to promote their narrative of exclusion, which is“ misleading ” and has no place in Saudi Arabia today.
Today, the Saudis mix their sects, tribes, families and cultures in different regions, cities and villages, where they work to overcome the culture of the ghetto, which has been enshrined in extremist sectarian discourses for more than forty years!
Today, Saudi Arabia ’ s major cities are a mix of Saudi sectarian, cultural and tribal mixtures. In many neighborhoods of these cities, they are adjacent to the homes of Saudi Shia and Sunni, tribal and urban Saudis, who are rebuilding their modern Saudi identity, an identity that believes that pluralism is an important symbolic and cultural capital, and one of the national riches that must be preserved and protected from calls for hatred, intolerance and violence.
Safeguard diversity!
This sectarian pluralism is legally protected in accordance with the provisions of Title III of the Basic Law of Governance, which came under the title "The components of Saudi society," where Article 12 stipulates that "the strengthening of national unity is a duty, and the state prevents everything that leads to division, sedition and division."
King Salman bin Abdulaziz
King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud, who assumed the reins of power in January 2015, stressed in more than one speech the importance of consolidating the concept of equality between citizens, saying: "Every citizen in our country and every part of our dear country is the subject of my attention and care, there is no difference between one citizen and another, nor between one region and another." The people of the homeland are equal in rights and duties. ”

(Geneva) – The International Air Transport Association (IATA) has revealed a slowdown in the recovery of the air travel industry in domestic and global markets in January 2022 compared to December 2021, as a result of travel restrictions imposed after the emergence of the mutant Omicron in November.
Note: In this report, we return to making comparisons on an annual basis rather than comparing results with those recorded in 2019, unless otherwise indicated.
Given the low levels of movement in 2021, some markets may show very high annual growth rates, although the size of these markets is still much smaller than in 2019.
· Total air travel demand in January 2022 increased by 82.3% (measured in passenger revenue per kilometre) compared to January 2021; however, it decreased by 4.9% compared to the previous month (December 2021) on a seasonally adjusted basis.
Domestic flights in January increased by 41.5% compared to the same period last year, but decreased by 7.2% compared to December 2021 on a seasonally adjusted basis.
Passenger revenue per kilometer for international flights increased by 165.6% compared to January 2021, but decreased by 2.2% month-on-month between December 2021 and January 2022 on a seasonally adjusted basis.
Willie Walsh, Director General of the International Air Transport Association (IATA), said: “The air transport industry continued to recover in January despite the emergence of the Omicron mutant.
Although stricter border controls have not been able to stop the spread of this mutant, public health systems have not been overstretched in areas where the population ’ s immunity has been strong.
“Many governments have also begun to adjust COVID-19 measures to bring them in line with those imposed on other endemic viruses, including the removal of travel restrictions that have had a negative impact on life, the economy and freedom of movement. ”
Global Passenger Markets
In January, European airlines increased international traffic by 225.1% compared to the same month a year earlier, slightly up from 223.3% in December 2021 compared to the same month in 2020.
Capacity increased by 129.9% and load factor increased by 19.4 percentage points to 66.4%.
Airlines in the Asia-Pacific region recorded a 124.4 per cent increase in global traffic in January compared to the same month in 2021, a slight decline from the 138.5 per cent improvement recorded in December 2021 compared to December 2020.
Capacity also increased by 54.4%, and load factor increased by 14.7 percentage points to follow the lowest levels among different regions at 47.0%.
In January, Middle East airlines recorded 145.0% higher demand compared to the same period in 2021, a significant decline compared to the 178.2% improvement recorded in December 2021 versus the same month in 2020.
Capacity in January increased by 71.7% compared to the same period a year earlier, and the load factor increased by 17.5 percentage points to 58.6%.
In January, North American airlines saw a 148.8% improvement in traffic compared to the same period in 2021, down significantly from the 185.4% increase in December compared to the same month in 2020.
Capacity increased by 78.0% and load factor increased by 17.0 percentage points to 59.9%.
Latin American airlines recorded a 157.0% increase in traffic in January compared to the same period in 2021, an improvement on the 150.8% increase in December 2021 compared to the same month in 2020.
Capacity in January increased by 91.2%, and load factor increased by 19.4 percentage points to 75.7%, the highest among regions for the 16th consecutive month.
Air traffic in Africa increased by 17.9% year-on-year in January 2022, down from 26.3% year-on-year growth in December 2021.
Capacity increased by 6.3% and load factor increased by 6.0 percentage points to 60.5%.
Domestic Markets
Japan ’ s domestic demand rose to 107%, the fastest recorded annual growth rate, despite travel in January 2022 falling 4.1% from December on a seasonally adjusted basis.
Passenger revenue per kilometer in India ’ s domestic market in January fell 18 percent year-on-year, marking the largest decline recorded among all IATA domestic markets.
On a monthly basis, these revenues declined on a seasonally adjusted basis by approximately 45% between December and January.
2019 vs 2022
Despite significant growth in travel in January 2022 compared to the previous year, passenger demand is still a far cry from pre-COVID-19, with total passenger revenue per kilometre in January down 49.6% compared to January 2019.
International traffic decreased by 62.4% and domestic by 26.5%.

Praise the slow pace of life.
Explore the fun of the world calmly
The idea of slow living negates the belief that a successful person should be busy or fast, and encourages the person to be present consciously at every moment.
Once the society is saturated with the new, it returns to the past, and this is what happens in art, decoration, fashion, and social trends.
From here, too, the slow pace of life can be seen as a return to the old calm in some way, after the rhythm of life has become too fast to keep up with.
The idea of a slow life can be a convenient orientation for those who are looking for a calm state of mind, trying to take a long-term view of life and the world away from constant stress, anxiety and gasping.
Slow living helps us live more consciously and clearly with what we value and need in life, where we do everything at the right speed, rather than constantly striving for speed.
The idea of slow living negates the belief that a successful person must be busy or fast, and encourages the person to be present consciously at every moment.
Life is better, not faster.
The idea of slow living is part of the broader slow movement that began in the 1980s in Italy.
After opening McDonald ’ s restaurants in the heart of Rome, Carlo Petrini and a group of activists formed a movement defending regional food traditions called Slow Food.
Over time, the movement has gained supporters in more than 150 countries, trying to encourage the enjoyment of good food and conscious consumption that encourages respect for seasonality, and to minimize the negative impact on the environment of food production.
Carlo Petrini ’ s idea began to take shape when he noticed the disconnect between farmer and consumer, due to the huge boutiques and fast food restaurants that fed central Rome and dramatically eroded local food traditions.
Carl Honoré, one of the most famous theorists of the idea of slow living, helped bring the idea to areas other than food when he published a book in Praise of Slow in 2004.
Awareness is growing about slow travel, slow thinking and slow action, all of which are examples of the different branches of the slow living movement.
Not all slowness is negative.
As more people were forced to slow down their lifestyle, interest in slow living increased during the epidemic period.
The search for the term slow life has increased by 4 times in Google and YouTube.
Although some of these images and videos depict a romantic rural life far from reality, for most people, the increase in research related to this content shows the desire to return to nature and seek hobbies closer to it, especially as a large number of people turned to remote work, which gave the opportunity to connect more with the self and search for what is truly pleasing, which is forgotten in the midst of a fast and breathless life.
The slow life movement gets rid of the negative connotations of the word "slow", which some may associate with laziness and non-productivity.
Carl Honoré explains the difference between good slowness and negative slowness, as good slowness is the deliberate slowness to do things at the right speed to achieve the best result.
On the other side, there is also good speed and bad speed.
Speed can be exciting and exhilarating in the right circumstances while the rush to finish things from just above the surface without going deep is just the opposite, because it causes distraction and is difficult to prioritize.
Essential elements of slow living
Slow living doesn ’ t mean we give up technology and fall back into old times, but it does help us give up distracting activities, make us reclaim our own time to become more present and aware of every moment in life, and help build stronger relationships and spend quality time with friends and children.
It also helps us build our own values, design the lifestyle that suits us, and dedicate time to what we ’ re really looking for, not what the fast-paced lifestyle of the planet forces us to do.
A slow life entails taking a break and redefining our relationship with things like a phone, tablet, or other gadgets like them, and then making room for screen-free time.
Honoré says, “The cornerstone of slow living is to form balanced and more humane relationships with modern technologies.
“We have to somehow learn when to go ahead with technology and when to slow down and stop moving between social media, the Netflix screen or even aimlessly surfing the internet. ”
Honoré also emphasizes the need to let go of the fear of rejection or being lost, and instead of trying to do everything, we should choose only what matters to us and touches us, without the worry of saying the word “no ”.
We must say no to everything that does not concern us and not increase the burden we place on ourselves.
We have to prioritize carefully and let everything else go, having grown tired of the speed with which we feel we are racing rather than actually living our lives.
We always wait for a moment other than the moment we live, which makes us feel that our lives are vanishing in vain.
Slow life solidifies deep pleasures and strong emotions, away from entertainment and shallow pleasures that fade away shortly and leave us burdened with feelings of frustration and loneliness.

World Government Summit aims to promote women ’ s empowerment in non-traditional fields
Dafni Arslan: Green technology is suitable for women 's skills
T + T - normal size
Efforts to enhance women ’ s participation in the energy sector continue to be challenged by the fact that, for long periods, the majority of workers in this sector have been men, with a low female presence, which is now gradually changing.
Many of the sessions held during the World Government Summit in Dubai focus on the empowerment of women in this sector, specifically in the field of green technology.
Daphne Arslan, senior director at the Atlantic Council, said: “I remember the first time I walked into an energy conference room.
I felt strange in the crowd dominated by men.
"I have to admit that the energy industry has long been monopolized by men, but it's starting to change, especially in green technology."
Enormous Opportunities
Studies by United Nations organizations indicate that women with applied scientific interest can now find tremendous opportunities for professional growth in the energy field.
By being rooted in their society, women can also play a vital role in building trust in the use of green technology.
Challenges
Arslan, who has worked for the US government for many years in the field of financial consulting, adds: “The situation is different in the financial field; women have long been there, but there are still great opportunities in the field of energy. ”
Women face some obstacles to accessing the education, training, financial services and loans they need to establish and sustain their own business.
They have little access to information on energy alternatives as well as commercial, administrative and technical aspects of renewable energy and energy efficiency technologies and alternatives.
Provision of information
In February 2020, the International Women ’ s Forum in Dubai discussed ways to overcome these challenges and stressed that achieving gender balance in the fields of conventional and renewable energy is a priority to promote the growth and sustainability of the sector.
Providing women with adequate information, supporting their academic achievement in technical and engineering fields and providing them with appropriate opportunities will ensure their active participation in this sector and thus enhance their contribution to building a better future for future generations.
Valerie Levkov, Executive Vice President, Middle East and North Africa, EDF, said: “It is important to stress here that more women and young people are involved in this sector at all levels of leadership and middle management. I have great confidence in the efforts to achieve gender balance in the energy sector, and I call on women to be ambitious in leadership positions. ”
