Analysis: Dust storms and their danger to Iraqis and their economy
Iraq is witnessing escalating waves of dust and dust storms that threaten to destroy the components of housing and living in different areas.
What are the reasons for exacerbating the problem, and why the efforts of stakeholders to address it do not appear to be at the level of responsibility?
Not only in Najaf, but in different parts of Iraq, life was interrupted by the severity of dust storms and the dust they carried with them.
Not so long ago, one could not have imagined that something like paralysis would occur more than once in an entire country due to dust and dust storms.
This is what happened in Iraq recently because of the severity of these storms and their unprecedented frequency.
Nine storms occurred in May and April, doubling the number of storms over the same period of years.
The consequences have not only been the closure of government and private institutions and the suspension of staff, but have also led to the closure of schools, the closure of airports and the curtailment of land and sea traffic.
The softness of storm-borne dust easily seeps into critical machinery and infrastructure, causing damage or destruction.
Annual economic losses from dust and sand storms in the Middle East are estimated at $13 billion, according to the World Bank.
Iraq is at the forefront of the worst affected countries due to the intensity and frequency of storms.
In addition to the losses, the storms are causing a lack of vision, difficulty breathing and thousands of people have been hospitalized not only in Iraq, but also in neighboring countries such as Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Syria and Bahrain.
In the short term, there is a lot of damage, not least of which is the migration of people from storm areas because of the difficulty of living in them.
Thousands of people have suffered shortness of breath from the dust storms that hit Iraq recently, and hundreds of them have been hospitalized.
Why did the problem get worse?
Experts attribute the occurrence of frequent dust storms at an increasing pace in the Middle East, especially in Iraq, to climatic changes accompanied by high temperatures, lack of rain and desertification affecting agricultural and pastoral lands.
The decline of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers in Iraq is compounded by Turkey ’ s construction of more dams that block the sources of the two rivers from Mesopotamia, which has depended on them for 90 percent for thousands of years.
Iran also diverted the sources of many of the tributaries that fed the Tigris River and irrigated many areas in the Iraqi areas adjacent to its borders.
In addition to external factors, there are internal factors that contributed to the worsening of the water situation, most notably the armed conflicts that led to the neglect of the maintenance and modernization of dams and irrigation canals, especially in the north and northwest areas where the two rivers cross.
Water consumption systems currently in place, whether in agriculture or for other purposes, waste a lot of water because of flooded irrigation methods, leakage of water from the networks and financial corruption, which disrupt and postpone the implementation of many urgent projects, including those involving scarce drinking water in the regions and cities of southern Iraq over the next few years.
Lack of water and rain have reduced the area of agricultural land and lost vegetation.
According to the Iraqi Ministry of Agriculture, the area affected by desertification during the past 10 years amounted to about 27 million dunums of arable and grazing land and about 2 million dunums of vegetation cover.
As the pace of climate change increases and the level of the two rivers decreases, the pace of decline is expected to accelerate.
One of the consequences of this desertification is the fragility and fragmentation of the soil, making it vulnerable to winds and storms that carry it to residential and industrial areas and disrupt life therein.
The major disaster will occur if the storms hit the oil extraction industry and its tankers through the Gulf waters, because the economies of Iraq and neighboring Gulf countries depend on black gold rates ranging from 40 to more than 90 percent.
Even dams have dried up in Iraq due to lack of rain water and the decline of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers
Counting losses instead of speeding up solutions!
Many Iraqi parties, such as the Ministry of Environment, are sounding the alarm of the escalation of sand and dust storms, which have become more powerful and intense before.
The problem is not only that, but also that the number of days with dust has risen to more than 270 days a year.
In light of this, calls are mounting for intensifying efforts that will reduce the decline of water sources and preserve them in parallel with the expansion of vegetation areas and the planting of dense trees that form windbreaks and sand around cities, communities and desert oases.
There are also increasing demands to dispense with traditional irrigation methods in favour of modern drip and sprinkler irrigation, to stop wastage of water, and to modernize and maintain artificial dams and lakes.
However, despite these demands and the gravity of the situation, the steps taken by the official bodies concerned are modest and do not rise to the level of addressing the problem, except for those related to counting the storms and the losses caused by them.
In the Iraqi Ministry of Agriculture, for example, several projects to combat desertification and stabilize sand dunes are advertised from time to time.
These projects include the rehabilitation of artificial forests and the establishment of dozens of nurseries to grow millions of shrubs and seedlings annually.
However, according to the Ministry's own sources, the implementation process is slow and unsustainable for many reasons.
Oddly enough, one is the lack of financial allocations in a country whose current monthly income from oil sales is now $10 billion a month.
Ibrahim Mohammed: Iraq needs regional cooperation to face dust storms that do not know borders
Regional cooperation needed to avoid the worst
The frequency and increasing severity of sand and dust storms complicates Iraq's basic problems, foremost among which is the deterioration of infrastructure, including water, and the provision of basic needs.
Every day that steps to address them are postponed, the danger to the lives, health and livelihoods of the population increases.
This confrontation is more important than ever in the light of the current global food crisis, which is exacerbated by the war in Ukraine and before by the consequences of the Coronavirus pandemic.
Its importance also comes from the fact that increasing its intensity threatens the areas of oil extraction and vital transport routes through the waters of the Gulf, Bab al-Mandab and the Suez Canal.
The closure of the canal in March 2021 due to the deviation of a ship as a result of a sandstorm is a lesson to be learned, especially as the damage to the economies of Arab countries and the global economy amounted to tens of billions in less than a week.
Because sandstorms know no borders, regional cooperation to reduce them between Iraq, the Gulf states and Egypt seems more vital to their economies than ever before.

The Middle Eastern threat no one talks about.
Category: Reports and Analysis
Date: 2022-05-30T20: 29: 58 + 0000
The Israeli newspaper "Haaretz" warned of the world's disregard for the phenomenon of sand storms in the Middle East, especially in Iraq, which causes economic losses of billions of dollars, and health damage to thousands of citizens, pointing out that this phenomenon is likely to increase significantly in the coming years.
After the newspaper pointed out in a report translated by the agency Shafaq News; that the sand storms in the Middle East are ignored by the world compared to other types of natural disasters, and thus ignore the increasing impact on the health of people and the economy of the region.
The report compared the scenes of the storm in Iraq with the scenes known as in the United States, saying that you are in the midst of a winter storm in an American city, where cars are slowly moving through the streets, and their headlights light light in the middle of the day, as if crossing a layer of snow, but adds that the place is already in Baghdad amid temperatures exceeding 30 degrees Celsius, and that the streets were not covered by white snow, but orange color of sand and dust. A Air, noting that there were similar scenes recorded in Iran, eastern Syria and most of the Gulf countries.
The report noted that sandstorms usually hit Iraq during the spring months.
But he added that the storm is the tenth since the beginning of April, an average of one a week, adding that it is a phenomenon that is growing in size and severity in recent years and is expected to worsen in the coming years.
In Iraq, nearly 1,000 people have been hospitalized for respiratory problems, the government has declared a holiday to urge people to stay home, and many airports have been closed.
The report also warned that the economic and health consequences of sandstorms have not been studied in the same way as specific studies of the effects of other natural disasters.
Oxford University academic Nick Middleton, who co-authored one of the first research studies on the issue, said the costs were too high: "Dust storms can affect tens of millions of people and have an economic impact of hundreds of millions of dollars."
Middleton said the link between health problems and sandstorms was not always clear, but it could be "enormous", adding: "There are strong links between dusty days, respiratory problems and some heart disease."
But one of the few estimates available on the economic costs of dust storms, from the World Bank, reported in 2019, is that the global cost of dust and sand storms increased by 63% between 1990 and 2013 to reach $3.6 trillion.
In the Middle East and North Africa, it increased by 123% to $141 billion.
This estimate reflects losses to the economy as a result of premature deaths due to excessive exposure to dust.
Since 2013, it has suffered an estimated 10,400 premature deaths from dust, costing the economy $15 billion, or 2.9% of GDP.
Among the direct costs are losses due to closed airports, crop losses and production disruptions, as well as government holidays, estimated by the World Bank at about $13 billion, which means that the total cost of losses in the Middle East and North Africa region from sandstorms exceeds $150 billion annually.
Orange Warning
The Iraqi Ministry of Environment monitored 122 dust storms and 283 dusty days during 2013 alone, but an official at the Ministry of Environment warned last month that Iraq may suffer 272 days of sand storms as an annual average over the next two decades, which could increase to more than 300 days by 2050.
In his paper, titled “The Comprehensive Causes and Socio-Economic Consequences of a Sharp Dust Storm in the Middle East, ” Middleton documented the fallout from a particularly large sandstorm in early April 2015 that hit an area of 10 million square kilometers, including Iraq, Iran and the Gulf, stretching east as far as India and the Red Sea to the west.
The storm forced officials to close schools in Qatar and parts of Saudi Arabia that had been declared a holiday for workers, Saudi and Iranian ports disrupted operations, and forced airports in seven countries to delay, reroute or cancel flights.
Open space construction has also stopped in the UAE, and Abu Dhabi cancelled the Desert Challenge because visibility was almost zero, and even solar plants stopped working due to the accumulation of too much dust on the panels.
According to the study, traffic accidents have increased in Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE, and cases of respiratory patients in hospitals have increased.
Israel is not immune to dust storms, though it does not suffer from any of the same severe pattern as Iraq and other neighboring countries.
The report pointed out that the phenomenon of climate change is responsible for the increase of these extreme weather events, but experts say that climate change is only one of the factors, but it will have a greater impact in the coming years because it causes increased desertification and more severe drought, pointing out that the sources of dust and sand storms are mainly due to natural and not man-made factors, but these factors are exacerbated by human activity.
Poor land management makes the soil unprotected after the harvest season, and wars have caused farmers to abandon their fields, creating large tracts of land where the wind can easily carry dust.
Population growth and urban sprawl are also reducing areas that previously contained plants that protected the soil.
In addition, large bodies of water have been affected by drought, such as the Aral Sea between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, and Lake Urmia in Iran, once the largest lake in the Middle East.
Dam construction projects have also drained rivers and reduced water flows to the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, with Saddam Hussein even playing a role in draining the marshes in the south.
Some scientists also believe that La Niña weather phenomenon may have contributed to the recent spike in dust storms in the Middle East.
Panfsha Kenoush, a researcher at the Middle East Institute in Washington, questioned whether Middle East governments were willing to make a major effort to address the problem, explaining that "sand and dust storms are often seen in the Gulf region as largely uncontrollable natural phenomena."
Some measures have been taken by governments in the region, with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman pledging to plant 10 billion trees in Saudi Arabia and an additional 40 billion in the region to combat sandstorms and desertification.
In 2016, an institute in the UAE launched a dust storm forecasting system that countries in the region can use to prepare for major storms.
But Middleton admits that even if governments work together, fighting sandstorms will not be easy, but he added that they could at least mitigate their effects and address the local factors that make sandstorms worse.

A submarine is tracking CO2 in the ocean.

In the cold, choppy waters of Easter Bay in Alaska, all eyes were staring at the gray waters, looking for just one thing.
It wasn ’ t a fountain flowing from humpback whales active in this magnificent fjord, or a beaver lazily relaxing on the water ’ s surface.
Instead, everyone on board the Nanoc, the research ship of the University of Alaska Fairbanks, was looking at where the tiny 1.52 meter submarine used under the sea (Sea Glider) for research appeared.
The submarine, believed to be the first to be equipped with a large sensor to measure carbon dioxide levels within the ocean, had just completed its first night mission.
Designed to dive up to 1,000 meters, roaming parts of the ocean far away, the autonomous vehicle was placed in the Gulf of Alaska this spring to provide a deeper understanding of the chemistry of the sea in the era of climate change.
The research may be a major step toward monitoring ocean greenhouse gases, because until now, carbon dioxide concentrations to determine ocean acidity have been measured mostly by ships, buoys and moorings tied to the ocean floor.
“Ocean acidification is a process by which humans release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere because of burning fossil fuels and changing land uses, ” says Andrew McDonnell, an oceanographer at the University of Alaska Fairbanks ’ School of Oceanography.
The oceans provide a valuable service by containing some of the carbon dioxide.
Otherwise, there would be too much of it in the atmosphere, absorbing the sun ’ s heat and raising the planet ’ s warmth.
“But the problem now is that the ocean is changing its chemistry because of this absorption, ” says Claudine Hawrie, an oceanographer at the University ’ s International Center for Arctic Research.
The vast amount of data collected to study ocean acidification that can harm and kill specific species of marine life is currently under review.
For several weeks this spring, the couple, Claudine and Andrew, worked with engineers from Kepers Subsea Services, which equipped the research submarine, and with a German company, 4H-Jena, which supplied the sensor attached to the submarine.
On most days, researchers have gone too far into Easter Bay from the coast of Seward to conduct tests.
After the first mission, the research submarine was towed to the ship.
The sensor is then pulled out of the submarine and quickly sent to the ship ’ s cabin to upload its data, and the sensor analyzes carbon dioxide, records the data and stores it within a temperature-controlled system.
Many sensor components use battery power to perform their work.
As far as industrial standards are concerned, this sensor is the same as any other vessel or laboratory measuring CO2.
Claudine says the use of this new technology was “a huge step towards accommodating such an avid enthusiast, and that ’ s what characterizes the current project. ”

A high-fat, low-carb diet that has become popular in recent years may extend life, according to a new study.

The cells were also able to move to other animals that were not fasting or followed the keto system.

People of the Internet...
We want a language that everyone understands.
When I was a kid, I never told my dad that, “When I grow up, I want to be an app developer using Ruby on Rails with a multi-tasking scope for work. ”
Nor did I dream of becoming an engineer using Python for programming, a user experience designer, a software engineer running computer servers, or a front-end designer for websites.
There's a reason behind all this.
The functionality in this software did not exist at the time.
And there was no such thing as the Internet, as we see it now, not even the incredible array of functions that emerged from it.
This is unfortunate, given the benefits of such a business.
On American online recruitment sites last week, salaries of up to $175,000 were offered to those who know that Python and Ruby are computer programming languages, and that UX is an acronym for user experience, just as it is for website experience.
These generous fees were also offered to those who became an expert in front-end programming for websites — what you see while shopping online — and programming the code that the servers run on is in the backend of the website that makes it work as it should.
There are other benefits.
One person can build a sustainable self-project once they have mastered the required software skills.
He can also oversee the project using his laptop from a convenient remote location on a beach, along with other digital nomads.
While this is all fun, there ’ s something to worry about about how quickly the online revolution has created a new generation of workers doing jobs that establish many aspects of modern life — but are baffling for non-professionals in the field.
For starters, what does a parent do when their teenage son comes home and asks if it ’ s worth learning Python?
It would be easy if parents themselves had done such jobs, but given the early age of many tech workers, that ’ s unlikely.
A global survey last year of more than 30,000 software developers found that 59 percent of them were not yet 30.
No wonder studies in England this year have shown that parents of children aged 11 to 18 feel powerless to give them career advice.
About two-thirds of those surveyed had a child who showed an interest in a career they knew nothing about, according to the Talking Futures (Talking about the Future), a job campaign that commissioned the study.
But the tech industry ’ s poor use of terminology is not helpful.
Separate research conducted by Babeltech in the UK last week showed that this prevents job seekers from applying for jobs that are difficult for employers to explain.
There ’ s also a bigger problem with digitally excluded people, who get confused when they suddenly have to use an app in order to find a parking spot for their cars, or when using a website to check their bank balance.
When my colleague, Andrew Hill, wrote in February about his attempts to help his elderly relatives handle online password requests and download documents from the websites of banks, insurance companies and pension providers, he was bombarded with sympathetic messages from colleagues with the same problem.
The same thing happened last month when another journalist, Pete Pavides, wrote about his late father being fined for a ticket for not being able to pay the parking fee electronically.
The story prompted activist Esther Rantzen to tell the BBC: “Too often, these decisions are made by people in their 40s who never understand that an older person feels differently about the decisions they make. ”
Even younger, tech-savvy people can get confused, too.
A 35-year-old American named Byron Clark told me last week: “I was frustrated when I used some apps on my mobile phone. ”
Clark was a recruiter for tech careers in New York City, but now runs his own website, Carrier Sidecake, to mentor job seekers.
Clark doesn ’ t necessarily believe that young software developers are responsible for designing apps that irritate older users.
Their bosses should, he says, make sure that online navigation is easy for everyone in everything related to life matters.
Having taught himself everything he needs in order to set up his website, Clark has some words of encouragement for those who fear that the digital revolution will leave many people behind.
He said, “I ’ m just optimistic about this.
There are opportunities that are increasing every year for everyone who pays attention to them. ”
I ’ m sure he ’ s right, but if everyone who takes advantage of these opportunities pays more attention to the needs of all users, and if they use language that everyone can understand, the stubborn online world will be much better than it is today.

King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) is conducting a collaborative study with engineers and scientists from the Japan Geo-Marine Science and Technology Agency (JAMSTEC), a leading Japanese deep sea science research institute.
The study aims to conduct a range of exploratory research in the Red Sea, specifically in shallow and deep water corals using sophisticated and specialized Japanese equipment, as well as KAUST ’ s research vessel Thule.
The first pilot projects between KAUST and JAMSTEC were launched with support and funding from Japan ’ s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) and KAUST ’ s Vice President for Research.
Such research projects foster cultural and international relations and scientific initiatives between Saudi Arabia and Japan, which make it easier for researchers from around the world to explore previously unexplored places in the Red Sea region.
Distinguished Professor Donal Bradley, KAUST ’ s Vice President for Research, spoke on the occasion of this collaboration and how it provides a multidisciplinary and multi-divisional platform for the exchange of international resources and expertise: “Jamstec has extensive experience in deep water research and infrastructure development, with a modern ship fleet and high-tech marine equipment that will be of great benefit to our research goals.
KAUST provides local logistical and technical support through our core laboratory for coastal and marine resources and, most importantly, our extensive knowledge of the Red Sea from geology to ecology. ”
Sean Tokzko, vice president of the Expedition Management Group at Jamstec ’ s Institute of Exploration and Geo-Marine Engineering (MarE3), said: “Japan ’ s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry is pushing for more technical and bilateral research cooperation with Saudi Arabia.
Our partnership with KAUST is a truly remarkable initiative that will enable us to have high quality results and interesting discoveries in the Red Sea. ”
Research Expeditions
KAUST and JAMSTEC scientists completed their first research trip in February 2022 in the Facial Reef Zone, a grouping of corals in the middle layer “middle light ” of the Red Sea (that is, the area 200 meters above sea floor level).
The coral reefs are located there above a thick creeping salt layer, which erodes, moves and partially sinks as salt infiltrates deep water.
The scientific team investigated one of the submerged coral reef populations from a sedimentary, biological and oceanographic perspective (oceanography).
The area was characterized by active volcanic vents, hot springs, mineral-rich salt basins, and a world of organisms that uniquely evolved to live here.
Temperatures in deep saltwater ponds in the Red Sea can exceed 70 ° C, the maximum that most industrial, scientific and medical electronic devices can withstand.
While KAUST team devices can corrode, melt, or float in such extreme conditions, Japanese team equipment is designed to withstand very high salinity, temperature, and pressure environments.
Moreover, they are accustomed to working at depths of 3,000 meters and more, conducting integrated geological and biological studies using specialized equipment such as remotely operated submarines and human-operated vehicles.
Jamstec engineers trained KAUST scientists on this equipment and how to make measurements of various parameters, collecting samples from sediments, water and plankton to analyze their biochemical and mineral composition and determine DNA sequence and absolute salinity.
The Jamstec cameras, which were lowered into the water by small remote-controlled submarines, also recorded high-resolution videos of a range of marine life and various natural phenomena.
It is noteworthy that the crew of the research vessel Thule and the KAUST Coastal and Marine Resources Laboratory performed outstanding performance in these cruises, reflecting their engineering expertise and great skill, especially in the integration and deployment of new devices and equipment from the ship.
Lloyd Smith, director of KAUST ’ s Coastal and Marine Resources Core Laboratory, said: “Our team has 13 years of experience in the Red Sea environment, a pressure and temperature lab to simulate and validate technical innovations, and extensive operational experience to help Jamstec build devices and equipment that can survive in extreme marine environments for long periods of time. ”
Data Analysis
With the first cruise completed, scientists from both teams are in the early stages of analyzing the collected data, which will be the building block for future research.
Hildegard Westphal, a visiting professor at KAUST who has expertise in carbon sedimentation, says the cruise was successful from a scientific point of view: “Facial reefs – which are in the process of drowning due to tectonic conditions – support the growth and prosperity of some marine organisms that have adapted to live in low-light and warm water conditions, such as some red algae and foraminifera.
We still don ’ t know much about the stages coral reefs go through when they sink, or the life that lives here.
"These sedimentary and biological data and video footage collected in this study provide unprecedented insight into marine life and the habitats of this unique region of the Red Sea."
Professor Thomas Finkbainer, Professor of Energy Resources and Petroleum Engineering at KAUST, who manages the components of the collaborative project between KAUST and Jamstec, explains that the layer deposited in the face area is interesting because of its close connection to the ground.
It has one of the largest valleys along the Red Sea.
When it rains, the valley can flood quickly, bringing huge streams of gravel, rocks and vegetation through its canals into the sea, and “studying the aquifers extracted from these deposits provides us with valuable information about the region ’ s ancient climates and more. ”
Professor Dougal Lindsey, senior scientist at the Institute for Advanced Science and Technology Research (X-star) at Jamestech, who leads studies of floating ecosystems, said: “The Red Sea has a combination of extremely high temperatures and salinity, which makes it a suitable environment for understanding the impact of climate change on plankton ecosystems.
"In this context, we plan to use plankton samples collected during the Thule cruise to study the scale of impact and resistance to climate change in marine plankton such as jellyfish, which, along with bacteria, are expected to be one of the most successful populations of organisms to resist ocean change."
Importance of Cruises
Adam and Spanali, drilling engineer in Jamstec ’ s expedition management team, confirm that Project Face is a first step for future strategic collaboration: “This initial journey is like an experiment for future journeys.
You have given us important information about salinity rate, temperature and pressure.
This information will undoubtedly help us determine what research equipment and methods should be used in the future.
We also learned a lot about how to work together, which in itself was a key objective of this project. ”
The KAUST and JAMSTEC teams see the importance of continuing deep-sea research to achieve a range of objectives, foremost among which is to study the tectonic features of the Red Sea and its surrounding crust.
In this context, the Jamstec team plans to work with KAUST as well as the Saudi Ministry of Investment to bring their marine research vessel Kaimi to the Red Sea on a six-month expedition to study the operations of the Red Sea seabed and its central basin.
A unique feature of the face reef is that it lies at a major fault zone that stretches across the Red Sea and meets land.
The fault is caused by the movement of tectonic plates that formed the Red Sea 30 million years ago when the Arabian Peninsula began to separate from Africa.
These tectonic plates are still in continuous motion and are expanding by 8-16 mm each year.
On this research trip, scientists will deploy a network of seismometers to the bottom of the Red Sea.
The longer these devices stay at sea, the more reliable the information collected about seismic activity in the area.
On the other hand, this will help to better understand the tectonic processes between the African and Arab plates and their impact on the occurrence of natural phenomena in coastal areas such as earthquakes, floods, tsunamis and landslides.
This data can also be used to assess the environment in coastal communities and prepare them for environmental disasters.
The collection of cores is a joint research area between KAUST and JAMSTEC.
Jamstec ’ s own BMS platform will be used here, a sophisticated robot that automatically drills to a depth of 60 meters, a depth that exceeds the range that KAUST equipment can currently handle.
“Bringing a Japanese vessel to the Red Sea with advanced deep-water research capabilities (from a depth of 7-8,000 meters) offers a great advantage for scientists and researchers to determine what is under the sea, ” he says.“ Analysis of previously collected aquifers will help us detect the conditions of the Red Sea plate and identify the early history of the Red Sea and its adjacent coasts.
It also highlights climate change in the region and its effects on biological evolution and the evolution of humans and other organisms, as well as the geological processes involved in the evolution of the sea itself.
Live encyclopedia of the Red Sea
The KAUST and Jamstec team are building an open-source encyclopedia or database of information collected, using artificial intelligence to identify fish, coral reefs, plankton and other organisms.
Professor Thomas Finkbainer explains that the aim is to create a living, interdisciplinary archive of Red Sea research that is scalable and accessible to students and researchers around the world, from a variety of disciplines and interests, such as biology, ecology, natural resources, environmental conservation, marine technology, oceanography, geology, geochemistry, geographical hazards, palaeoclimatic and palaeobiology.
“We hope to create an encyclopedia that marine scientists can contribute to and that the public and researchers can use to study the great mysteries of the Red Sea, such as the forces that shaped it, the origin of life and biodiversity, as well as newly discovered organisms, current geological features and patterns, water circulation, and the potential impacts of climate change on coral reefs and the world ’ s future oceans. ”
Professor Finkbainer also stressed that the Kaust-Gamstec initiative will help fill critical gaps in Red Sea data.
These data are important and central to mega projects in Saudi Arabia, especially in guiding government regulations and legislation related to the development and protection of the Red Sea.

Can you stand on one leg?
This ability may be related to longevity.
HEALTH
Publish
6 minutes read
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates (CNN) -- The inability to stand on one leg for 10 seconds later in life may be linked to double the risk of death from any cause over the next decade, a new study shows.
The research, published Tuesday in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, suggested that a simple balance test may be useful in routine physical tests for middle-aged and older people.
The research pointed out that while aging leads to a deterioration in fitness, muscle strength and flexibility, balance remains well maintained until the age of 50, when it begins to decline relatively quickly.
Previous research has linked the inability to stand on one leg to an increased risk of falls and cognitive decline.
The study involved 1,702 people, aged 51 to 75, living in Brazil, who were asked to stand on one leg without support during the initial screening.
Participants were given three attempts to test their balance on either foot.
The ability to balance on one leg is important for older adults for many reasons, and it also reflects broader fitness and health levels, said study author Dr. Claudio Gil Araujo at the CLINIMEX Exercise Medicine Clinic in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
Araujo explained that there is an urgent need to stand on one leg, for example, when getting out of the car, when going up or down the stairs, and so on.
Not having this ability or being afraid to do so may be associated with loss of independence, inability to exercise, and other things.
Poor balance and longevity
The average age of the study participants was 61 years, and a third of them were men.
About 1 in 5 people failed the balance test on one leg for 10 seconds at the initial screening.
The researchers followed the study participants after the initial examination for seven years, during which 123 of them died, or about 7%.
The mortality rate among participants who failed the test, 17.5%, was significantly higher than among participants who managed to pass the 10-second balance test, 4.5%.
The study found that for those unable to complete the balance test, there was an 84% higher risk of death from any cause, and this link remained even when other factors — including age, gender, body mass index, pre-existing conditions, or health risks such as coronary artery disease, high blood pressure, obesity, high cholesterol, and diabetes — were all taken into account.
However, the researchers were unable to include other variables in their analysis such as the recent history of falls, the pattern of physical activity, exercise, diet, smoking, and drug use that may interfere with balance.
The research was based on observation, and did not reveal cause and effect.
The study did not investigate any possible biological mechanisms that might explain the link between poor balance and longevity.
Dr Navid Starr, a professor of metabolic medicine at the University of Glasgow ’ s Institute of Cardiovascular and Medical Sciences, said the research was interesting, but not definitive.
Starr, who was not involved in the study, added that "because standing on one leg requires good balance, associated with brain function, good muscle strength and good blood flow, it is likely to integrate the muscle, blood vessel and brain systems, so it is a global test for the risk of future death."
Improved balance
Overall, participants who failed the test had poor health, and included a higher percentage of people with obesity and / or heart disease, high blood pressure, and unhealthy blood fats, according to the study.
The study was conducted between 2009 and 2020, and was part of a broader research project that began in 1994.
The inability to complete the balance test increased with age, more or less doubling during subsequent 5-year periods of the age range between 51 and 55 years and beyond.
More than half (54%) of the 71-75 year olds were unable to complete the test, compared to 5% in the lower age group who were unable to pass it.
There were no clear trends in mortality, or differences in cause of death, between those who were able to complete the test and those who were unable to do it.
Araujo explained that balance could be significantly improved through specific training, which he was working on with patients participating in a medically supervised exercise program.
However, he said he did not have data yet to assess whether improved balance affects longevity.
And if you want to test your ability to balance on one leg for 10 seconds, Araujo advised that it ’ s best to stand near a wall, table, or anyone else for support.

Saudi Arabia affirmed that it is determined to achieve the effective and real empowerment of women and enable them to play their role in building the nation with the full support and assistance of their fellow Saudi citizens without discrimination, disruption or neutralization.
This came in a speech delivered by the Chargé d'affaires of the Permanent Delegation of Saudi Arabia to the United Nations, Counsellor Mohammed bin Abdulaziz Al-Ateeq, during the annual session of the Executive Board of the United Nations Women and Gender Equality.
Al-Ateeq expressed Saudi Arabia ’ s appreciation for the report issued on the implementation of the Strategic Plan 2018-2021, which many governments have aligned in line with their orientations in order to achieve the goals of women ’ s empowerment and equality.
In the past few years, Saudi Arabia has witnessed extensive reforms in the field of human rights, and the field of women's rights has received the largest share of these developments and reforms, as many laws, regulations and legal bases have been promulgated and amended to ensure that women enjoy their rights on an equal basis with men, and a number of measures have been taken to promote women's rights and empowerment.
He pointed out that many legal frameworks have been amended and promulgated to achieve equality between women and men, most notably the Traffic Regulations, the Travel Documents Regulations, the Civil Status Regulations, the Labour Regulations and the Social Insurance Regulations.
As a result of these accelerated reforms in the file of Saudi women, the World Bank ’ s Women, Business and the Law report for the years 2020 and 2021 respectively ranked Saudi Arabia among the most countries in the world in implementing reforms related to laws and regulations related to women, and Saudi Arabia achieved a full score of “100 ” in five indicators: mobility, workplace, entrepreneurship, retirement and wages.
Al-Ateeq pointed out that Saudi Arabia has taken a number of special measures to accelerate equality in various fields through the launch of several initiatives aimed at accelerating the achievement of concrete and effective achievements in this regard.
He said: The initiative was launched by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development, the launch of the "National Platform for Saudi Women Leaders" in cooperation with Princess Nourah bint Abdulrahman University, where the number of registered women in the platform reached 9077, and the launch of "Qara" program to support the transport of working women. From a program of 13,950 beneficiaries to the third quarter of 2021.
He added that the measures taken include the "Support for Self-Employment" program, which expands the circle of opportunities to increase women's income according to their skills, the "Partial Work" and "Remote Work" programs, which enable women to achieve a balance between work and family, as well as empowering women in rural and remote areas to enter the labor market.
It is noteworthy that the economic participation rate of Saudi females has been increased by 94% from 2017 to 2020, and the launch of the Women Empowerment Program at the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology to increase their participation in the digital sector, and to enable access to leadership positions in the sector. By encouraging companies to commit and pledge to support women ’ s access to senior positions in their organizations and encouraging other companies to join, more than 30 companies in Saudi Arabia have joined the alliance.
Al-Ateeq explained that the Human Resources Development Fund (HDF) has launched a number of initiatives, including Tamheer Program, which reached 70,000 beneficiaries until 2019, Doroob, a national e-training platform where women accounted for 53.8% of the total trainees in the second quarter of 2021, and the Employment Support Program, where the Fund provides financial support for targeted employment. Beneficiary.
He stressed that work has been done to empower women to occupy senior positions, so that Saudi women have reached senior positions in government institutions, universities and others, where they occupy leadership and supervisory positions in a number of ministries and government institutions, and the percentage of women in senior and middle management positions increased from 28.6% in 2017 to 41.4% in the first quarter of 2021.
He reiterated that women are active partners in the political and public life in Saudi Arabia by participating in decision-making or elections and running for election. Saudi women have been included in their participation in the Shura Council, and the number of women working in the Council has reached 97. Women also participate in municipal elections and in running for and election to the Council of Chambers of Commerce.
At the international level, Saudi women have held senior international positions and participated in international and regional organizations, including the United Nations, where a Saudi woman was the Executive Director of UNFPA and the Assistant Secretary-General of the United Nations, and a Saudi woman was the Assistant Director-General of the World Health Organization, in addition to her participation in the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, the League of Arab States and the Cooperation Council for the Arab States of the Gulf.

"International Day of Women in Engineering".
Engineers refuse to limit their creativity on the pretext of social heritage
There are a number of obstacles behind the weak representation of women in the practice of engineering, especially the field side, the most important of which are customs and traditions in Arab societies.
DOHA – Some social legacies still prevent many women and girls from engaging in many field occupations, which has caused a decline in the participation of women in some fields of engineering, regardless of their qualifications and skills.
Although 54% of engineering graduates in the Arab world are women, their chances of fieldwork do not exceed 5%, while men occupy 95% of the job opportunities, due to several obstacles that prevent women engineers from obtaining field work and heading only to the field of office engineering.
During a ceremony organized by the Women Engineers Group in the Middle East and North Africa in Doha, Qatar, on the occasion of the International Day of Women in Engineering, participants highlighted the mechanisms that ensure that women engineers receive an appropriate share of fieldwork, as well as the importance of recognizing women ’ s achievements and promoting diversity, equity and inclusion.
Poor representation.
The President of the Qatari Women Engineers Society, Dr. Hanan Farhat, said that there are many obstacles that stand behind the weak representation of women in the practice of engineering, especially the field side, the most important of which is the customs and traditions in our Arab societies that reject the presence of women in sectors that are almost entirely subordinate to men.
In an interview with Al Jazeera Net, Farahat pointed out that these legacies have entrenched the idea that women cannot pursue such difficult or male-dominated professions, as well as that workplaces in the fields of engineering are designed for them only, which contributes to reducing job opportunities for women.
It reveals that many female engineers have had to turn to areas such as product manufacturing or marketing in order to overcome the obstacles they face.
The President of the Qatari Women Engineers Society believes that to overcome these obstacles, laws must be enacted and measures taken to improve working environments and make them attractive to women, which is lacking in many of our Arab societies despite the existence of laws in this regard.
She stresses that women can work anywhere as long as they have qualifications and maintain their customs and traditions, but at the same time society is required to change its outlook and highlight the female role models that have contributed to the achievements.
Promulgation of legislation
Farahat explained that in order for women engineers to have a fair proportion of jobs, it is necessary to pass legislation obliging companies and employers to hire a certain percentage of women, expressing her hope that the proportion of women engineers in our Arab societies will rise to 30% of the workforce in engineering by 2030.
Despite the obstacles faced by girls and women in the labor market, the demand to enroll in engineering colleges and similar in the Arab world is large, and the President of the Qatari Women Engineers Association justifies the large number of Arab women to study engineering, science and mathematics because these fields are fun and women see them as a challenge.
Digital technology has made it easier to enter and innovate in these areas, but the problem begins when access to the labor market and many companies refrain from hiring women because of women ’ s family obligations and caring for their children.
She concluded that engineers have the power to change the situation through more efforts, noting that for this reason, several groups such as the “Women Engineers in the Middle East and North Africa Group ” have been established to help women develop themselves and to provide and exchange information as the most powerful weapon to learn about their rights, in addition to continuous communication to adopt and qualify new cadres for the labor market.
Facing difficulties
For her part, Qatari engineer Sarah Ahmed, who works for one of the international oil companies, said that the practice of engineering contributed to the refinement and building of her personality, and enabled her to face difficulties through the experiences gained in the field of work.
She says to Al Jazeera Net that despite suffering a bit at the beginning of her work, she was able to overcome this quickly because of her desire to prove herself and achieve her goals without regard to any obstacles, but she was able to progress in her job.
She notes that she practices the profession of engineering as an adventure and views the obstacles she faces with challenge and happiness, saying that despite the suffering of working in the field, the participation of women brings about a change in the profession and creates an atmosphere of compassion and compassion.
Sarah hopes that employers will understand the different nature of women and their different way of thinking, which may bring more benefits and creativity to work, and expressed her gratitude to many companies that respected customs and traditions, respected the culture of society and created the right conditions for the work of women engineers without resorting to marginalizing them or confining them to office work.
Difficult areas
As for Qatari engineer Zulekha Abdullah, she stressed that since joining an international oil company, she is keen to learn everything to prove to everyone that Qatar is able to break into all difficult fields.
She told Al Jazeera Net that Qatari women engineers have succeeded in practicing difficult disciplines such as petroleum engineering, construction and infrastructure, and have been able to face the challenges boldly.
Zulekha praised the efforts of the Qatari government to enhance the presence of women engineers in various fields, overcome challenges and enable them to reach leadership positions.
She pointed out that the engineering profession has made her more distinguished in everything and added to her personality a lot, stressing that she is now more proud of the engineering profession and strongly encourages girls to attend engineering colleges and not to succumb to the wrong legacies that prevent them from joining them.
Women in Engineering Day was first launched in the UK on 23 June 2014 by the Women ’ s Engineering Society (WES) to celebrate its 95th anniversary.
Since then, the celebration has grown so dramatically over subsequent years that it received UNESCO sponsorship in 2016.
In 2017, Women in Engineering Day became global because of the interest and enthusiasm shown by the international public and its participants during previous years.

China ’ s Largest Airbus Order Since Coronavirus Outbreak
Three of China ’ s largest airlines have signed a landmark contract to buy 300 aircraft from Airbus, described as the country ’ s largest since the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Air China and China Southern Airlines have announced in separate disclosure documents filed with the exchange that they will each purchase 96 A320neo aircraft worth $12.2 billion at advertised prices.
China Eastern Airlines also said it would buy 100 aircraft of the same type, worth $12.8 billion.
Deliveries are expected to begin in 2023 and continue until 2027, with the bulk to be delivered in 2024.
Air China said its purchase would represent a 10.4 percent increase in available tonnage (ATK) capacity, while China Southern expects a 13 percent increase in capacity.
China Eastern said the new planes are narrow-body and will be deployed mostly on domestic routes and on flights to neighboring countries such as Japan, South Korea and Southeast Asia.
Major airlines usually get big discounts for the price list, with China Eastern confirming that the discounts were bigger than usual.
The recovery of Chinese aviation
China ’ s aviation industry has recovered in recent weeks from the blow it suffered after authorities shut down the huge city of Shanghai in April due to the new wave of the pandemic.
As well as the crash of a Boeing 737-800 in March, which killed 132 people on board, in the worst air disaster on the mainland in 28 years.
The 737 MAX, Boeing's primary model, has not resumed commercial flights in the country, although airlines are making test flights after China's aviation regulator lifted a grounding order late last year.
Boeing sold a quarter of the planes it makes annually to Chinese buyers, and China was its biggest customer, before the MAX was grounded after accidents in Indonesia and Ethiopia.
The massive order is expected to significantly boost the European aircraft maker, Airbus, in a key market.
Airbus said the orders showed positive momentum for the recovery and a booming outlook for the Chinese aviation market.
It added in a statement that once the relevant criteria are met, the backlog of applications will enter.
Shares in Airbus rose more than 3% following the news, while those of US rival Boeing fell 1.2% ahead of the market.
Its net profit more than tripled in the first quarter to 1.2 billion euros ($1.27 billion) compared to the same period last year.
Airbus jumped 3.02% to $95.24 at press time.

July 2, 2022 01: 38
Taha Hassib (Abu Dhabi)
Motivating people to protect the environment is a central goal of the Environment Awards. Caring for the planet is no longer a luxury. Preserving its natural balance and biodiversity is now the focus of attention for politicians, scientists and activists through inspiring individual initiatives.
Climate change, its consequences and ways to address it, is moving towards a trend that is emerging day by day at the international level through climate conferences and summits, as well as at the national level, where most countries of the world are developing their policies to be more committed to protecting the environment, and more ready to shift to carbon neutrality (zero carbon).
The focus on the role of the individual in protecting the environment is clearly reflected in the Goldman Environmental Prize, which they call the "Green Nobel", founded by Richard and Rhoda Goldman in San Francisco, California, in 1989, to shed more light on environmental problems and their effects, and to draw the attention of the global public to the need for action in the field of environmental protection.
Richard Goldman, the founder of the award, believes that “people from ordinary backgrounds are doing extraordinary things to save our planet. ”
By rewarding ordinary people for outstanding environmental achievements, the Prize seeks to inspire others in the same direction.
The first edition of the Goldman Environmental Prize was launched on April 16, 1990, and was also the founder's 70th birthday.
The award is given to individuals who have made continuous efforts to protect and enhance the natural environment, often in the face of significant personal risks.
A more sustainable future
The $200,000 prize seeks to motivate candidates from all continents, Asia, Africa, Europe, North America, South America and the island states, and to ensure that the categories are diverse in terms of age, gender, ethnicity and language, all united in their commitment to building a more sustainable, equitable and biologically diverse future.
Since its inception, the prize has awarded $28 million to 213 winners from 93 countries, and 95 women have won the prize.
Nomination Criteria
Candidates are often leaders in a grassroots campaign that results in significant impact at the regional, national or global level, as well as those who provide significant inspiration to other environmentalists or the public.
The award pays attention to individuals who will be greatly helped to complement their current efforts to protect the environment.
The most likely element to win lies in recent achievements that have strengthened the environment, prioritizing individuals over executives of large NGOs.
Government employees can run when the work they have submitted falls outside their official responsibilities.
The 33rd edition of the Goldman Environment Prize was broadcast in a virtual ceremony on May 25.
The event was presented by the famous American actress and environmental activist Jane Fonda, who has won several awards, including two Oscars, two BAFTA awards, seven Golden Globe Awards, the Primetime Emmy Award, the American Film Institute Award, and the Honorary Golden Lion Award.
In 2019, Jane Fonda moved to Washington, D.C. and founded her grassroots climate change movement, Fire Drill Fridays, where every Friday she hosted events on Capitol Hill calling on political leaders to take action to address the climate emergency we are in.
Climate action requires as fast as firefighters move to put out a fire in a house, and that ’ s what the connotations of a phrase from Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg: “This is a crisis.
We have to act like our house is on fire, because it is.
Jane Goodall.
Dr. Jane Goodall, the world ’ s most famous wildlife conservationist who has spent decades studying chimpanzee behavior, is convinced that “there ’ s a secret to real change: when we have reason to hope, we have reason to act. ”
Her latest book, The Book of Hope: A Survival Guide for Trying Times, and her podcast, Jane Goodall Hopecast, both deliver inspiring messages.
In 2021, Dr. Goodall received the Templeton Prize, which is awarded to people who harness the power of science to explore the deepest questions about the universe and human existence, in recognition of her work integrating science with spirituality and compassion.
Inspiring and environmental advocates
The winners of the 33rd edition are described on its website as outstanding individuals who have taken action to defend their communities and environment: Shima Williams of Nigeria, Niwat Ruikau of Thailand, Marjan Menesma of the Netherlands, Julian Vincent of Australia, Nalele Cobo of the United States, and Alex Lusitante and Alexandra Narviz of Ecuador.
Oil spill.
In Nigeria, despite the oil wealth of the Niger Delta, residents face the dilemma of environmental degradation caused by oil spills.
Each year, around 240,000 barrels of crude oil leak from pipelines and oil wells, polluting water supplies and crops.
In the wake of the catastrophic oil spills in Nigeria, environmental lawyer Chima Williams held Royal Dutch Shell responsible for the widespread environmental damage caused.
This is the first time a Dutch multinational has been held responsible for violations by its subsidiaries in another country.
Prevention of climate change
In an unprecedented victory, Marjan Menesma leveraged public input and unique legal strategy to secure a successful ruling against the Dutch government, requiring her to enact specific preventive measures against climate change.
In December 2019, the Dutch Supreme Court ruled that the government had a legal obligation to protect its citizens from climate change and ordered, by the end of 2020, to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 25% below 1990 levels.
The decision by the Dutch Supreme Court marks the first time citizens have successfully held their government to account for its inability to protect them in the face of climate change.
Abolition of coal financing
Australian Julian Vincent led a successful populist campaign to abolish coal financing in Australia, a major coal exporter.
Thanks to its activity, Australia ’ s four largest banks have committed to ending funding for coal projects by 2030, and major insurers have also agreed to stop underwriting new coal projects.
No to oil in urban areas
Nalili Kobo, 21, grew up in southern Los Angeles and started her business when she was 9 years old after noticing foul smells emanating from an oil well across the street from her home.
Over the years, she has suffered headaches, nosebleeds and heart palpitations caused by pollution from the well.
At the age of 19, Nalili Kobo led a coalition to permanently shut down her community ’ s oil exploration site in March 2020.
She began attending meetings and gatherings with her mother, and at the age of nine, she gave her first public speech on the issue, eventually becoming the main spokesperson for the Los Angeles oil embargo.
Protecting the Mekong River
In Thailand, Niwat Ruikau and his community successfully ended the project to blow up the upper Mekong slopes, which would have destroyed 248 miles of the Mekong River to deepen shipping channels.
This is the first time that the Thai government has cancelled a cross-border project because of the environmental damage it could cause.
repercussions of gold mining
In Ecuador, the duo Alex Lusitante and Alexandra Narviz were able to galvanize indigenous efforts to protect their ancestral lands from the fallout from gold mining, preserving 79,000 acres of pristine and biodiverse rainforest at the headwaters of the Ecuadorian Aguarco River, a sacred place in Cován.
Jury
Wangera Maathai, a Kenyan Nobel Peace Prize laureate in 2004 for her contributions to sustainable development, democracy and peace, and for her role in protecting the environment, especially her 1977 founding of the Green Belt Movement to plant 30 million trees in Africa.
Among the judges of the award is Alvaro Umana, the former Minister of Environment of Costa Rica, the first minister to hold this portfolio, during 1989 and 1990, and Yolanda Cacapades, the former Minister of Environment of Ecuador, who from 1990 to 1992 coordinated the participation of civil society organizations in the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development during the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro in 1992.

Poisonous sunscreen.
UV filters can harm aquatic life
DBA
Published on: Saturday 9 July 2022 - 4: 05 PM | Last updated on Saturday 9 July 2022 - 4: 05 PM
Warmer temperatures attract people to beaches and water, but large amounts of sunscreen get into the water with bathers – UV filters and nanoparticles from creams and sprays can damage coral reefs and other marine organisms, more and more studies are currently showing such effects.
And replacement solutions are in the works – but until then, it ’ s up to the users themselves.
Up to 14,000 tons of sunscreen end up in the seas each year, of which 4,000 to 6,000 tons reach coral reefs, according to researchers at the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
How this affects the marine environment has not been conclusively explained, but the UV filters included in these condoms are particularly worrisome.
NOAA observed that these substances inhibit the growth of green algae, lead to abnormalities in young mussels, and harm the immune system and reproduction of sea urchins.
For dolphins, these substances can accumulate in cell tissues and be passed on to small animals, while they can reduce fertility in fish and cause genetic changes.
But UV filters pose a particular threat to coral reefs — along with stressors such as rising sea temperatures.
A 2016 US study suggested that an organic chemical filter, oxybenzone, in particular, could damage the genetic material of sensitive caterpillars and cause their larvae to encapsulate and die in their skeleton.
The results of studies like this prompted the US state of Hawaii to pass a law banning the sale of sunscreens containing oxybenzone and octinoxate from 2021.
Similar regulations apply in Key West, Florida, the Virgin Islands, the island nation of Palau, the Thai Maritime National Parks, the Caribbean island of Bonaire, and some holiday areas in Mexico.
How the corals were damaged by oxybenzone was determined by a recent US study published in the journal Science, where scientists from Stanford University used a type of coral and a type of marine anemone for this purpose, added "oxybenzone" in high concentrations within fish ponds, and then exposed them to various light radiation.
The effect was surprising: only organisms exposed to the simulated rays of the sun died.
Lead author of the study, William Mitch, said: “It was strange to see that oxybenzone makes sunlight toxic to corals – as opposed to what it ’ s supposed to do. ”
Oxybenzone, like other chemical UV filters, is actually used as a sunscreen because it absorbs ultraviolet rays that fall on human skin and then releases them as harmless heat.
However, the researchers observed that anemones and corals metabolized the filter in such a way that the resulting material formed harmful roots when exposed to sunlight, turning the filter into a phototoxin.
Scientists also note that algae, which live in symbiosis with corals and give them their colorful appearance, apparently protect their host by trapping toxins produced from oxybenzone.
Thus, the currently prevalent coral bleaching phenomenon, along with oxybenzone in the water, could have even more deadly consequences for corals.
Bleaching occurs when stressed corals expel their “algae ” partners, thus exposing their white skeleton.
According to the study, these bleached corals are more susceptible to "oxybenzone".
In addition to oxybenzone, another organic chemical candidate is under discussion, octocrillin.
According to studies, this substance is suspected to harm water fleas, ciliary and zebra fish by affecting the balance of their hormones, among other things.
In addition, this water-insoluble substance is difficult to decompose and therefore can accumulate in living organisms.
According to various studies, UV filters can now be found in both tropical coral reefs and in the Arctic Ocean – as well as in the Baltic Sea: Catherine Fish of the German Leibniz Baltic Research Institute in Farnmunde conducted measurements on the German Baltic Sea coast in 2016, and found there 30 nanograms of UV filters per litre of Baltic Sea water.
In rivers that drain into the Baltic Sea, the amount was sometimes as high as 836 nanograms per liter.
Although these quantities are small, they may have a long-term impact on marine organisms.
Germany has no nationwide monitoring to measure pollution of water bodies with UV filters, and there are no specific upper limits on their allowable amounts.
In response to the potential environmental risks of chemical UV filters, more and more manufacturers are offering “coral-safe ” or“ coral-friendly ” metal sunscreens.
These protectors contain zinc or titanium dioxide – molecules act like tiny mirrors on the skin, reflecting UV light.
Some manufacturers are trying to reduce this effect by reducing metal dyes and relying on nano-sized particles, but Spanish researchers showed in 2014 that these nanoparticles act as catalysts that make sunlight produce highly reactive hydrogen peroxide from water, which can harm microorganisms.
Research is currently underway on alternatives in which compounds from algae, seaweed and other marine organisms act as UV filters.
Until these products are ready for the market, the best green sun protection is likely to be one that relies on reducing the amount of condoms used without cutting them out altogether — given the risk of skin cancer.
The consumer magazine "UMID" of the German Federal Agency for the Environment recommends the use of metal filters in non-nano-form and advises exposure to the sun in the afternoon or just before sunset, stay in the shade and protect the body with appropriate clothing and bathing at home, thus reducing the UV filters that end up directly in the water.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman during his visit to the British government headquarters in London 07 / 03 / 2018 - Alastair Grant / AP.
Saudi Arabia ’ s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is leading his conservative kingdom with ambitious radical reforms and accelerated social changes that began with his ascension to the leadership ladder five years ago.
In parallel, he worked to fortify his position as the de facto and future ruler of the world ’ s largest oil state by silencing all dissent.
However, US President Joe Biden ’ s visit to Saudi Arabia this week indicates that bin Salman remains the country ’ s main international modernizer.
After a quick jump to the top in one of the world ’ s wealthiest countries, the brutal murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi at his country ’ s consulate in Istanbul in 2018 cast a shadow over Mohammed bin Salman ’ s one-year tenure as crown prince.
Khashoggi was writing articles critical of the prince ’ s performance in the Washington Post.
American reports concluded that bin Salman ordered his death, and this entailed attempts to isolate him on the international scene, although Saudi Arabia has repeatedly denied any involvement in the operation.
But the visit of the US president, who during his election campaign pledged to treat the kingdom as a “pariah state ” against the backdrop of its human rights record and the killing of Khashoggi, to Saudi Arabia appears to reopen external doors for Prince Mohammed.
Prince Mohammed bin Salman is strong, with a trimmed black beard and a hoarse voice.
One of his most prominent mega-projects as he seeks to diversify the kingdom ’ s oil-based economy is the construction of the futuristic mega-city of Neom at a cost of $500 billion.
But he is also seeking to cement his country ’ s position as a powerful regional power.
He has been the driving force behind Saudi Arabia ’ s military intervention in Yemen, the Arabian Peninsula ’ s poorest country, to support government forces against Iranian-backed Houthi rebels.
The 36-year-old crown prince, said to be fond of fast food and video games, is also extremely wealthy, owning a $500 million yacht and a mansion in France, while reports suggest he is the owner of a controversial painting by Leonardo de Vinci.
Unlike other Saudi princes who speak English with a British accent, wear elegant suits and have university degrees from foreign universities, the crown prince has clung to his nomadic roots.
He often wears a traditional robe and sandals, and takes friends and relatives to roast lamb meals in luxurious desert breaks.
After his meteoric rise, he oversaw the biggest shift in modern history for the kingdom, the world ’ s largest crude oil exporter and home to Islam ’ s holiest sites in Mecca and Medina.
"Master of everything."
As part of his reform drive, the Commission for the Promotion of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice, which served as a powerful religious police, was dismantled, cinemas reopened and tourist visas issued for the first time to visit the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia has organised a film festival, a Formula One race, free wrestling matches and concerts.
Women were allowed to drive.
In contrast, during his reign, Saudi Arabia witnessed a crackdown on activists and the increasing number of dissidents by imprisoning them.
As part of an anti-corruption campaign, dozens of princes and businessmen were detained at Riyadh ’ s luxury Ritz-Carlton hotel in 2017 for months.
In his book “The Rise of Mohammed bin Salman to Power, ” the journalist Ben Hubbard says,“ Bin Salman is a deeply divisive figure.
His supporters praise him as a long-awaited game-changer in a region that yearns for it, and his enemies abhor him as a ruthless dictator in the making.
The prince is “determined to give the Saudis a bright and prosperous future and has an unwavering willingness to crush his enemies. ”
Born on August 31, 1985, Prince Mohammed is one of hundreds of descendants of Saudi Arabia ’ s founder, King Abdulaziz Al Saud.
He grew up in a palace in Riyadh with his mother Fahda, one of his father ’ s four wives, and has five brothers.
“As the sixth son of the founding king ’ s 25th son, there was little reason to expect him to rise to prominence, ” Hubbard writes,“ for most of his life, few people expected it. ”
Mohammed bin Salman received a law degree from King Saud University.
Upon graduation, he served as an adviser to his father, then governor of Riyadh.
When King Salman came to power in early 2015, he appointed him defense minister.
Within a few months, the young prince became responsible for coordinating economic policy and overseeing Aramco ’ s oil company and his country ’ s military intervention in Yemen.
Prince Mohammed ’ s positions have been so numerous that diplomats in Riyadh have called him “master of everything. ”
Unlike many princes in the royal family, Prince Mohammed is married to only one woman and has three sons and two daughters.
People close to him say he works 16 hours a day.
A torrent of ideas.
On 21 June 2017, with the support of his father, he was able to remove his cousin Mohammed bin Nayef and replace him.
In March 2020, bin Nayef and the king ’ s brother Prince Ahmed bin Abdulaziz Al Saud were arrested on charges of orchestrating a coup.
Since coming to power, bin Salman has vowed to lead a "moderate, free" kingdom that is open to other religions.
Explaining the philosophy of change, he said during an investment forum in Riyadh in 2017, “We want to live a normal life, ” adding,“ We are just going back to what we were, to Islam that is open to all religions, traditions and peoples. ”
"Seventy percent of the Saudi people are under the age of 30, and frankly we will not waste 30 years of our lives dealing with any extremist ideas that we will destroy today," he said.
As his star began to shine, the crown prince toured the United States and was praised by the White House, Wall Street, Silicon Valley and even Hollywood.
New York Times columnist Thomas Friedman spoke of a "flood of new ideas to change his country" that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke of in an interview.
At the start of his reign, Prince Mohammed escalated the confrontation with Tehran, led a three-year boycott against neighboring Qatar, and reportedly detained former Lebanese Prime Minister Saad Hariri for days before French President Emmanuel Macron intervened.
Mohammed bin Salman has had a close relationship with the White House under former President Donald Trump, especially with the president ’ s son-in-law and adviser Jared Kushner.
But in early 2021, with the arrival of Democratic President Joe Biden in the White House and allowing the publication of an intelligence report that concluded that the crown prince authorized the killing of Khashoggi, relations between Saudi Arabia and Washington cooled.
Biden ’ s visit is an implicit admission of the inability to bypass Prince Mohammed.
This may be an admission that bin Salman could rule Saudi Arabia for half a century or more.

The latest forecast by the U.S. planemaker rules out any possible future deliveries to buyers from Russia, which has already been excluded from the global aviation market due to sweeping sanctions imposed by the United States and other countries following its invasion of Ukraine.
Boeing predicted last year that Russian customers would make up about 1,500 aircraft sales over the next two decades.
Holst told reporters before issuing the forecast: “Russia is not a viable market for us. ”
Demand for commercial aircraft
Despite widespread concerns, demand for cargo aircraft remains strong, with the global fleet expected to grow to 3,610 aircraft in 2041, from 2010 aircraft in 2019.
Sales of new aircraft are expected to be strong over the next decade, as airlines strengthen their fleets to meet the burgeoning demand for air travel after the coronavirus pandemic.

Avocado fruit has a delicious taste and versatility, so that some do not get tired of eating it every day, and it also reduces the level of cholesterol, according to a new study.
In the study, recently published in the Journal of the American Heart Association, 500 participants were asked to eat a large avocado each day, while another 500 participants were not asked to do so.
In addition, 500 people who did not make fruit a regular part of their diet were asked to eat less than two avocados each month.
When the six-month time frame expired, participants who consumed avocado regularly ate a generally healthy diet and ended up with lower cholesterol levels.
Nutritionist Sarah Glaser told Sputnik, “Overall, this is a good study because it ’ s randomized and controlled by a large number of people. ”
Participants in each group also had a similar basic diet and scored about 50% on the healthy eating index.
Regarding how avocados lower cholesterol levels, Glaser says that this fruit “speeds up the breakdown of triglycerium-rich lipoproteins and prevents the liver from producing more VLDL (a type of bad cholesterol), which means there is less low-density lipoprotein (“ LDL cholesterol ”) in the bloodstream in general. ”
