Anthropology or Anthropology: Anthropology and its Relation to Medicine and Health / 11
Anthropology or Anthropology: Anthropology and its Relation to Medicine and Health / 11
Translated by Ahmed Mogheer
Medical Anthropology: Definition, History and Concerns
Medical anthropology is a specialized branch of anthropology whose main interest is in the relationship between cultural factors, perceptions and beliefs on the one hand and health disorders on the other.
Medical anthropology is a branch of applied anthropology, which studies diseases, the health care system, theories of disease and treatment from a pluralistic, sociocultural perspective.
Medical anthropology, in general, has grown very rapidly as a specialized field of study in anthropology, especially since the 1950s and 1960s.
The growth of this field is mainly due to: (1) the growing interest of social scientists in general and anthropologists in particular in health and disease, and (2) the increased awareness of medical professionals and health policy makers about the role of social sciences in the health issue.
Arguably, when anthropology arose in the 19th century, investigating health and disease issues seemed not to be among the dominant concerns of cultural anthropologists.
However, sociologists in general and anthropologists in particular have begun to develop academic and practical interests in the study of health and disease in social and cultural contexts.
At the root of the emergence and development of medical anthropology also lies the need to study the world of health and disease from evolutionary and ecological perspectives.
Medical anthropologists attempt to address fundamental questions such as:
What is the evolutionary basis for the difference in how different populations deal with the disease?
What are the main factors that affect children ’ s growth and development?
What is the impact of modernization on the local population?
Medical anthropologists are also interested in:
Investigate the interrelationship between human health, nutrition, cultural beliefs and practices; and how people ’ s dietary behavior and sexual habits affect the spread of pathogenic organisms;
Multicultural aspects of nursing care;
the social and cultural contexts of disease; health-related behavior of people, and the social and cultural associations of such behavior;
The social, behavioral, demographic and biological characteristics of people who develop the disease.
Some of the main theories of health, culture and society
A brief overview of key perspectives in the anthropology of health and disease may be appropriate at this juncture.
Medicine as an institution and the question of health and disease have been explained through different perspectives.
The following are crucial theories:
Functional Perspective: This perspective views medicine and healthcare systems as important social institutions; it focuses on the functions and roles that the institution plays in maintaining stability in society.
Medical institutions, whether scientific or traditional, and various practitioners exist to meet the needs of individuals and society.
Medical Ecological Perspective: This perspective focuses on human biological and behavioral adaptations to diseases in different ecological and environmental contexts.
Thus, diseases evolve in line with specific ecological niches, and people ’ s responses to health problems have evolved in the context of their specific local ecosystems.
Cultural Interpretative Perspective: This is also called the “symbolic interaction ” approach.
This approach focuses on the social and cultural constructs of health, disease and illness.
According to this theory, diseases and health are not just things that exist “out there ”; they are a product of complex social interactions; and health and disease are largely shaped by the way people as representatives give meaning to them and how actors respond to them in social and cultural ways.
Critical perspective: This theory is also called “radical political economy. ”
It is an approach that emphasizes social and economic inequality in power and wealth, which in turn has a significant impact on health status and access to health-care facilities.
Individuals, groups, communities and even nations thus tend to have an unbalanced share of health resources; this often results in an unequal distribution of morbidity and mortality patterns among a given society; those in power and dominance enjoy better health, and marginalized groups suffer the burden of disease.
The roles of anthropologists and contributions of anthropology to health
Applied medical anthropology is strongly interdisciplinary in its nature and approach.
Medical anthropologists often work with academics in the field of sociology, medicine, psychology, and demography.
Applied medical anthropology brings with it the comparative framework of anthropology that helps medically trained people avoid one limited cultural perspective, to see how social and environmental factors affect health, and to be familiar with alternative ways of understanding and treating disease.
In general, medical anthropologists play the following two important roles:
work in collaboration with health professionals, researchers and other professionals, as consultants, consultants and researchers;
They work in the field of health and disease and participate in their own independent research, in order to advance anthropological knowledge.
Some specific applications or contributions of medical anthropology in health and disease include:
-They help hospitals and health agencies to deliver health care more effectively to people.
They assist national and international health organizations by providing anthropological data on the cultures of the peoples of the world.
They work with epidemiologists in identifying the effects of cultural practices and beliefs on disease transmission.
-They help health professionals in disease prevention and control.
They are involved in the fields of international health, promoting mental health in different cultures.
They assist in the areas of public health education efforts related to family planning, maternal and child health, improving community sanitation and nutritional counseling.
They help promote community involvement in disease prevention.
-They help people understand the psychosocial factors that affect prevention, and participate in the identification of cases and treatment.
They help health workers overcome restrictions on large-scale drug administration or vaccination as well as in overcoming cultural constraints on health education programs and dealing with them.
Anthropologists work with epidemiologists and psychiatrists in the areas of cardiovascular problems and mental disorders.
Disease, society and economic activity
Understanding social and cultural behaviors as important factors in the causal relationship, spread, and distribution of many diseases is critical.
Anthropologists argue that how people live, how they behave, what and how they eat, what they believe and practice, what they value and what technology they possess, etc., are important determinants of their individual and collective health.
Different societies have different concepts of health and disease.
The standards that people set for health vary from culture to culture.
Behaviors and lifestyles that are considered healthy vary from one community to another, and from time to time.
People ’ s understanding of health and perceptions of the nature of diseases also vary from culture to culture.
Anthropologists argue that, on the basis of cross-cultural research (i.e. research conducted relatively in different cultures) perceptions of good and bad health are constructed, along with culturally significant health threats and problems.
Thus, the production and distribution of health and disease are strongly influenced by sociocultural and political-economic factors.
Different ethnic groups and cultures recognize different diseases, symptoms and causes and have developed different health care systems and treatment strategies.
Anthropologists also argue that diseases vary between cultures and types of economic activity.
Systems of economic activity prevalent in a given society greatly influence the characteristics of morbidity and mortality.
For example, some infectious diseases such as malaria, typhoid, cholera, etc., are more common in settled communities (peasants and urban communities).
Diseases such as schistosomiasis are associated with certain economic activities.
They are widespread in communities that practice irrigation systems.
Other infectious diseases, particularly sexually transmitted diseases, including the HIV / AIDS pandemic, are more common in urban cultures than in rural areas and along highways.
There are also what anthropologists call development diseases which are those health problems that arise in a given society after the introduction of development projects, or when indigenous people are integrated into global political and economic systems, certain types of diseases can be introduced to people.
These diseases may include bacterial or parasitic diseases that occur in an area due to changes in the environment following development-related activities and other categories of development diseases may include “diseases caused by poverty, undernutrition and poor sanitation, reflecting the failure of development programs to integrate people into large-scale communities in a satisfactory manner. ”
Causality theories of disease
The biomedical theory of the causality of disease is just one of the different theories of diseases that people carry.
The methods by which people try to treat the perceived disease are based on their beliefs about the cause of the disease.
People from different cultures have developed for themselves different ways of interpreting how diseases and misfortunes (bad luck or disaster) occur.
It seems that such theories for centuries have worked for them very efficiently.
In fact, the peoples of the world relied on such kinds of explanations (and still not a few societies continue to do so) until the modern scientific theory of medicine emerged a few centuries ago.
Anthropologists have classified the various causal theories of diseases that exist between different cultures in the world into: 1) theories of personal diseases, 2) theories of natural diseases, and 3) theories of emotional diseases.
The causation theory of personal illness attributes disease to causative agents that are considered intelligent beings.
This theory is particularly common among most non-Western societies.
Even if a person knows that a mosquito bite causes malaria, it is often believed and believed that the cause of the disease is due to the force and evil action of such factors as evil spirits, witches and witches, ancestral spirits, curses made by elders, the wrath of supernatural beings, etc.
The causal theory of natural diseases is also referred to as Western or scientific medicine.
This attributes diseases to such non-personal and scientifically proven factors as viruses, bacteria, fungi, parasites, etc. and toxic substances.
This theory explains the causes of diseases from a natural point of view.
That is, diseases are natural events, not supernatural things.
Non-Western cultures also use natural disease theories.
For example, some people believe that eating or drinking hot or cold substances may create a health problem.
For example, a menstruating woman is not supposed to eat pineapple in some cultures.
Because they think pineapple is a “cold ” thing and menstruation is a“ hot ” thing, the two will collide and cause illness.
The causal theory of emotional illness states that illnesses are caused by some severe negative emotional experience.
A number of ethnographic studies have found that there are, for example, mental illnesses that are unique to certain cultural environments.
Such diseases caused by certain cultural environments and traditions are described as syndromes associated with culture.
In some cultures, emotional experiences such as anxiety and fear may cause a disease called susto, or what is also called "soul loss" in anthropological literature.
A person who thinks they have this mental illness may develop symptoms such as lethargy (fatigue or weakness), loss of activity, wandering, distraction (or thinking disorder), etc.
In Africa, which is predominantly a traditional society, traditional, non-scientific explanations of disease are very important in the diagnosis, treatment and management of diseases.
Belief in the power of various intelligent agents such as Djinn, Mitch, Devil, Ganel, etc. to cause various mental and physical illnesses is very common in most African cultures.
People in some cultures do not go to a modern health care center to seek help for certain types of diseases.
Treatment of diseases is also closely related to the type of causal relationship of diseases that people carry.
In psychosomatic illnesses such as Soto and other culture-specific illnesses, people prefer to go for treatment to a traditional medical professional, rather than a modern health facility.
Perspectives on the causality of disease carried by people are therefore very important in determining people's health care seeking behavior and the type of diagnosis and treatment.
This is why it is critical that healthcare professionals be culturally sensitive and have some basic understanding of social and cultural anthropological knowledge when dealing with the care of patients from different cultural and religious backgrounds.
Health Care Systems
Health systems vary across time and space.
Since time immemorial, people have developed different health care systems.
The modern system of health care and its provision as practiced in the contemporary modern world is a modern phenomenon.
People have treated the sick and developed means of caring for the sick and disabled in various traditional ways, and these means of providing health care are still prevalent in almost all non-Western societies. In short, all societies have some form of health care system.
A health care system can be defined as beliefs, habits, specialists and techniques aimed at promoting health and preventing, diagnosing and treating diseases.
Traditional societies have their own medical practices and specialists who often rely on what is suggested by a specific causal theory.
Traditional healers play important roles in treating patients with various health problems.
Magical rituals and prayers are often used in the production of medicines and their use on patients.
They are highly respected in their communities.
Patients believe in their knowledge and skills (often much more than they believe in the expertise of modern doctors) and their consultation.
Traditional Medicine
Traditional medicine can be referred to as a system of medicine in particular societies with a range of causal views of diseases, mechanisms of diagnosis and treatment, and roles of specialists, where the prevailing model of disease and health differs significantly from scientific medicine.
It may commonly be seen as medical beliefs and practices that were used from time immemorial by human societies before the advent of modern medicine, and are still used by most non-Western societies.
Traditional medicine embodies a system of medical care that is based on ideas about pathogens and treatment of diseases that have evolved over a longer period of time and that is shaped by people's own experience in terms of their environment, and their pattern of beliefs about human, environmental, and supernatural relationships.
A broader term such as alternative medicine can also be used to describe this type of medicine.
In this sense, all medical opinions and practices outside of traditional scientific medicine, such as acupuncture, healing by faith, healing through prayer, etc., fall into this category.
Traditional medical practitioners acquire and employ a wide range of medical knowledge that includes astrology, healing by faith, massage, folk psychotherapy and folk psychiatry, exorcism, herbal medicine, various magical acts and amulets to treat the sick.
Traditional disease care systems represent experimental attempts by indigenous people to control associated diseases and calamities and to maintain health and well-being in a given environment.
These systems express deep-rooted attitudes towards health and disease, popular drug concepts, the activities of indigenous healers, the role of kinship groups in maintaining health, and so on.
Biomedicine
This medicine is referred to interchangeably as “scientific ”,“ Western ” and “modern ” medicine.
It is based on the model of disease and health as concepts, explainable and subject to natural assumptions.
Biomedicine aims to link disease to scientifically proven factors that do not carry any personal malice towards their victims, as seen by people who hold a personal causal theory of disease.
Comparison and contrast between traditional and scientific medicine
It may be appropriate to say that medicine has always been recognized as a social biological science.
When we look at the history of medicine, prominent thinkers from Hippocrates to Sigmund Freud tend to view human health as being strongly influenced by social, cultural, environmental and other non-biological factors.
Health and disease have been understood to be inextricably linked to the way humans live and their social and cultural environment.
However, the contributions of sociocultural factors to pathogens and their roles in healing processes have been greatly undermined until recently and have not received systematic analyze.However, starting in the 1950s, social sciences and medicine began to show increased interest in cooperation.
The place of traditional medicine in the health care sector, which has so far been neglected, is now being appreciated.
There now seems to be a growing acceptance of the contributions of traditional medicine by modern medical and health planners.
Modern health care professionals rejected traditional or alternative medical systems as useless until recently but now this position is being changed.
Anthropologists argue that the two systems can complement each other.
In many African societies, modern health-care professionals recognize traditional medical practitioners, and collaborative efforts are being made in research and practice in areas such as HIV / AIDS, and in the identification of various plants of medicinal value.
Traditional medical practitioners may be more effective in treating diseases that have psychological causes, such as mental problems.
People often consult them and get treatment that may not be possible by modern psychiatrists.
Patients often receive more psychological / emotional comfort and social support when treated by traditional healers.
But in modern medicine, the context of treatment is often one of isolation, alienation (separation), and separation from the group.
Western medicine may learn a lot from traditional medicine in which the “relationship between therapist, patient and community ” is important.
In such cases, the patient is not an expatriate and has the necessary emotional and social support.
Unlike Western medicine, traditional medicine sees the patient as not just a biological person, and pays attention to social and spiritual aspects as well.
Traditional medical practitioners effectively treat patients as whole beings, using any combination of methods that prove useful.
This is not usually the case in modern medicine.
There is no doubt that Western medicine is better than traditional medicine in many respects, as many of its achievements are based on scientific facts.
As such, traditional medicine has a lot to learn from it.
It is true that traditional medicine may not be as effective against bacteria as antibiotics.
Advances in scientific medicine have made it possible to combat many permanent (persistent and recurring) health problems.
Countless drugs have been made and are effective in the treatment of various diseases.
However, anthropologists still draw our attention to some problems in Western medicine.
They argue that the growth in medical science and diagnostic and treatment techniques has occurred at an alarming rate.
But many of the procedures and practices of modern medicine lack convincing justification and logic.
They report instances of bias, lack of a personal relationship between patient and doctor, and interactions between doctor and nurse.
Despite the dominance of modern scientific medicine, and in some cases its apparent superiority in quality and utility, it is better to consider the two systems of medicine as complementary to each other, rather than competing and undermining one another.
The reality on the ground is that even in industrialized societies people often consult with both modern and traditional systems of medicine.
Medical pluralism is still an ever-present phenomenon.
Medical anthropological research suggests that even in urban settings where there are Western scientific medical facilities, people often consult traditional medical practitioners.
Both cosmic and supernatural scientific perspectives regarding health and disease continue to play important roles in influencing people ’ s health-seeking behavior.
Many countries are now developing policies whereby their national health-care system integrates both scientific and traditional medical care systems.
It is appropriate to describe briefly the social and cultural implications of medical pluralism, particularly in the context of developing countries. One such developing trend is that the health-care system in developing countries is largely dominated and biased by the biomedical model, despite the multiplicity of natures.
This is usually manifested in the fact that biomedical dominance and the medical care system enjoys a higher status and the traditional medical system is often not recognized as a viable alternative, although some steps have been taken in this regard.
Other issues associated with this medical pluralism also include:
Although it has a higher status, the Western medical system, on the other hand, is criticized for its bias towards curative rather than preventive and promotive medicine.
Its heavy reliance on Western countries for institutional, professional and technical support is also another point of criticism.
Most importantly, hierarchical medical pluralism in the Third World represents the basic social stratification.
The few elites with the greatest privileges often benefit from the dominant scientific medicine, while the majority of the population benefit from the popular medical services.
Another prevalent fact worth noting is that there is often a dual use of medical care; the elite rely primarily on the biomedical system and may resort to popular medical assistance as a last resort; on the other hand, the masses generally rely on the popular medical system and may also benefit from the biomedical sector at its lower end.

What do the longest living people do?
What do the longest living people do?
September 24, 2022 01: 19
I'm sorry.
Sherif Arafa
Although people around the world suffer from psychological stress, it leads to increased rates of diseases such as heart disease and diabetes.
Some people have better mental and physical health, and the average age of people in some parts of the world is longer than others.
Researchers call the “blue zones ” those places around the world where people live decades longer than life expectancy.
These include: Islanders of Ikaria (Greece), Sardinia (Italy), Okinawa (Japan), Nicoya Peninsula (Costa Rica), and Loma Linda, California (USA).
What brings together the people of these different regions?
A recent study
In a study titled “Lessons from Blue Zones and the Pillars of Lifestyle Medicine and Beyond: An Update on the Contributions of Behavior and Genetics to Well-Being and Longevity, ” published recently in the American Journal of Lifestyle Medicine, scientists found common factors among residents of these areas, including the presence of specific genes, FOXO3A- ApoE2 - HLA.
But they also found many factors that humans can control.
They are:
1) Move a lot
The common lifestyle of the inhabitants of these areas includes a lot of physical activity that is done naturally throughout the day, on a daily basis.
As a normal part of their normal way of life.
In general, scientists advise adults to exercise at least 150 minutes a week of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, and at least twice a week of body muscle training.
But how many people actually do that?
Fewer than 25% of adults in developed countries are engaged in this physical activity that is supposed to be practiced by a normal person on a daily basis, while in blue areas it is considered a daily routine.
“Eat wisely. ”
According to the study, residents of the Blue Zones routinely eat healthy, balanced foods and whole grains.
It seems that the inhabitants of these areas do not overeat too much, on the contrary they stop before reaching the stage of overcrowding.
For cultural reasons, Okinawans stop eating when their stomach is only 80% full, which prevents them from overeating calories.In this study, the researchers discussed different diets among the blue zones, and reviewed the potential benefits of eating different fish and vegetables to support brain health.
This points to the health benefits of the Mediterranean diet in particular.
3) Dealing with pressure
The study says that chronic stress has become a major problem in developed countries in the 21st century, usually associated with work and earning a living, but the accumulation of the stress hormone cortisol increases the risk of cardiovascular disease and digestive disorders and may lead to death.
The study adds that trying to “avoid stress ” is now an unrealistic goal.
While the most realistic is the habit of dealing with and relieving these pressures, and recovering from them, in different ways from one person to another.
Such as strengthening social bonds, laughter, recreational activities, sports, breathing techniques, meditation, yoga, tai chi, activities that reduce stress and increase relaxation...
and so on.
4- Sleep well
The study says that older adults in blue areas follow the sun cycle, sleeping in the evening and waking up early, and repeat that they always strive to get plenty of good sleep.
7 to 9 hours each night.
The study also points to the importance of the day of napping for the elderly, as most of them in these areas slept a little during the afternoon as a regular habit.
The study also noted that poor sleep quality is associated with an increased risk of arterial hypertension, type 2 diabetes, depression, overeating and obesity.
5) Maintain social ties
Loneliness leads to bad consequences for physical and mental health.
Older adults who feel lonely and isolated are more prone to chronic diseases and higher rates of depression.
A sense of belonging and connectedness, in family and social relations, contributes to the improvement of the quality of life.
They found that older people in these blue areas often live in the family, among their children and grandchildren, which improves their mental health and enhances their physical health.
Respect the planet!
Having a cohesive meaning of life has a great role in improving the mental state.
The researchers believe that the cultural beliefs adopted by the residents of these areas prevent them from polluting the place where they live, improving their quality of life and their physical health as well.
Respect for the environment leads to behaviors that contribute to the overall cleanliness of their city, reduce pollution in their waterways, and reduce chemicals on their farms, leading to a balanced food chain, ecosystem, and healthier plants and animals.
A concern for the environment may make people more inclined to eat natural foods.
In this study, scientists associate it with aversion to negative habits such as smoking.
He proposed further studies to examine the relationship between environmental concern and longevity.
Now tell me, dear reader.
How much of this advice do you actually apply in your life?

Doha World Air Transport Summit charts path to further recovery
Losses are expected to fall to just $9.7 billion this year.
Recommendations for greater collaboration between parties to achieve sustainability goals

“Sustainability, environmental conservation and the road to greater recovery. ”
Words summarizing the most important points discussed by the fourth edition of the International Air Transport Association (IATA) Global Finance Symposium, which was hosted in the Qatari capital Doha this year, with the participation of senior officials and aviation industry experts worldwide.
Al Mal attended the event, which is the largest in the industry since the outbreak of the Coronavirus epidemic at the end of 2019, in which more than 50 officials, experts and leaders representing all aspects participated and discussed the most prominent challenges and financial strategy to advance the future of the industry during the coming period.
The participants described the recent crises in the air transport sector as one of the biggest problems in its history, especially given the complexity of the situation with the outbreak of the Russo-Ukrainian war.
The World Air Transport Association estimated that the sector's losses by the end of this year alone amounted to $9.7 billion, a significant decline as a result of the lifting of travel restrictions, after witnessing a series of losses with the repercussions of the Coronavirus amounted to about $190 billion.
Participants said the sector is likely to return to profitability by 2023, but certainly at lower levels than before the pandemic, pointing out that the high level of corporate debt due to borrowing will remain the biggest challenge for financial managers, especially as companies commit to achieving their zero carbon targets by 2050, which will require greater investment in this aspect and pressure the financial resources of entities.
Participants stressed that the path to sustainability and achieving the industry ’ s goal of zero carbon emissions – Fly Net Zero – will require the cooperation of all stakeholders – airlines, financial managers, employees and government officials.
The seminar was held in the presence and patronage of the Minister of Transport, Jassim bin Saif Al-Sulaiti, and a number of officials. Wali Walsh, Director General of the International Air Transport Association (IATA), and Akbar Al-Baker, Chief Executive Officer of Qatar Airways, also participated in the opening session.
This was followed by dozens of dialogue sessions over the course of two days, in which the most prominent participants were: « Mohammed Bakri, Senior Vice President of Financial Settlement Services at the International Air Transport Association, and Mary Owens Thompson, Chief Economist at the Union ».
In addition to the participation of: Duncan Naismith, Chief Financial Officer of Qatar Airways, Teresa Parejo, Head of Sustainability at Iberia, Eric Soelheim, Chairman of the Financial Advisory Board for Industry, Chief Financial Officer of KLM, Caroline Dreschell, Head of Joint Responsibility at Lufthansa Group, and others.
Wally Walsh, director-general of the International Air Transport Association (IATA), said sustainability in the aviation sector was crucial, but it ran counter to the policy of taxing airlines for failing to commit to cutting carbon emissions.
Mr Walsh said: “Taxes are not particularly used to reduce carbon and therefore add nothing to the environment. ”
He believes that the benefits of preserving the environment are less than the risks of disruption of communication between the world through aviation, predicting that airlines will not see a hydrogen-powered aircraft before 2040 or 2050.
Numerous studies have shown that border closures have done nothing to protect citizens; for example, China ’ s zero-covid policy has lost its position as a global aviation hub.
He pointed out that the current high oil prices will certainly reflect on the prices of airline tickets, expecting companies to return to profitability rates in 2023.
Akbar Al Baker, Chief Executive Officer of Qatar Airways and Chairman of Qatar Tourism Authority, said: “The circumstances of the sector have made us meet more than once in a short time, not long ago we held a General Assembly meeting here in Doha to discuss resilience after the epidemic. ”
“Today, we are focusing on the future of the industry, companies and the entire planet as part of our mission to eliminate carbon emissions by 2050, and airlines around the world are taking serious steps to reduce these emissions. ”
The biggest challenge for the world ’ s aviation industry is political unrest, followed by inflation, fuel prices, employment and infrastructure in later stages.
He explained that the industry went through the Coronavirus pandemic as a major challenge before going through successive obstacles due to high oil prices and manpower shortages, as well as a decline in investment due to restrictions imposed on airlines due to a commitment to support the climate issue.
He pointed out that governments place restrictions on aviation, claiming that it is the main cause of carbon dioxide emissions, although it contributes only 3% of total carbon emissions.
He said that the market lacks human talent in managing the energy sustainability portfolio in the aviation sector, stressing that there is a large role for politicians to help the aviation sector with regard to the climate.
He explained that the oil companies have a great commitment in terms of the production of sustainable aviation fuel (known as SAF), pointing out that Qatar Airways will buy from it if provided at an appropriate price.
SAF fuel is three times more expensive than kerosene and is purchased as a sign of the airline ’ s commitment to mitigating environmental impacts.
Al-Baker stressed that hydrogen and hybrid electric propulsion still have many years to go, making increasing the production of sustainable aviation fuel even more important for the industry.
He said that investment decisions, especially in the field of sustainability, will have a significant impact on the financial affairs of companies in the short and long term and affect their future solvency.
He stressed the need to make huge investments in aircraft and new technologies, which have been hampered by financing in the field of sustainability and environmental solutions due to global regulations.
He said that the years following the coronavirus epidemic are the most successful in aviation history, pointing out that time is still dangerous and we do not know how things will develop as there is a possibility that tourism and travel will be affected by demand processes.

Mohamed Al Bakri, Senior Vice President of the International Air Transport Association for Financial Settlement and Distribution Services, said that the real test for the sector is the lessons learned from the crises it has experienced over the past two years through the application of the collective action mechanism.

He pointed out that learning from the mistakes of the two years is moving forward positively, and now we look forward to more support from policymakers and try to continue on the road to recovery, especially as the demand for travel continues.
He stressed that the new reality must focus on our customers and their needs, the customer is still the first choice for us, stressing the need to be financially flexible and companies stronger financially.
“We have to be financially able to continue to deliver the benefits and values we have shown because the world needs us, and aviation is no longer a luxury or an option but a necessity for human life. ”
The airline ’ s CFOs are working to rebuild balance sheets after the losses of the past two years by creating capital structures that support the ambitions of the plan to reach zero carbon emissions by 2050 and attract the necessary funding.
He stressed the need for continuous reporting on the environment, in addition to working on the digital transformation and transformation of the retail model of airlines and the impact of all this on the systems and capabilities of the financial departments of the sector.
Mary Owens Thompson, chief economist at the International Air Transport Association (IATA), said the recovery in the travel sector was supporting expectations of a return to 2019 levels by 2024.
Future bookings remain strong, with international bookings accelerating despite continued coronavirus travel restrictions in Asia, particularly in China.
Global gross domestic product (GDP) growth is expected to reach about 3 percent this year, half the growth achieved in 2021, and emerging economies will bear the brunt of the challenges this creates.
“Job growth should help mitigate the impact of rising inflation and interest rates. ”
It sees forecasts of a compound annual growth rate in the sector of 3.4% between 2019 and 2040.
Aviation is a necessary component of economic development and was recognized more than 75 years ago in an agreement signed in Chicago, she said.
Qatar Airways Chief Financial Officer Henk Jan Hogendoorn said geopolitical turmoil was the aviation industry ’ s overriding concern and that it had translated into an economic crisis after rising oil prices and rising inflation as consumers had less purchasing power.
Demand for travel is likely to continue to suffer, but there are still some residual effects of the epidemic as well, most notably the ongoing travel restrictions in certain parts of the world, especially with concern that these restrictions will increase with the advent of winter in the northern hemisphere.
Zoom and other forms of online meetings and conferences had little impact on the crisis, but what is becoming more apparent is the growing environmental awareness that is likely to continue as airlines and the industry as a whole will need to do more to educate the public about the environment.
He stressed that the rise in the value of the dollar will also have an impact on many airlines as they incur more costs, especially in fuel, and therefore the exchange rate has a negative impact on net income.
He predicted that costs will continue to rise, especially in the labor sector, which is poised for a sharp increase, not only because of the shortage of manpower but also because of regulations in force around the world.
He said there had been an increase in interest on investment funds in aviation, with good prospects for rising air freight revenues and a recovery in travel traffic.
Daniel Culver, market participation officer at Platts, an energy data provider, said: “With sustainable jet fuel as a key component of an airline ’ s cost base, hedging will be vital to avoid negative impacts from these companies appearing on their balance sheets.
He pointed out that airlines hedge to secure their profit margins and protect against losses, making financial planning more accurate and difficult.
He added that the difference between the price of crude oil and jet fuel is expected to remain high throughout 2023, after reaching record levels during the epidemic period as producers changed levels of jet fuel production during those periods.

King Abdullah University of Science and Technology selects Hewlett Packard Enterprise to build the most powerful supercomputer system in the Middle East
King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) has announced the selection of Hewlett Packard Enterprise, a leading global ICT company, to build the next generation Shaheen 3 supercomputer to deliver the latest supercomputing and artificial intelligence capabilities and advance scientific research in many fields including food, water, energy and the environment.

Artificial intelligence.

Hewlett-Packard Enterprise ’ s supercomputing capabilities enable AI at scale by combining massive computing power with the specialized capabilities required to build machine learning models and train large amounts of data. It will enhance KAUST ’ s AI mission at scale by integrating the Machine Learning Development Environment, an improved software suite for model training and development. AI models faster and larger for increased accuracy.

At KAUST by more than half of the faculty, students, postdoctoral fellows and researchers from more than 20 institutions in Saudi Arabia.
The Shaheen 3 supercomputer system will be fully operational in 2023. The new system will process unique data sets in focus areas such as clean combustion, Red Sea ecosystems, climate modelling and Arabian tectonic plates, while delivering high-resolution analysis, modelling and simulation. KAUST users plan to target a range of applications, including the design of new materials for low-cost, high-performance solar photovoltaics. It will also be used in the areas of personal preventive health care, new drug discovery, increased hydrocarbon recovery with lower environmental and economic costs, and the use of genetic and genomic approaches to enhance plant tolerance to drought and resilience in desert environments.
Equipped with more than 2,800 NVIDIA Grace Hopper Superchips and tightly interconnected CPU / GPU accelerators, the Shaheen 3 supercomputer will enable the development of new and scalable technologies in core AI areas such as deep learning, enhanced learning, unified learning, visual computing, natural and language processing, as well as providing unique opportunities to scale up traditional high-performance computing workloads. The accelerator section of the GPU will facilitate the widespread use of applied AI in science and engineering applications, including computational chemistry, biology and materials science, which were previously futile due to the large-scale nature of the data sets produced and used in KAUST.
Over the coming years, applications will increase, with Shaheen 3 expected to deliver 100 petaflops / s performance and outstanding AI modeling capabilities.

Before you freak out about the term “autophagy, ” you should know that this process is the body ’ s way of cleansing itself and occurs spontaneously.
But you can also boost this process in your body in a few ways, to reap its many health benefits.
What is autophagy of the body?
In short, the term “self-eating ” consists of two words: auto and phagein, and this process is a mechanism of the body that occurs immediately from birth without conscious effort.
Colin Champ, an assistant professor at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, said: “Think of it as our body ’ s innate recycling program.
When in autophagy mode, body cells create membranes that find dead, sick or worn out cells, devour them and use the resulting molecules for energy or to make new parts of cells.
Benefits of autophagy
A 2012 study in mice found that autophagy can protect against:
- Cancer.
- Neurodegenerative disorders
- Infections
- Inflammatory diseases
- Aging
- Insulin resistance
Another study showed that removing the autophagy gene in mice caused weight gain, lethargy, high cholesterol and impaired brain function.
According to Timesofindia, “Autophagy makes us more efficient machines to get rid of defective parts, stop cancerous growth, and stop metabolic imbalances such as obesity and diabetes. ”
How can I increase autophagy?
Autophagy is a response to stress, so stimulating it requires you to put your body into some hardship, and basically you need to starve your cells of energy.
Once your body enters autophagy, it will begin to repair damaged cells and break down old ones for energy, and you can increase autophagy through exercise, intermittent fasting, or the keto diet.
The ketogenic state occurs when your body doesn ’ t have enough carbohydrates to burn for energy, so the idea is to reduce the body ’ s carbohydrates to low levels so that the body has no choice but to use fat for energy.
The keto diet is high in fat and low in carbohydrates, and can help people lose body fat while retaining muscle, fighting cancer tumors, reducing the risk of diabetes, and preventing brain disorders, according to some studies.
“Ketosis is like penetrating autophagy, and you get a lot of metabolic changes and benefits of fasting without actually fasting. ”
But it ’ s best to consult your doctor first before following the keto diet, especially if you have any health condition such as kidney or liver problems.
Intermittent fasting is another great way to induce autophagy, but to enter the autophagy phase through intermittent fasting you need to fast for at least 14 to 16 hours.

While exercise exhausts your muscles, especially intense workouts and weightlifting exercises, your body rushes to heal from them, and therefore regular exercise enhances your body ’ s self-cleansing process.

Transferring Human Brain Cells to Rats
New research shows that human neurons implanted in the brains of rats continued to grow, forming connections with the brain cells of animals and helping to guide their behavior, raising ethical and scientific questions as to whether it would result in a superorganism or an improved rat with unique abilities.
According to a study published in the journal Nature, clumps of lab-grown human brain cells were transplanted into the brains of newborn mice, showing that these cells grew and merged with rodent neural circuits, eventually making up about one-sixth of their brains.
The researchers say these animals could be used to learn more about human neurological and psychiatric disorders.
The team used organics made from skin cells.
These cells were synthesized into stem cells in the lab before being encouraged to form layers of cells similar to those found in the human cortex, the folded outer part of the brain that contains areas responsible for thought, vision, hearing, memory and sensing the environment, among other things.
This process took about two months in the lab.
The resulting three-dimensional organelles were then injected into the brains of day-old mice through an incision in the skull, the organelles were implanted into the sensory cortex, an area that plays a role in helping animals feel their environment.
Within four months, brain scans showed that the organelles had grown to about nine times their original size and made up about a third of the cerebral hemisphere.
The cells appear to have formed connections with mice ’ s brain cells and were integrated into brain circuits.
Stanford University ’ s Sergio Pashka said: “It ’ s just a very big step. ”
In another experiment, the team specifically fired human cells using optogenetics — a technique that involves shedding light on brain cells that have been genetically modified to respond to light.
By doing so, the researchers were able to influence how often the mice sought a reward.
Bashka hopes that studying human brain organelles in mice could help researchers understand human diseases.
In another experiment, his team created organelles using cells taken from people with Timothy syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that affects the brain and heart.
These neurons looked different from healthy cells, and they seemed to work differently as well.
The research team is currently testing potential new treatments for the syndrome in these mice.
But the more important question is, are mice with brain cells still mice?
The participating researchers believe they are, and Paschka says the animals showed no signs of enhanced cognition or any human-like behaviors.
Another co-researcher says the human brain is incredibly complex — far more so than rat brains, even with a fraction of human cells in it.
Julian Savulescu, a bioethicist at the National University of Singapore, who was not involved in the study, commented on the experiment, “It ’ s an important step forward in advancing toward [understanding] and treating brain diseases. ”
But evolution also raises ethical questions, he says, especially regarding what it means to “humanize ” animals.
He sees that mice, at least at the cellular level, are no longer fully mice.
However, Savulescu has no ethical concerns about the study, because only a small portion of the cells were transplanted and placed in a part of the brain that deals with sensing the environment, rather than consciousness.
But in the future, scientists should be aware of the potential effects of growing larger organoids in other areas of the brain, "it raises the possibility of creating an improved rat that may have greater cognitive abilities than the average rat," he says.

Fish are becoming more suicidal due to climate change.
Archival Image
A recent scientific study revealed serious risks to fish stocks in various seas and oceans around the world, as a result of climate changes, where greenhouse gas emissions lead to increased acidity of water, prompting fish to commit suicide, attracted to large predatory fish.
The study, conducted by a team of researchers at James Cook University in Australia, aims to assess the impact of greenhouse gases that cause climate change on the coral reef area off the coast of Papua New Guinea, in the southwest Pacific Ocean, where the region is witnessing volcanic activity.
The results of the study showed that the high rate of acidity in the ocean waters, as a result of the escalation of carbon dioxide from repeated volcanic activities below the depths, leads to the loss of species of fish, on which fishing activity depends, their ability to survive, making them easy prey for other predatory species.
The study, published on the site « Nature Climate Change », that fish in general can smell the smell of large predatory species, which helps them to get off track, but surprise that in the area under study, it turns out that fish are attracted to the smell of predatory species, making them easy prey.
Lead researcher Professor Philippe Mendai said the acidity effect of the water has also been shown to cause fish to wander aimlessly into the water and go to areas far from where they live, putting them at risk, where they are more likely to be attacked by predatory fish.
The main author of the study pointed out that these threats to fish are not limited to volcanic activities, noting that about 30% of the carbon dioxide emissions in the atmosphere are absorbed by water bodies, leading to increased acidity of the seas and oceans.
The researchers also warned that the acidity levels in the coral reef area in question have reached very high levels and are expected to spread to other areas, and may include the entire Pacific Ocean by the end of this century, as the phenomenon of climate change worsens.
The study concluded that fish that live for long periods of life exposed to high levels of carbon dioxide, could not cope with the changes caused by high acidity in the water, as a result of exposure to high levels of carbon emissions permanently.

12% of the total demand for fossil fuels from the aviation sector
2022 / 10 / 22 | 15: 16 - Source: Yes Iraq
(This is news from Iraq.)
YES IRAQ: FOLLOW
A virtual seminar hosted by the King Abdullah Petroleum Studies and Research Center (KAPSARC) discussed the drivers of increased energy demand in the aviation sector and the future of jet fuel.
The participants revealed that fossil fuels dominated the demand of the global aviation sector, accounting for about 12% of the total energy demand in the transport sector, second only to the road transport sector, noting that the traditional fossil fuels used in the road transport sector are being replaced by low-carbon alternatives.
The ICAO Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Plan for International Aviation has long-term objectives for the aviation industry, based on developments in aircraft technologies, operational and infrastructure improvements, and measures that include compensatory mechanisms, sustainable jet fuel and low-carbon jet fuel.
According to the seminar, the aviation sector transported more than $7 trillion in goods in 2019, in addition to transporting 4 billion passengers, as the pace of demand for aviation increased significantly in regional, local and international markets, creating about 70 million jobs in aviation and related industries in the world, but the pandemic caused the largest decline in the pace of demand in recent decades.
Before the COVID-19 pandemic, the aviation industry was characterized by affordable travel for consumers, leading to increased connectivity rates, while airlines made efforts to enhance efficiency through the passenger load factor, but it did not apply to cargo, noting that lower consumer prices increase efficiency and unit performance, i.e. lower emissions per passenger per kilometer.
They added that it is difficult for airlines to raise prices to increase revenues because the airline industry has become highly competitive even for routes they own, and the potential entry of new airlines and network structures puts more pressure on airlines, explaining that the pressure comes from rival airlines that go to the same destinations, but using alternative routes and as a result, competition in the aviation sector has intensified.
The participants pointed out that airlines aim to buy more airlines to control the market, avoid losing market share, and turn them into larger organizations using a variety of business models, noting that technical development, increased operational efficiency and the spread of alternative fuels in the future will play a critical role in creating more efficient aviation systems around the world. is an ongoing challenge in the years ahead.
They explained that the development of urban air mobility solutions through electric vertical take-off and landing technology of the future will depend to a large extent on the right policy framework being implemented.
They noted that the aviation industry and manufacturers are still working to address the current challenges associated with market evolution, new technologies and the use of fossil fuel-based fuels, and the deployment of non-fossil fuels and other alternative sources such as hydrogen and electric power, calling for policies and incentives to play a major role in supporting the global transformation of aviation to become more environmentally sustainable.
Participants stressed that the use of renewable energy at the stages of the low-carbon aviation fuel supply chain can reduce the carbon intensity of low-carbon aviation fuel, noting that this includes the use of renewable energy sources in oil fields and refineries and carbon capture and storage to reduce refinery emissions.
Recent studies of the world ’ s 9,000 oil fields and refineries at 500 refineries have shown that carbon intensity can be reduced by three factors: innovation-oriented policy formulation, the development and consumption of low-emission fuels, and the use of different technologies to reduce emissions.
Low-carbon jet fuel is at least 10% less carbon-intensive than commercial jet fuel.
They pointed out that the use of cooking oil as a biofuel for aircraft depends on the quantities used more than once, which may be limited availability, while electronic fuel has a low carbon intensity due to the level of emissions of commercial aircraft to zero in the combustion process, as well as the use of this type of fuel for renewable energy sources.
Participants noted that there is only one commercial technology for sustainable aviation fuel: the path of hydrogen-treated esters and fatty acids, so these esters will remain the main source of sustainable low-carbon aviation fuel over the next decade, while other technologies rely on facilities that are either under construction or at an early stage of commercial readiness.
Colloquium participants predicted that fully commercial technologies would be three to four times more expensive than the cost of the path of hydrogen-treated esters and acids.
While the price gap between sustainable jet fuel and conventional jet fuel is significant, the production of sustainable jet fuel through co-processing, which is not widely used in existing refineries, will become critical, particularly in areas where raw materials are available.
They pointed out that the main obstacle to sustainable aviation fuel, which prevents it from benefiting a real environment, is the way it is produced, pointing out that although sustainable aviation fuel is a key enabler to meet the industry ’ s emissions reduction aspirations, it helps the industry achieve the maximum reduction of carbon emissions.

On July 10, 2020, a Turkish court overturned a 1934 ministerial decision that turned Hagia Sophia into a museum, paving the way for it to be used again as a mosque after an 86-year hiatus.

Announcement

Europe is the most affected!

And then, globally, the second most affected region is the Mediterranean. ”
"In the Arctic, melting ice is contributing to this warming.
In the Mediterranean, the atmosphere is drier, so there is not enough evaporation to mitigate this warming that usually occurs. ”
The oceans shield the planet.
According to experts, the warming we see on land would be faster without the oceans, which absorb up to 90% of the excess heat in the atmosphere trapped by greenhouse gases.
Asked by Euronews about the effects that could result from repeated heatwaves in the Mediterranean, oceanographer Jean-Pierre Gattuso said:
“The main effect of marine heatwaves is the massive mortality of invertebrates, plants, molluscs, sponges and corals.
Between the surface and a depth of 50 meters there are many invertebrates and plants that are adversely affected and die. ”
Gattuso also stressed that “the ongoing negotiations at the COP27 summit are extremely important.
Scenarios predicted by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change show that if the Paris Agreement is implemented quickly and fully, we can stabilize temperatures and ocean acidification.
That doesn ’ t mean we ’ ll go back to the way it was before.
It means we can stop global warming and stop acidification. "
Those gathered at the summit know that the opportunity is coming to an end with regard to the goals of the Paris Agreement and limiting global warming to less than 2 degrees Celsius, and in the context of increasing greenhouse gas concentrations, emissions expert Claire Vesson says, “Unfortunately, greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere are still rising.
A recent estimate put the concentration of carbon dioxide at 416 parts per million.
This is higher than last year, and this is higher than in the history of human civilization.
“This is a very worrying trend, because as carbon emissions continue to rise, the effects of climate change will continue to worsen. ”
It's up to humans.
Fyson says that changing these data depends on the decisions that are made and the steps that will be implemented over the next 10 years.
“If we reduce emissions to zero, then yes, we will see stabilization in those concentrations and we will see a rise in temperature that starts to plateau and the impacts of climate change stop to get worse, ” she says.
“Recent assessments suggest that we ’ re actually going to be heading for about 2.4 to 2.8 degrees of warming.

Even with the rapid decline in emissions in the next few decades, some of the impacts of climate change will persist for centuries to come.
These include sea level rise and melting of the cryosphere.

Food spoiled by storage in the refrigerator
When we want to save food, the refrigerator is the first place that comes to mind.
However, the refrigerator is not always suitable for all foods.
Some of them can only be placed on the shelves.
Because storing some of them can produce mycotoxins, according to the Brightside website.
1. Avocado
Often when we buy avocados it is not quite ripe.
In order for them to mature, they should be placed at room temperature and not in the refrigerator.
Cooling is only necessary if the fruits are already ripe and you don ’ t want to eat them right now.
This is because once they are placed in the refrigerator they immediately stop ripening.
Avocado fruits take between two to four days to ripen, so it is best to leave them on the table.
After they are ready, they can be kept in the refrigerator for up to 7 days.
2 apples
Apples stay fresher at room temperature which can range from 30 to 35 degrees Fahrenheit (i.e. from about 1 ° C below zero to 2 ° C above zero) however a fresh vegetable drawer in the refrigerator can make apples fresh for longer.
But before storing it in the refrigerator, it should be placed in a plastic bag with small openings or alternatively can be covered with a wet paper towel to absorb the moisture of the refrigerator and if not done, the temperature and humidity level of the refrigerator will change the texture and taste of the apples.
3. Herbs
Herbs need to retain their moisture without being exposed to too much oxygen.
In order to properly store green herbs, they must be placed in a loose bag.
And if they have to be placed in the refrigerator, they should be completely covered with a wet paper towel.
Dried herbs are best stored in a jar, a sealed container, or a plastic bag with a zipper to keep air and oxygen away.
4. Watermelon
Watermelon stops ripening once picked and harvested, however, studies suggest that storing watermelon in the refrigerator may negatively affect its nutritional value.
At a temperature of 55 (about 13 ° C), watermelon retains more antioxidants for 14 to 21 days.
After cutting it, it can be put in a plastic bag with a zipper and kept in the refrigerator.
In this case, it should be noted that it is advisable to consume it within two to three days.
5. Bread
Bread in general is not a food that can be kept for a long time.
Keeping bread for a long time at home will spoil it or change its condition.

Explain why storms are increasing in the Southern Hemisphere
Science and Technology
Expressive Image
Copy Link https: / / www.rt.com / ubnt
For the first time, scientists at the University of Chicago have been able to explain the phenomenon of increased storm strength in the southern hemisphere compared to the strength of storms in the northern hemisphere.
According to the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), since they discovered South America, sailors have realized that storms in those regions are stronger than those in the Northern Hemisphere.
This is what the researchers were able to confirm by satellite, where the results of studies and follow-up showed that the strength of storms in the southern half is 24% stronger than the storms in the northern half.
But they could not determine the cause.
To identify it, the experts gathered comprehensive satellite data and follow-up results, as well as available theories, and combined them into a climate model.
They then omitted the different variables and determined the effect each had on storms.
Topography was the first variable: large mountain ranges obstruct the flow of air currents, reducing storms.
In the northern half there are many large mountain ranges.
When the researchers removed these chains in the model, half of the storm force difference between the two hemispheres disappeared.
The other half turns out to be connected to ocean currents: water moves around the globe like a slow but powerful conveyor belt.
It descends from the North Pole, passes through the ocean floor, rises near Antarctica, and then moves near the surface.
And that makes a difference between the two hemispheres.
When scientists removed this flow from the model, they noticed that the second half of the differences in storm intensity disappeared.
In addition, after analyzing follow-up data over recent decades, the researchers noted an increase in storm asymmetry compared to the 1980s.
That is, the southern hemisphere became more active, while the changes were minor, in the northern hemisphere.
According to the researchers, this is due to oceanic changes in the Southern Hemisphere, which are similar to those in the Northern Hemisphere.
But this effect in the northern hemisphere is offset by the absorption of sunlight due to melting sea ice and snow.

Is Biden ’ s diplomacy working in Africa?
Osman Mirghani
Posted in: Last Updated:
Reading mode
100% font size
Over the course of three days, the US-Africa summit called by the administration of President Joe Biden was held in Washington, and concludes today with many expectations and challenges for both sides.
The United States says it wants to build a strong partnership, and the summit is meant to show its “enduring commitment to Africa, ” while African leaders speak of their aspiration to build strong relationships“ beyond the politics of diktat. ”
What is no secret is that the summit comes in the context of America ’ s strategy to curb the Chinese and Russian influence that has grown dramatically on the African continent over the past two decades.
The Biden administration has been keen to invite all African countries, including some that have reservations about its policies, and has excluded only Sudan, Mali, Guinea and Burkina Faso because of the military coups that took place in them.
Africa is important in the context of the US-China competition for influence because it is the second largest continent after Asia, with a population of 1.4 billion people, 60 percent of the population is young people under the age of 25, a figure that is increasing.
U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris said that Africa is the fastest-growing continent in the world and is increasingly in need of education, technology and infrastructure, with a population increase that means a $2.1 trillion purchasing power for the global economy.
The question is, will America succeed in curbing Chinese influence in Africa?
It's certainly not going to be easy.
China has become Africa ’ s largest trading partner in the last decade.
According to official figures released by Beijing, the volume of its trade with Africa increased by 35 percent in 2021 to $254 billion, in addition to Beijing being the largest lender to African countries.
At a time when trade between the United States and Africa is estimated at $64 billion, placing America fourth in the list of trading partners with Africa.
While Western investments in the African continent appear slow and cautious, often tied to estimates and political factors, China is pouring huge money into African countries in the form of loans to finance massive infrastructure projects, from ports to roads and power plants, making it difficult for the United States and other Western countries to compete.
In its efforts today to make a strong return to Africa, what the administration hears most from African leaders is that they want from Washington a strategic partnership away from dictatorial politics, or, as Senegalese President Macky Sall, whose country holds the current chair of the African Union, they want a partnership “without anyone telling us what to do, or what not to do. ”
Many African governments may see China as comfortable in dealing because it does not interfere in their political affairs and does not raise issues of human rights and democracy with them.
But this does not negate that they also raise their concerns when their debt burdens accumulate and they are unable to pay, because China will not hesitate - as it has shown in several cases - to seize their resources or national assets such as ports and airports, in exchange for these debts.
Too often, loans have been squandered by waste, corruption, and lack of transparency and accountability, putting these countries at the mercy of creditor nations.
China, however, prioritizes its interests, which are acquiring natural resources and raw materials, while marketing its products, expanding and diversifying its trade so that it is not too dependent on trade with the West, amid the new Cold War on the international stage and the growing strategic conflict with America and the West.
Washington may not be able to keep up with Beijing ’ s massive infusion of money without monitoring or demanding transparency, but it appears to be working on several fronts to try to build strong ties with Africa.
Since the first day of the summit in Washington, the Biden administration has announced a series of decisions to emphasize its seriousness in building a new partnership strategy, including a $55 billion investment in Africa over the next three years in the areas of food security, education, health, environment, infrastructure and renewable energy.
To counter previous criticism that many of the recommendations and promises are not being implemented, Washington appointed former Assistant Secretary of State Johnny Carson, who has also served as ambassador to a number of African countries and in the Department of African Affairs at the State Department to follow up on the implementation of the decisions and initiatives emanating from this summit.
At the same time, Biden signed a resolution establishing a presidential advisory board to promote the involvement of African expatriates in the United States and to advise the White House on how to strengthen U.S.-African ties.
This suggests that the US administration is counting on a large role for expatriates and residents of its territory coming from Africa, who represent a large proportion of the African diaspora around the world.
At the same time, Washington seems interested in focusing on Africa ’ s youth, who represent the highest percentage of its population, whether by supporting education programs, training opportunities, or investments in areas to create employment opportunities for young people.
Washington is trying to distinguish its support and investments by asserting that, unlike China, it does not link its investments to the recruitment of American workers, for example, while China often brings its workers to carry out its projects.
The Biden administration was also keen to reaffirm its support for the African Union ’ s accession to the G-20, and for Africa to be given a permanent seat on the Security Council as part of the reforms that several countries are calling for in the structures and work of the United Nations.
These steps are important, but are they enough to restore momentum to U.S.-African relations?
Much will depend on the implementation of the decisions, on the steps America takes to strengthen relations, to develop trade cooperation and investments, and to show that it is adopting a new strategy of strong and sustained relations with African countries that have long complained of Washington ’ s neglect or fluctuating relations with the continent.
The administration of former President Barack Obama had shown similar enthusiasm to that of the Biden administration, and organized the first African-American summit in Washington in 2014, on the basis that those summits will continue periodically, which did not happen, but relations deteriorated under the administration of Donald Trump, who showed no interest in the African continent, and even showed clear contempt for it in some of his statements.
Africa is also waiting for Washington to help with debt relief, support development projects, grant tax concessions and exemptions for African exports, and obtain compensation for the damage caused to the continent by climate change.
In any case, international relations are always subject to calculations of interests, this applies to China as it does to America, and Africa cannot expect to receive free support, and if it wants to get rid of the pressure, its governments must better employ loans and aid in real development projects, and make better use of its resources.
The policy of borrowing to fill budget deficits, financing ill-conceived projects, and squandering money in the absence of transparency and widespread corruption is a disastrous recipe that has contributed to the impoverishment of Africa and undermined its stability.

Saudi authorities continue to discriminate against women as second-class citizens with an unchanging authoritarian guardianship system and strict disobedience laws and rules that restrict the rights of unmarried women.
Since Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman launched the so-called “social and economic reform ” dubbed Vision 2030 in April 2016, the status of women has changed dramatically, with the network seeing that some laws were in favor of women and others headed for the worse.
While women activists like Loujain al-Hathloul were jailed for three years following a drive for women to drive, the relevant legislation was changed in 2018 — and according to research firm Statista — within a year and a half, more than 175,000 women applied.
Driving license in Riyadh.

Lina al-Hathloul, the sister of women ’ s activist Loujain al-Hathloul, who is the head of communications and surveillance at the London-based ALQST Human Rights Organisation, said: “The regime of repression is still in place ” in Saudi Arabia.
Because of the male guardianship system, girls and women still rely on male guardian consent for most decisions.
In case of disobedience, these guardians, who could be fathers, husbands, brothers or sons, are entitled to be sent to so-called “care homes ” — forever, al-Hathloul said.
Moreover, this year, three court rulings starkly emphasized the Saudi ambivalence between men and women.

Verbal sexual harassment of a woman.

This came during the statements of the Minister of Environment to the media at the end of her inspection tour of environmental sanitation projects in companies operating in the oil sector in the Gulf of Suez, which is the first inspection tour of the Minister at the beginning of the new year 2023; to ensure compliance with the Environment Law No. 4 of 1994, as amended by Law No. 9 of 2009 and its executive regulations and their amendments.

NASA is working to design new, more fuel-efficient aircraft with Boeing
Thank you for reading the news about technology: NASA is working on designing new fuel-efficient aircraft with Boeing and now with details
CAIRO (Reuters) - NASA has announced that it will work with Boeing on a new type of fuel-efficient single-aisle aircraft for commercial use, with the aim of reducing fuel emissions and reducing the climate impact of aviation, according to theverge ’ s report.
“It ’ s also a climate agency, ” NASA Administrator Bill Nelson said at a press conference,“ NASA is monitoring the Earth from space — using tools like satellites to monitor global weather and water systems — and developing technologies to reduce carbon emissions.
But NASA is also developing aircraft, such as its X-57 Maxwell electric plane and Super Guppy transport plane, and that includes developing flight technologies that eventually make their way into the types of commercial aircraft that most of us use today.
"When you fly in any type of aircraft, you're surrounded by NASA technology," Nelson said, and advances in aircraft design such as winglets, small vertical extensions of wings, were created by NASA in the 1970s and are now ubiquitous on passenger planes.
The agency hopes its sustainable aviation project will deliver a similar kind of innovation in the form of a new wing structure called the voice-assisted wing, and will work with Boeing to design and build the new aircraft, which should be more fuel-efficient and can use up to 30% less fuel than current aircraft designs.
The concept is an aircraft with more efficient engines and wings that sit high on the fuselage and are longer and less wide, supported by a brace that comes from the bottom of the body, this creates less resistance, while both the wing and the brace provide lift power.
Bob Pierce, associate director of NASA's Flight Research Mission Directorate, said: "The aerodynamics of this type of configuration have already been known for a long time.
“If you increase the aspect ratio of a wing, it ’ s normal to lower that aircraft ’ s induced drag — drag from lifting, and we know that if we do that, you ’ ll get better aerodynamics, you ’ ll get less drag, and you ’ ll burn less fuel. ”
The challenge, in this case, is to create the desired structure for this wing shape without adding too much weight to the aircraft.
Boeing unveiled the first version of the concept in 2019, but it will take several years to integrate other technologies and move from demonstration to practically usable.
The idea is that unlike NASA ’ s supersonic X-59 QueSST, which is also currently under development but will never carry passengers, this will not only be an experimental aircraft.
NASA wants to develop a technology that can be used commercially, Nelson said, “This project aims to revolutionize the type of aircraft that the public frequently uses when flying in the sky. ”
NASA aims to launch its first prototype in 2028 and to be commercially used by 2030.
