US-China technology war threatens scientific progress
US-China technology war threatens scientific progress
The world is currently witnessing an escalating technological war between the United States and China, while Europe is also participating in it, but only timidly, as its efforts to maintain technological supremacy decline due to stagnation in this area.
As the major powers in that war seek to protect themselves from technological dependency, it could threaten the world ’ s progress and prosperity by fragmenting it into competing technological worlds.
Hiba Muhyi
German writer Wolfgang Hearn published a book in 2024 entitled “The Technological War between China and the United States and the European Position on Competition ”, in which he discusses the historical role of these major powers in supporting the march of technological progress, and the most important technological fields that are grappling with, especially quantum computing, artificial intelligence, biotechnology and others, as well as the dangers of this conflict and the feasibility of cooperation between powers in the technological field.
The book traces the knowledge and technological contributions of the United States, China and Europe, noting that Washington established modern global technological development when the Second Industrial Revolution began with the discovery of electricity and the Third Industrial Revolution with the introduction of computers.
This was followed by innovations such as the Internet and electronic chips.
According to a report published by the Future Institute for Advanced Studies and Research, this American success is due to the availability of elements of knowledge (universities and research bodies) and capital.
China contributed to historical technological development during the period (960 – 1279 AD) through the invention of paper, printing art, powder gunpowder and magnetic compass, followed by a rapid decline due to, inter alia, the Opium Wars, the end of the Empire, and civil wars, until China intensified efforts to achieve a slow recovery beginning in 1978, and then a strong rise during the last two decades.
Europe experienced the first industrial revolution a hundred years ago, as it pioneered natural sciences and medicine at the time, but there is now a marked decline in several technological areas when compared to Beijing and Washington, and this affected leading European industries, such as the automotive industry; where leading companies, such as Volkswagen, lag in the areas of autonomous and automated driving.
The book offers several technological areas in which conflicts between major powers arise, as follows:
Artificial Intelligence: Artificial intelligence applications aim to simulate the human mind in its patterns of thinking and processing of data, which makes the performance of complex tasks entrusted to it.
The United States provides support to companies involved in this field, resulting in the launch of ChatGT in 2022, which can be used to obtain high-quality and accurate answers on various topics.
China has banned the app and created its latest emulator, Ernie Bot, which was launched in 2023.
European efforts to invest in artificial intelligence appeared disappointing, with the German minister of research presenting a plan of action aimed at investing about 1.6 billion euros by 2025 in the field.
Semiconductors or electronic chips are used in various low-tech devices, from washing machines to missiles, a US invention that emerged in the 1950s, but two companies currently monopolize the field: Samsung in South Korea and TSMC in Taiwan, and Beijing, Washington and Europe cannot compete, at least in the near term.
Digital transformation: Digital transformation aims to embed technological technologies into business and social processes and interactions.
Washington and Beijing dominate this area, the first is the main founder of the four Internet giants Google, Apple, Facebook and Amazon, while the second contributed three rival giants, namely: Baidu, Alibaba and Tencent, while Europe is at the bottom of the list of leading companies such as: Zalando and Otto.
Quantum computing and quantum theory: The field of quantum computing is based on combining disciplines, such as computer science, physics and mathematics, using quantum theory to achieve sophisticated analytical processing of data that ordinary computers cannot process with the same speed and accuracy.
This contributes to breakthroughs in many fields, such as medicine, by making it possible to diagnose and treat diseases cheaply such as Alzheimer ’ s, epilepsy and Parkinson ’ s.
It also alters war strategies by creating a radar based on quantum technologies that can track and locate an adversary.
China tops the list of investors in this new technology.
According to U.S. consulting firm McKinsey, Chinese investment reached $15.3 billion in 2022.
It was followed by Europe with $7.2 billion and the United States with $3.7 billion.
• Energy generation: States are seeking to exploit technology to provide promising and safe ways to generate energy from it, nuclear fusion (the production of an artificial sun), which is based on the idea of merging two light atomic nuclei of hydrogen isotopes such as deuterium and tritium to produce one heavier atomic nucleus of a new element, helium, as happens on the surface of the sun.
This fusion is accompanied by the emission of four times the amount of energy produced by nuclear fission reactions.
However, there are obstacles to the actual implementation of this technology, such as the need to provide high temperatures of up to 100 million degrees Celsius to ensure that no long-term greenhouse gases or radioactive waste is produced.
Despite the difficulty of using fusion in power generation in the near future until 2050, countries are sparing no effort to develop this technology; China has developed several nuclear fusion reactors, the latest of which is the advanced experimental Tokamak designed to provide temperatures of up to 120 million degrees Celsius in 2022.
The United States is also interested in supporting related research and partnering with Japan this year to accelerate nuclear fusion development.
Europe is also making concrete efforts in this area through the joint European-Japanese project JT-60SA in 2022.
Biotechnology and medicine: applications of digital health care, genetic foods, and genetic scissors (Chris BR), which refers to a technique used to cut and modify DNA in a targeted way; genes can be inserted, removed, or disabled, whether in plants, animals, or humans; making its use ethically accountable, especially if applied to humans.
China uses it in agriculture to ensure the production of genetic foods and provide needed food for its people, while the United States approved the first treatment for sickle cell disease late last year, and the use of the technology in Europe faces strict legal rules according to the judgment of the European Court of Justice in 2018.
Space travel: The United States, China and Russia have paid special attention to space by sending missions and spaceflight to the Moon and Mars.
But competition between Washington and Beijing has now subsided as Moscow has been hit by financial crises.
The technological impulse of Washington and Beijing supports the economic impulse in this area: the need to mine space and reveal its resources that can be used, and for Europe it does not yet have an ambitious and practical policy to invade space.
Patents and people: The United States tops the list, with its universities, research centers and capital, while China filed nearly 3 million patents in 2023, of which only 10 percent were accepted.
Germany is a European power in the field of patents, but has been in decline recently, according to the German government ’ s report on the future strategy for research and innovation.
Because the human element is the most important link in the development of technology and the registration of patents, the major powers take several ways to prepare the human element, especially in the fields of mathematics, computer science, natural sciences and technology, but suffer a huge gap between supply and demand.
But China has two competitive advantages: huge numbers graduate each year from universities, and an active policy of sending students and scientists abroad to study and train and then calling them back when needed.
According to the book, the technological struggle between major powers cannot be confined to the former; there are other promising areas.
In the military field, combat drones and autonomous military robots can be built that make decisions on the battlefield autonomously without the need for human intervention.
At the urban level, smart cities can be created that rely on the Internet of Things to do their functions quickly and with a high degree of accuracy, such as facilitating traffic in those cities, rationalizing the energy used and environmental monitoring for any potential environmental risks.
Technology cooperation between China, the United States and Europe is crucial, especially in the circumstances of climate change, energy crises and migration, especially as the continuation of the technological war will lead to a global rise in prices, a decline in welfare rates and a decline in global total production by 7 percent, according to economists at the International Monetary Fund.
It is expected that the current technological war between Beijing and Washington will lead to technical fragmentation, as two different technological worlds, one American and the other Chinese, may arise, as has already happened with the Internet, resulting in increased costs for consumers and producers and a slowdown in the desired development to prevent the exchange of knowledge and technology between the two worlds.
While the writer understands the need for countries to protect their economies and technological progress from falling into the trap of dependence, the solution is to take an approach aimed at reducing those risks by diversifying relations with many international actors and forming alliances rather than cutting trade and technology ties, as happened between the United States and China in the trade war launched by former US President Donald Trump.

But entering any body of water below 15 ° C (59 ° F) – the temperature often matched by the UK ’ s oceans, rivers and lakes – without preparation can have serious and potentially fatal consequences.
Cold water shock is a term that refers to the sudden and drastic measures that the human body is exposed to when it is flooded with extremely cold water.
The reality of ice diving.
While these instinctive and involuntary measures are, in theory, designed to help keep us alive in freezing temperatures, they can put us at risk of death, the first thing that happens after the body is suddenly exposed to cold water is the sudden gasping to breathe where the body needs oxygen.

Hoff claims that it fights stress, helps people recover from exercise faster, improves sleep, helps achieve fitness goals and boosts creativity and mental abilities.
However, it can significantly increase the risk of cold water to the heart - and Hoff himself warns on his website that the two should not be combined.
Experts estimated that people with arrhythmias due to cold water were 1-3% more likely to develop up to 63% if they held their breath before being submerged.
Professor Mike Tipton of the University of Portsmouth, who has been studying the effects of cold water on the body for 40 years, told the Sunday Times that combining cold water with holding breath can be dangerous.
What are the deaths associated with cold water and breathing exercises?
One death that grieving families have linked to Hoff's techniques is the death of Kelly Ball, a mother of three, who collapsed and died in a river in Derbyshire after adopting the trend.
In April 2022, the 39-year-old joined her friend Victoria Fielding at the Jowett River in the Peak area for a two-hour class on the method, and shortly after entering the cold water she began complaining of headaches before collapsing.
She was pulled out of the water and another member of the class tried to resuscitate her, but she died at the scene.
Her investigation concluded that she had an undiagnosed heart condition and that cold water "may have had an impact on heart function and may be associated with sudden death."
A report to prevent future deaths was released to warn that some people may "suffer from a physiological adverse reaction to immersion in cold water" that may threaten their lives, another death in the same year was of a 17-year-old girl, Madeleine Metzger.
In August 2022, Madeleine drowned in her family ’ s swimming pool in California while trying, as her father believes, to imitate Hof ’ s method, her father, Rafael Metzger, found her face in the water and pulled her out, tried to perform CPR and call paramedics but sadly died.
It was later discovered that Madeleine had been looking for the method since 2020, and that she had downloaded the Hoff app just a month before her death.
Her father has filed a £67m lawsuit and is seeking an injunction to stop Hoff and his companies from promoting his breathing technique in California.
Metzger says Hoff was negligent in promoting his style and caused death by failing to properly warn people of the risk of drowning.
So what are the benefits of snorkeling in an ice bath?
Hoff and his family have built a multimillion-pound empire using his techniques, whose website claims it can help reduce inflammation, boost the immune system, relieve conditions like arthritis, lower blood pressure, burn fat, and help fight depression.
Studies show that swimming in cold water for 30 minutes can relieve symptoms of depression and anxiety by increasing the production of mood-boosting hormones such as dopamine.
Scientists think it ’ s related to how the brain swells during a particular type of breath, holding your breath while also trying to exhale aggressively, such as when swimming in cold water.
Some of the risks of immersion in cold water can be mitigated by slowly getting into the water and allowing your body to overcome the “shock ” of exposure.

Current AI voice technology can mimic human voices
How does the brain distinguish between the human voice and the voice of artificial intelligence?
Research shows that people struggle to recognize artificial intelligence from human voices, but the activities of their brains vary and respond in a unique way to each sound type.
People assume that happy voices are real voices, and neutral voices are artificial intelligence.
The sounds generated by artificial intelligence have become so advanced that they are almost indistinguishable from real human voices.
Fraudsters have used this technology to imitate the voice of a person who appears to be in distress to trick victims into transferring money, and while machine learning experts are developing technological solutions to detect AI sounds, little is known about the human brain ’ s response to these sounds.
People associate happiness with being more human-like.
Attempting to identify sounds
New research involved 43 people who were asked to listen to human voices and voices from artificial intelligence expressing five different emotions: neutrality, anger, fear, happiness, and pleasure.
They were asked to identify whether the sounds were artificial or human while studying their brains using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to detect changes in blood flow within the brain, indicating which parts of the brain were active.
Participants were also asked to rate the characteristics of the sounds they heard.
Participants correctly identified only 56% of human sounds and 50.5% of AI sounds, meaning they were equally bad at identifying both types of sounds.
People were more likely to correctly identify a “neutral ” voice as an AI voice, and for human happy voices, the correct identification rate was 78%, suggesting that people associate happiness with being more human-like.
Differences in brain response
Current AI voice technology can mimic human voices
Looking at brain imaging, the researchers found that human voices elicited stronger responses in brain regions associated with memory, while AI sounds elicited stronger responses in areas related to error detection and attention regulation.
The results showed that we are not very precise in determining whether sound is human or caused by artificial intelligence.
Participants also often expressed how difficult it was to distinguish between votes.
This suggests that current AI voice technology can mimic human voices to such an extent that it is difficult for people to reliably distinguish between them.
This increases the risk of using this technology to defraud and deceive people.
However, there are potential benefits as well, such as providing vocal replacements for people who have lost their natural voice.
Artificial intelligence sounds can also be used to treat some mental health conditions.

Health & Fitness
Tips for staying fit in your 60s
Thank you for reading about tips to keep fit in your 60s and now with the details
Cairo - Samia Sayed - written by Fatima Khalil
Wednesday ، 03 July 2024 11: 00 AM
As we age, our bodies undergo a range of changes that can affect our overall health, and maintaining optimal health becomes vital, from prioritizing fitness through regular exercise and a balanced diet to mental health care through social networking.
1.
Exercise regularly:
Regular physical activity is vital to maintaining muscle strength and flexibility and cardiovascular health, aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity each week, along with muscle strengthening exercises for two or more days a week.
Activities such as walking, swimming, cycling, and yoga can be particularly beneficial, and this helps maintain cardiovascular health, strength, and flexibility.
2.
Balance and Fall Prevention:
Combine exercises that improve balance and reduce the risk of falls, such as balance training.
3.
Management of chronic conditions:
If you have chronic conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes or arthritis, it is necessary to manage them effectively, it is necessary to follow the advice of a health expert, take prescribed medications as directed, make the necessary lifestyle changes and regular monitoring can help prevent complications and maintain your quality of life.
4.
Keep your body hydrated:
Dehydration can be a common problem as you get older, as your sense of thirst may diminish, aim to drink at least 8 glasses of water a day, and more if you are physically active or live in a hot climate.
Staying hydrated helps maintain energy levels, supports kidney function, and keeps your skin healthy.
5.
Stay Socially:
Engage in social activities and keep in touch with friends and family to prevent isolation and depression.
6.
Reducing Tension:
Practice mindfulness techniques such as deep breathing exercises to manage stress and anxiety.
7.
Cognitive stimulation:
Engage in mentally stimulating activities such as reading, puzzles or learning a new skill to maintain cognitive function.
8.
Regular health checks:
Schedule annual health checks to monitor your health status and detect any potential problems ahead of time.
9.
Tests and vaccinations:
Stay up to date with the latest recommended tests such as mammograms, colonoscopies, and flu vaccinations.
10.
Dental Care:
Maintain good oral health through regular dental check-ups and hygiene practices.
11.
Balanced diet:
Focus on unprocessed whole foods such as fruits, vegetables, whole grains and lean proteins to maintain a balanced diet.
12.
Adequate sleep:
Aim to get 7-8 hours of sleep each night to help regulate your physical and mental health.
By following these healthy habits, people in their 60s can maintain physical and mental health, reduce the risk of chronic diseases, and enjoy a healthy and active life.

The book is not just a theoretical exposition, it is a fictional journey into the quantum world, involving chapters with dramatic titles that rob the passionate reader: Into Quantum Land, Heisenberg Bank, Institute of Mechanics, Copenhagen School, Fermi-Boz Academy, Virtual Reality, Atoms in the Empty, Rutherford Castle, Particle Concert Masquerade, and the City of Experimental Physics Games.
Quantum Alice is similar to the Alice created by the novelist Lewis Carroll (who had an in-depth experience in mathematics).
It is a novel whose protagonists are electrons, neutrons, protons, photons, and quarks.
Alice goes to the Quantum Country — an entirely new version of Wonderland, smaller than an atom — and each landmark she frequents there illustrates a different aspect of quantum theory; there Alice encounters a number of extraordinary characters, through which she learns the uncertainty principle, wave functions, Pauli principle, and other concepts. Baffling, with a new intake that makes them all easy to absorb.
Along the same lines, Dan Brown introduces elements of particle physics and electronic engineering into his novels, as shown in The Lost Symbol and The Origin.
Braun blends scientific facts and literary fiction to create interesting worlds that help readers explore these fields without feeling overwhelmed; in Angels and Demons, Braun offers particle physics in an exciting way, tackling the story of antimatter smuggling, which prompts the reader to dive into this complex field of science, in an interesting narrative that highlights the challenges and adventures associated with this science.

I feel very grateful for this type of novel and its authors as much as I am for scientists and their discoveries, and I hope that it will be more popular in our Arab societies, whether by specialists in the scientific field or others, as a space for fun and learning.

What science fiction novelists do in their series is try to shift one ’ s mind from the superficial, fragile, transitory levels of thought to the higher horizons, which may seem invisible or intangible to many; understanding the basics is the foundation of every sober science, the necessary first step to contribute to intellectual and societal advancement, and not to dwell in the corners of indifference away from the scientific revolutions around us.
I feel very grateful for this type of novel and its authors as much as I am for scientists and their discoveries, and I hope that it will be more popular in our Arab societies, whether by scientific professionals or others, as a space for fun and learning, to turn on the disrupted senses, and to take a look at the worlds around us.

Fans of classic films are now able to revive the voices of their late stars thanks to a new and controversial technology.
The British company Eleven Labs, launched by two Polish entrepreneurs, announced the development of an artificial intelligence tool capable of cloning the voices of late movie stars to be used to record audiobooks, articles and electronic documents.
Scary technique.
The new technique is based on the use of "generative" artificial intelligence models that are trained using real voice recordings of actors.
These models are able to analyze the acoustic patterns and recognize the subtleties that characterize the sounds of these stars, and then use this data to produce new recordings that are accurate and realistic.
Reviving the voice of Judy Garland
Judy Garland, best known for her timeless performance of "Somewhere Over the Rainbow" in the 1939 film The Wizard of Oz, was one of the first names to use the technique to revive her voice.
Lisa Minnelli, daughter of Judy Garland, expressed her delight at the move, noting that “it ’ s exciting to see our mother ’ s voice available to countless millions of people who love her. ”
Collaborating with celebrity heirs
The British company not only limited itself to Judy Garland, but also reached deals with the heirs of Sir Laurence Olivier, James Dean, and Burt Reynolds.
These deals allow fans of these stars to listen to audiobooks, novels and articles recorded with their voices.
Controversy and fears
Besides the enthusiasm aroused by this technique, there are also many concerns.
Last year, Hollywood saw a 118-day strike by actors who feared movie studios would replace them with technology.
These concerns are not unfounded, as the technology clearly demonstrates the ability of artificial intelligence to imitate human voices with astonishing realism.
Other uses of artificial intelligence in music
The initiative is part of a wider wave of artificial intelligence in the music and entertainment industry.
For example, Paul McCartney and film director Peter Jackson used an AI tool to isolate John Lennon's voice from an old recording, allowing them to finish "The Beatles' Last Song."
The live performances also saw the use of holographic technology to revive the performances of Michael Jackson and rapper Tupac.
Continuous development
Eleven Labs, founded by Matty Staniszowski and former Google engineer Piotr Dabkowski, has been a huge success and has raised millions of pounds, raising its value to more than $1 billion (£783 million).
The company also offers a wide range of other synthetic sounds, such as “middle-aged American male ” and“ optimistic millennials. ”
A controversial future.
As for the future of this technology, the question remains: will it still be a way to revive the legacy of late artists or will it spark further debate about the impact of technology on art and creativity?
It seems that artificial intelligence will continue to advance, which will allow us to rethink the concept of originality and creativity in the digital age.

The UK ’ s largest public sector experiment to test work four days a week has delivered tremendous benefits as fewer waste pickers quit, there were faster planning decisions, and problems were addressed faster, independent research has found.
Research revealed that South Cumbridgeshire County Council ’ s experience of a shorter work week led to performance improvements in 11 out of 24 districts, little or no change in 11 districts and performance deterioration in two districts, according to a productivity analysis before and during a 15-month trial by academics at Cambridge and Salford Universities.
The experiment by the Liberal-Democratic-controlled authority drew angry reactions from the Conservative government, with one minister asking the region ’ s leader, Bridget Smith, to “terminate your experiment immediately ” and complaining that it would not give value for money to local taxpayers.
Former Conservative MP Anthony Brown, who was defeated by the Liberal Democrat in last week's general election, attacked the experiment as an "ideological crusade".
The multi-year study of the experiment, which included about 450 office employees as well as waste collectors, found:
The staff shift-rate decreased by 39%, helping to save £371,500 per year, mostly from agency staff costs.
Regular family planning applications were decided about a week and a half earlier than usual.
Key planning implementation decisions are almost 15% completed within the correct timeline, compared to the previous one.
Reduced time taken to process changes in housing benefit claims and council tax benefit claims.
On the negative side, rental collection for Council housing deteriorated slightly, although this was due to the cost-of-living crisis.
The speed of rehabilitation of empty council houses decreased slightly, from 28 to 30 days on average.
The results were adjusted to match the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Joe Ryle, director of the 4 Days a Week campaign, said the results herald “a great opportunity for councils and organisations across the public sector to start planning for a four-day work week. ”

Decline in the amount of dust in the atmosphere by 2023
Every year, about 2,000 million tons of dust enter the atmosphere, "blocking the sky and damaging air quality" in areas thousands of kilometers apart.
(Getty)
The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said Friday that the amount of dust in the atmosphere fell slightly in 2023, warning that environmental mismanagement increases the risk of sand and dust storms.
Every year, about 2,000 million tonnes of dust enter the atmosphere, "blocking the sky and damaging air quality" in areas that may be thousands of kilometres apart, but also affecting economies, ecosystems, weather and climate, the UN agency warned.
But in 2023, the average concentration of surface dust was slightly lower than in 2022, mainly due to lower dust emissions in North Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, northern India, central Australia, the Iranian Plateau and northwest China.
However, the UN agency explained in a report released on the occasion of World Day against Sand and Dust Storms on July 12 that “annual average surface dust concentrations over West Central Asia, Central North China and southern Mongolia were higher in 2023 than in 2022. ”
The heaviest sand storm in 2023, according to the World Meteorological Organization, was the one that swept through Mongolia and northern China in March, and whose violent winds and dust gave the sky a worrisome orange color.
The organisation said this had "led to a dramatic deterioration in air quality" in some areas, in excess of "9,000 micrograms per cubic metre".
According to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), “sand and dust storms have significant impacts on the environment, economy and health, ” and“ poor land and water management exacerbates the problem. ”
Secretary General of the World Meteorological Organization Celeste Saolo said: “Scientific data indicate that human activities affect sandstorms and dust storms, for example, rising temperatures, drought and increased evaporation lead to a decrease in soil moisture. ”
But “not all the news is bad, ” the agency said, noting that“ the accuracy of monitoring and forecasting has improved in recent years, ” and that the transportation of sand across oceans has had some positive aspects.

Al-Tuwaijri said: The Kingdom adopts the principles of equality, dialogue, cooperation, neutrality, objectivity and transparency, which the Kingdom seeks to be a basic pillar and a common ground for any interaction and joint action between countries in the field of human rights.
The President of the Human Rights Commission delivered the speech of Saudi Arabia at the Human Rights Council in Geneva, discussing the most prominent reforms and developments achieved in her country in the field of human rights and related to the topics of recommendations submitted to it.
She added that more than 150 legislative, institutional, judicial and procedural reforms and developments have been achieved since the adoption of Vision 2030, and these reforms have not stopped even during the circumstances that hit the world, represented by the Coronavirus (COVID-19).
The Kingdom's efforts have shifted from commitments to best practices in the field of human rights, through its own experiences, stemming from its established values, the will of its leadership, and the awareness of its society, in addition to sharing experiences with others.
In light of the Kingdom's belief in the principle of integral equality between men and women and that the integration of the relationship between men and women is an ideal way to promote and protect human rights, including women's rights and eliminate discrimination against them, its regulations derived from Islamic law have adopted the principle of ensuring equal opportunities and reducing inequalities by eliminating discriminatory practices and promoting appropriate legislation, policies and procedures in this regard.
The Kingdom's regulations do not contain any distinction, exclusion or restriction that results in the weakening or thwarting of women's recognition of human rights and fundamental freedoms in all fields.
Equality between men and women in the areas of human rights is absolute, such as the right to work, education, health, economic rights, and others.
In an effort to strengthen this trend, the Kingdom has issued and amended several laws, policies and regulations that support equal opportunities and reduce inequality; among them, several reforms that empower women, which exceeded 50 reforms, and allow them to participate fully and effectively in various fields, including the establishment of the Center for Gender Balance.
The Kingdom has promulgated the Law on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, which aims to protect and promote their rights and ensure their equal access to all services.
It promulgated a system of rights and care for older persons, which seeks to enable them to live in an environment that preserves their rights and dignity, organizes and implements appropriate programmes for them, and rehabilitates facilities to suit their needs.

Aware of the consequences of "trafficking in persons", which is the use, attachment, transfer, harbouring or reception of a person for the purpose of abuse, the Kingdom has paid great attention to this issue and has worked to develop its legal and institutional structure.
It has also strengthened the prosecution aspect through the establishment of specialized prosecution offices in all branches of the Public Prosecution to investigate these cases, and judicial chambers in the courts of first instance and the courts of appeal to hear cases of trafficking in persons.
To promote this policy, the Kingdom has formed a committee to combat trafficking in persons within the Human Rights Commission, comprising the Ministries of the Interior, Foreign Affairs, Justice, Human Resources and Social Development, Information, Public Prosecution, Education, Health and Human Rights.
Its functions include coordinating with the competent authorities for the return of the victim to his or her country of origin in the State to which he or she is a national, or to his or her place of residence in any other State if he or she so requests, and recommending that the victim remain in the Kingdom and regularize his or her status so as to enable him or her to work if necessary.
In addition to the legal system, the Kingdom has acceded to a number of international conventions and protocols, signed several memorandums of cooperation with relevant international organizations and bodies, in addition to local cooperation between the Human Rights Commission, government agencies and civil society organizations to strengthen efforts to prevent and combat trafficking in persons and take national measures to counter such crimes.
These regional conventions and instruments include the Arab Protocol to Prevent and Combat Human Trafficking, the Arab Charter on Human Rights, the Arab Convention on Combating Transnational Organized Crime 2010, and the Arab Comprehensive Strategy to Combat Human Trafficking Crimes.
Reference is also made to the international conventions and instruments to which the Kingdom has acceded, including the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime of 2000, the Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, Especially Women and Children, and the United Nations Global Plan of Action to Combat Trafficking in Persons 2010.

As Chairman of the 14th Summit of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), Saudi Arabia has strengthened its commitment to promoting human rights in the Islamic world, strengthened international cooperation in this regard, and addressed pressing humanitarian issues.

“When the victim hears the voice or watches a video of a friend or family member, the scam becomes more believable. ”
Erin Corpuz
Avoid questions that answer “yes ” or“ no. ”

She told the Khaleej Times: “Be careful if you get a call from an unknown number, especially if the caller starts a conversation with questions that require a yes or no answer. ”
How do fraudsters use this technique?
Corpuz explained this by saying, “Fraudsters can initiate calls using automated chat software, and when the software confirms the transaction request with a question:“ Would you like to start the payment process?
Is that true? "
Here, scammers can use the answer recorded as “yes ” or“ no. ”
So, avoid responding with affirmations like “yes ” or“ no ” to unknown callers.

“The fraudster will say, ‘ The first numbers of your Emirates ID are 784-19 and then …? ’ ”
Note that the fraudster is trying to make you fall into the trap by presenting the remaining numbers of your Emirates ID card, once they convince you that it is legitimate, they can then implement their technique.
Most of the phishing callers also pretend to be from banks, central banks, police and service companies. ”
What should you notice?
J.D. Ackley, CEO of Raizor, which specializes in deploying interactive AI services, told Khaleej Times: “There are things to watch out for, but first, be aware of any unwanted calls.
“Usually scammers will look for any reason why you might respond to a call from them and their hypothesis will be general and they will focus on the things you mentioned, because robots are programmed to respond based on your responses. ”
“Fraudsters always have a vague idea of your demographics and nothing is clear and specific, except what you tell them, if they ask investigative questions about your identity or habits, be careful and ask them why they need to know. ”
J.D. Ackley
The second thing to be careful about is asking for payment on unusual terms.
Akli said: “The legitimate company will not ask for payment of any kind of gift card or money transfer. ”
Akli, a veteran call center expert for more than 25 years, added: “Finally, if this is something you really need to address, ask for a number to call back and tell them you ’ ll call them back.

Don't be distracted.

Explore the possibilities of time travel.
Fact or science fiction?
Time travel: scientific and literary theories that refute or confirm the idea
News from Libya 24
Time travel is an idea found in science fiction and supported by some physical theories.
Black holes and wormholes are key to understanding the possibility of time travel.
The ethical dimensions of time travel address its effects on society and history.
Scientific literature offers a fantastical but airtight conception of time travel.
Time travel is an idea that has long fascinated scientists and writers alike.
This concept has long been the focus of scientific literature and fiction, but it is no longer just fiction but has become a serious topic in modern scientific studies.
In this article, we will review the theories of modern physics about time travel, the evidence that supports or disproves its feasibility, take a look at the ethical and social dimensions of this idea, and review how the scientific literature has addressed this topic.
Modern physics theories about time travel
Scientific theories dealing with time travel are mainly divided into two parts: the first is based on Albert Einstein's theory of relativity, and the second is based on quantum mechanics.
Theory of relativity and black holes
Einstein's theory of relativity is one of the scientific foundations that provides a theoretical framework for time travel.
The theory talks about time dilation and the effect of gravity on time.
Black holes, which represent massive concentrations of gravity, are key to understanding the possibility of time travel.
According to some scientists, black holes can create wormhole tunnels that connect different time points.
In relativity, the effect of time deceleration by approaching the velocities of light is known as the phenomenon of "temporal expansion."
The closer we get to the speed of light, the more time collides with respect to the moving person compared to the stationary person.
This theory provides a basis for the idea of future travel, where a person traveling at close to the speed of light can return to Earth after a few years to find that time has passed slowly for him and fast for people on Earth.
Quantum Mechanics
Quantum mechanics, on the other hand, introduces new and unfamiliar concepts related to time travel.
Quantum theory talks about the existence of parallel universes and multiple possibilities of events, which opens the door to the idea of moving between these universes.
One of the theoretical frameworks used to explain quantum phenomena is the plurality of worlds, where the theory assumes that every probability of an event actually happens in a parallel universe.
This theory posits the possibility of traveling between these multiple worlds, where time travel can be just a transition between these parallel universes.
Literature and science fiction
Time travel has always been a popular topic in literature and science fiction.
One of the most famous novels on the subject is The Time Machine by Herbert George Wells, in which the novel depicts how man can travel to the future or the past using a time machine.
Other writers, such as James Click, have approached the idea from a scientific perspective and put forward interesting theories about the possibility of time travel.
In The Time Machine, Wells describes how time travel can reveal the evolution of humanity and the effects of time on society.
This novel is a classic that has inspired many writers and scientists to think about the possibility of time travel.
Other novels, such as “Nervous Time ” by Philip Dick and“ A Double History ” by Stephen King, deal with time travel from different angles, examining the effects of time travel on individuals, communities, and history.
Scientific experiments and hypotheses
So far, scientists have not been able to conduct practical experiments that confirm the possibility of time travel.
But scientific hypotheses still exist.
One of these hypotheses relates to black holes and time tunnels that connect different time points.
If scientists can prove the existence of time tunnels, this could be the first step towards achieving time travel.
Experiments such as the famous CERN experiment with the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) are aimed at a deeper understanding of quantum mechanics and relativity.
Research conducted there may provide new evidence to support or deny the possibility of time travel.
Scientists are exploring elementary particles and fundamental forces that may be key to better understanding time and space.
Ethical and social dimensions
Time travel is not just a purely scientific matter, it carries with it great moral and social dimensions.
What would happen if man could go back to the past and change the course of history?
How can this affect the present and the future?
These questions are widely debated among scientists and philosophers.
An ethical dimension of time travel is the concept of “time paradox, ” where change in the past can create time discrepancies that lead to unexpected results.
For example, if someone goes back to the past and kills their grandfather before they meet their grandmother, that person will never be born, creating a complex time paradox.
Social Dimensions
Socially, time travel can lead to drastic changes in the structure of society.
It can lead to conflicts over who has the right to time travel and who can benefit from this technology.
This may create new social inequalities and reshape political and economic forces.
CONCLUSION
In the end, the question of the possibility of time travel hangs between reality and fiction.
While physical theories offer some hope for the realization of this dream, practical scientific evidence remains elusive.
Scientific literature offers us fantastical but compelling insights, prompting us to think deeply about what the future could be if we could navigate through time.
The big question remains: Can humans travel and travel through time?
Maybe the future holds the answer.

Loss of memory loss
By Michael C. Levin, MD, College of Medicine, University of Saskatchewan
Reviewed first spring 1445
Memory loss can be a symptom of brain dysfunction and is one of the most common reasons people, especially adults, visit a doctor.
Family members sometimes notice and report memory loss.
The most common concern for a person, family members, and doctors is whether memory loss is the first sign of Alzheimer ’ s disease, an advanced and incurable form of dementia (a type of brain disorder) where people with dementia lose the ability to think clearly. Usually early.
Did you know...
Most people with poor memory don ’ t usually have dementia.
Memories can be stored in short-term or long-term memory, depending on their type and importance to the person.
Short-term memory holds a small amount of information that a person temporarily needs, such as a list of things to buy at the grocery store.
Long-term memory, as its name suggests, stores memories (such as a person ’ s high school name) for a long time.
Short-term or long-term memory is stored in different parts of the brain.Long-term memory is stored in a number of areas of the brain.One part of the brain (the hippocampus) helps sort out new information, linking it to similar information already stored in the brain.This process converts short-term memories into long-term memories. It's about to become long-term memories.
Causes of memory loss
Common causes
The most common causes of memory loss are
Age-related memory changes (most common)
• Simple cognitive impairment
• Dementia
• Depression
Age-related memory changes (called age-related memory impairment) refer to the slight natural decline in brain function that occurs with age. [1] Most adults have some memory problems. [2] Recovering or remembering new things, such as the name of a new neighbor or how to use a new computer program, takes longer. But for them, unlike those with dementia, the ability to do everyday activities or think doesn ’ t wane.These people usually remember things when given enough time, although sometimes it happens later than the right time. Early Alzheimer's.
Simple cognitive impairment is an inaccurate term used to describe impairments in mental function that are not severe enough to affect daily functioning.
Memories are actually lost, and it ’ s not just slow recall, as happens in people with age-related memory changes.People with mild cognitive impairment have trouble remembering recent conversations and may forget important dates or social events, but they always remember past events.
Their attention and ability to perform daily activities are not affected, but more than half of people with mild cognitive impairment develop dementia within 3 years.
Dementia is a much more serious decline in mental function.
Memory loss, especially for recently acquired information, is often the first symptom, and it worsens over time.People with dementia can forget whole events, not just details.
• Difficulty remembering how to do things they ’ ve done so many times before, and how to get to places they ’ ve often been
• Do not continue to perform tasks that require a lot of steps, such as adhering to a prescription
• Forgetting to pay bills and keep appointments
They forget to turn off the stove or close the house when they leave, or take care of a child left in their care
But as dementia worsens, unlike those with age-related memory changes, they become unaware of their memory loss; they often deny that they have such loss or impairment.
Finding the right word, naming things, understanding the language, and doing, planning, and organizing daily activities are all the more difficult.
People with dementia become lost, do not know the time or even the year or where they are, and their personalities can change, as they may become more irritable, anxious, falsely (aggressive), stubborn or destructive.
There are a number of forms of dementia, but Alzheimer ’ s is the most common condition, and most forms of dementia gradually worsen until a person dies.
Some conditions that increase the risk of cardiovascular disorders (such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol levels and diabetes) seem to increase the risk of dementia.
Depression can cause a type of memory loss (called pseudodementia), similar to dementia.
Determining whether dementia or depression is the cause of memory loss can be difficult, but people with depressive memory loss, unlike people with dementia, recognize and complain about their memory loss. Many), lethargy or lack of appetite.
Stress can interfere with the formation and retrieval of memories, which preoccupies people to some degree, thus preventing them from paying attention to other things.But, in some cases, it enhances memory, especially when the intensity is light or medium and does not last long.
The less common cause.
Many disorders can cause mental function to deteriorate into a dementia-like condition.
Some of these disorders may be corrected with treatment. They include:
Other disorders can only be partially reversed; how much can be corrected depends on how much tissue is damaged.
In people with these disorders, treatment can sometimes improve memory and mental functions.If the damage is more extensive, treatment may not improve mental function, but it can often prevent further deterioration.
Memory is affected when delirium occurs, but amnesia is not the most obvious symptom.
Instead, people with delirium experience severe cases of mental confusion, confusion, and disconnection.
Severe alcohol abstinence (delirium tremens), severe bloodstream infection (sepsis), hypoxia (which can be caused by pneumonia) and a number of other disorders cause delirium, similar to the use of illicit drugs.
Assessment of memory loss
When assessing memory loss, doctors first determine whether the cause is delirium or another (treatable) reversible cause.
Doctors then focus on determining whether memory deficits are caused by natural age-related changes in the brain, mild cognitive impairment, depression, or early dementia.
Warning signs
Some symptoms are a concern in people with memory loss, such as:
• Difficulty performing normal daily activities
difficulty paying attention and fluctuations in the level of consciousness - symptoms that indicate delirium
depressive symptoms (such as loss of appetite, suicidal thoughts, difficulty sleeping, slowing speech and general activity)
When to see a doctor
People who show warning signs should see a doctor and should see a doctor immediately if they do.
They are unable to pay attention and appear to be in a state of intense mental confusion, lack of concentration and confusion (disorientation) - symptoms that indicate delirium
• Have depression or think of harming themselves
have other symptoms that indicate a problem with the nervous system, such as headaches, difficulty using or understanding language, tardiness, vision problems, or dizziness
Those who do not have warning signs, but are concerned about their memory or have difficulty performing basic daily activities should contact their doctor.The doctor determines how quickly a person should check, based on other symptoms and the severity of these symptoms.
What's the doctor gonna do?
Doctors inquire about a person's symptoms and medical history; they then conduct a clinical examination.
The presence of a family member is helpful, as people with memory difficulties may not be able to accurately describe their symptoms.The results of the medical history and clinical examination often indicate the cause and the tests that may be necessary (see table of some causes and features of memory loss).
Doctors often talk to the person and their family members separately, because family members may not feel free to explicitly describe the symptoms in the person's presence.
Doctors ask specific questions about memory loss or lack:
The types of things a person forgets (e.g., whether a person forgets or loses words or names)
When did memory problems begin?
What if memory loss is getting worse?
How memory loss affects a person ’ s ability to perform at work and at home
Doctors also inquire about other symptoms, such as difficulty using or understanding language and changes in eating, sleeping or mood habits.
They ask about all the disorders a person has, all medications, illegal drugs, over-the-counter medications, and supplements the person is taking to check for possible causes.Doctors also ask the person about any unusual eating habits.
Information about a person ’ s education, functions, and social activities can help doctors better assess their previous mental function and measure the degree of the problem.
During a clinical examination, doctors evaluate all body systems, but focus on the nervous system (neurological examination), including mental function (mental state tests).
In mental status tests, people are asked to answer questions or perform specific tasks to assess various aspects of mental function, such as:
Finding the time, place, and person: Identify the current date, place, and people.
Attention: Repeat a short list of words.
• Focus: Spelling the word “world ” backwards or repeating the phone number in two directions, naturally and vice versa.
Short-term memory: Recover a short list of words after a few minutes.
Long-term memory: Answer questions about events from the distant past.
Using language: naming common objects and body parts, and reading, writing, and repeating certain phrases.
Ability to understand spatial relationships: copying simple and complex structures (e.g. using cubes), drawing a clock, a cube, or a house.
These tests also assess abstract thinking, comprehension, the ability to follow orders, solve mathematical problems, ‘ illness perception ’ and mood.
TABLE
Exams
Doctors can usually determine if the cause is age-related changes, mild cognitive impairment, or early dementia, based on the type of memory loss and associated symptoms.
However, when the diagnosis is unclear, neuropsychological tests can provide more information.These tests are similar to mental state tests, but are more detailed.
Full tests can take hours.
These tests should be performed by a trained or licensed psychiatrist or psychiatrist with amnesia.These tests may not be useful for people over the age of 65.
If doctors suspect dementia or detect any abnormalities during a neurological exam, they usually perform magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or computed tomography (CT) if MRI is not available to check for any abnormalities, such as brain tumor, hypotensive hydrocephalus, and damage from a head injury. cerebral.
Doctors may also conduct blood tests to measure levels of vitamin B12 and thyroid hormones to determine whether vitamin B12 deficiency or thyroid disorder caused memory loss.
When a brain infection is suspected, doctors usually perform a spinal tap (lumbar puncture) to draw samples from the fluid around the brain (cerebrospinal fluid) and analyze them.
Treatment of memory loss
Treating any disorders that contribute to memory loss can help restore memory; for example, vitamin B12 deficiency is treated with B12 supplements, and hypothyroidism is treated with thyroid hormone supplements.
For depression, treatment includes medication, psychotherapy, or both.
Doctors choose to use antidepressants that do not aggravate memory loss, such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). To treat hypotensive hydrocephalus, a shunt can be placed through a surgical procedure to drain excess fluid from the periphery of the brain. She's on other meds.
If the only reason is age-related memory changes, doctors assure people that the problem is not serious, that these changes do not mean that mental function will decrease significantly, that there are ways to compensate for the loss, and perhaps improve mental function (see Basics for Older People).
General measures
General health measures are often recommended for people worried about memory loss:
• Exercise constantly
A healthy diet that includes eating plenty of fruits and vegetables
• Getting enough sleep
• Avoid smoking
• Reduce the use of alcohol or other substances (such as marijuana)
• Participate in stimulating social and intellectual activities
• Perform regular check-ups
• Avoiding exposure to high levels of psychological distress
• Protect the head from injury
These measures, along with controlling blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar levels, tend to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disorders.Some evidence suggests they may reduce the risk of dementia, but this effect is uncertain.
Some experts recommend that:
Learning new things (such as a new language or playing a new musical instrument)
doing mental exercises (such as memorizing lists, solving word puzzles, playing chess, bridge, or other games with strategy)
• Reading
• Working on the computer
• Doing manual work (such as sewing and sewing)
• Use tags to help remember and organize things
These activities can maintain or improve mental function, perhaps because they strengthen the connections between nerves.
Stronger connections between nerves help slow the decline of mental function caused by changes in the brain, and thus help to compensate for this deficiency.
Medications
For dementia, medications called cholinesterase inhibitors (such as donepezil, galantamine, and rifastigmine) may be used, especially in people with Alzheimer's disease or Lewy body dementia.
These medications may temporarily and slightly improve mental function in some people, including memory.
Another type of medication, memantine, may also be useful, and can be used with a cholinesterase inhibitor.
Adukanumab is used to treat Alzheimer's disease, but there are many experts who disagree on who should use the drug or even whether the drug should be used in the first place.
Lycanimab and Donimab are newer drugs that may be used in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.
Mild cognitive impairment can be treated with donepezil, a medication used to treat Alzheimer's disease.
This medicine may temporarily improve memory, but it appears to be of little use.
SAFETY AND SUPPORT MEASURES
There is no treatment that can restore mental function or completely stop the deterioration of dementia.
Dementia treatment focuses on keeping the person safe and providing support when their condition deteriorates.
If memory loss is relatively severe, or if family members are concerned about a person ’ s safety, the person ’ s home can be evaluated by physical or professional therapists who can recommend ways to prevent falls and other accidents, and may suggest preventive measures, such as hiding knives, disconnecting the stove and hiding car keys.
A supportive environment is characterized by the following characteristics:
• Promote frequent conversion (e.g., through large calendars and clocks).
• The public atmosphere should be cheerful and bright.
• Follow a regular routine.
Provide some stimuli (such as television or radio) and fun activities.
Eventually, you may need a housekeeper, a home health assistant, or you may need to move into a one-story house, a life support facility, or a skilled diagnostic facility.
Some of the key things for seniors: poor memory
Some memory problems begin to appear in most people as they get older.
Memory impairment is usually caused by normal age-related brain changes that do not lead to dementia.
Understanding such changes can reduce anxiety, and in doing so help older people cope and compensate.
Estimates of the number of people with mild cognitive impairment vary, but are common.
Some studies suggest that 7% of people develop it by the age of 70, and 25% of people develop it after the age of 80.
Dementia occurs when:
About 1% of people aged 60-64 years
• 3% of people aged 65 to 74 years
• Approximately 15% of people aged 75 to 79
About 25% of people aged 80 to 84 years
• 30-50% of people over 85 years of age
• 60-80% of the elderly home population
ADAPTATION
Strategies that may help people cope with memory loss include:
• Creating lists
• Maintain a detailed calendar
• Set a routine
Link or link new information to previously known information, such as linking the name of a new person to the name of a movie star
Repeating information, such as repeating a new person ’ s name several times
Focus on (or pay attention to) one thing at a time
Improve organizational skills, such as keeping frequently used items such as putting car keys in the same place
Making sure older people can hear and see well can help them stay connected with others and participate in social activities.This involvement helps older people maintain their self-confidence and often improves their mental function.
MAIN POINTS
Memory loss and fear of dementia are common concerns among adults.
Memory loss usually occurs as a result of natural age-related changes in the brain, which slightly slow down mental functions without significantly weakening them.
Dementia-induced memory loss usually interferes with the ability to engage in daily activities and worsens gradually.
People who have poor memory may not have dementia.
Doctors can usually determine the cause based on the results of the scan, imaging tests (such as MRI or CT), and other tests, including systematic tests of mental function.
A healthy lifestyle, maintaining mental activity, and participating in social activities may help maintain mental function, or slow its decline.
Using menus and other memory enhancers, focusing on one thing at a time and organizing, can help adults compensate for age-related memory changes.
Medications called cholinesterase inhibitors (such as donepezil) can also help memory, especially if people have Alzheimer's disease or Lewy body dementia.

Researchers turn immune cells in the body into tiny monitoring machines
Scientists at the University of Southern California have discovered a way to turn the body ’ s B cells into tiny monitoring machines and antibody factories that can pump out antibodies specifically designed to destroy cancer cells or HIV, two of medicine ’ s worst enemies.
The research, published in the journal Nature Biomedical Engineering and reported by Eurik Allert, describes a technique for editing the genes of immune cells called B cells, and charging them to fight even the most intrusive invaders.
This work is an important advance in harnessing the power of antibodies to treat conditions ranging from Alzheimer's disease to arthritis.
Lead author Paula Cannon, a professor of molecular microbiology and immunology at the University of Southern California ’ s Keck School of Medicine, said: “In some diseases or cases, the normal antibodies made by B cells are not good enough.
"HIV is a very good example of this.
It mutates constantly, and remains one step ahead of any antibodies that are released to it.
We thought checkmate ’ s move might be convincing for B cells to produce an antibody so broad in its ability to “see ” HIV that HIV can ’ t easily mutate around it. ”
B cells produce antibodies, which are proteins that recognize and adhere to foreign bodies such as cells invaded by viruses and bacteria cells.
A B cell is programmed to produce one specific antibody, and when a B cell encounters the virus or bacteria for which it is programmed (called an antigen), this leads to the production of antibodies.
The antibody matches the antigen just as the key matches the lock, and when it does, the foreign object is identified for destruction, and it is then identified by the T cells that attack and kill it.
Wide range of antibodies
The beauty of this technique is that it can be adapted to produce a wide range of different antibodies.
Researcher Jeffrey Rogers said: “It ’ s a technique for reprogramming B cells that can be applied to almost anything you can imagine dealing with an antibody.
We believe we will be able to fully personalize everything related to the antibody. ”
B cells act as a security system and manufacturer of antibodies, where they are present for a long time in the bone marrow, lymph nodes and spleen, and are active when needed.
To manufacture these small fighters, Cannon and Rogers used CRISPR gene-editing methods to place custom antibody instructions at the specific location in B-cell DNA where antibodies are naturally synthesized.
This trick means that B cells can be reprogrammed as bio-factories that make custom antibodies.
As normal antibodies respond to vaccination, reprogrammed B cells can also be stimulated to increase their production.
Researchers are working to license the technology for commercial use.

How did Muslim scholars refute the flat Earth theory a thousand years ago?
The flat earth is currently one of the most famous scientific myths widespread in the Arab world, and has private groups on social media met by supporters from all over, and in recent days has been controversial because of statements by the Egyptian artist Mohamed Sobhy.
There are two histories to this theory, not one; the first is ancient and the second is modern.
A number of Greek philosophers believed that the earth was flat, and the ancient Scandinavian and German peoples also believed that the earth was flat and surrounded by oceans, and the common belief in ancient China was that the earth was square and flat while the sky was spherical.
But it ’ s really surprising to know that early astronomers assumed its sphericity, and they were from almost every culture: Pythagoras, who lived about 2,500 years ago, proposed the sphericity of the Earth based on his observations of the moon during the eclipse.
Pythagorean's observations are still evidence of a refutation of the flat Earth theory: Pythagorean observed that the shadow that the Earth casts on the Moon during the eclipse is always round.
Regardless of the moon-facing part of the planet, eclipses occur everywhere in the world.
The idea of a lunar eclipse is simple: put a big lamp in the middle of your room and turn off the rest of the lights, stand at a distance of one meter from it, now turn around while you reach your hands in front of you with a tennis ball, when you give your back to the lamp and pass the tennis ball in the shadow extended in front of you because of your body, this is the eclipse.
To Eratosthenes
Eratosthenes, born 276 BC, was the first to measure the circumference of the Earth using a simple method involving the angle of the Sun at different locations.
Eratosthenes was astonished to read that the columns in the ancient Egyptian temples of Aswan on the afternoon of June 21 of each year did not leave a shadow under them, and the mystery of the wonder was that the columns in Alexandria left a shadow under them on the afternoon of the same day.
Eratosthenes came to the conclusion that the earth must be convex and not flat, otherwise the columns in Alexandria would appear shadowless, and then after reflection Eratosthenes came to the clever idea that we could measure the length of the shadow in Aswan which is zero, and its length in Alexandria, and then measure the distance between Alexandria and Aswan, and infer the circumference of the earth.
The story goes that he sent a man to measure the distance, so that with some simple geometry he could measure the circumference of the Earth, which he concluded was about 39,348 kilometers.
Eratosthenes' account was transferred to the Arabs from among the sciences they translated.
According to Carlo Nelino in his book "Astronomy: A History of the Arabs in the Middle Ages", the Caliph al-Ma'mun al-Abbasi (who ruled from 813 to 833 AD) asked two teams of astronomers to test these calculations and come up with the most accurate measurement of the Earth's circumference....
The safe astronomer.
The method adopted by the Arabs is to go out into a perfectly flat desert, and then rely on the inclination of the polar star in the sky.
The ancients realized that the position of stars in the sky is affected by your place on Earth, the further you travel south, the lower the polar star in the sky until it disappears completely after the equator, and the more you travel north, the higher the polar star sky until it became above your head in the North Pole, which means that the Earth is round, otherwise the position of stars in the sky changes with your place on it.
The height of the polar star (and all other stars) is measured in degrees, and it is like to put a protractor in front of your eyes, the horizon is at zero, and then look at the protractor from the side to find at what degree the polar star stands, and this is something you can do exactly as the ancients did, and now astronomical software is easily available.
Al-Ma'mun astronomers measured the height of the polar star, then moved north once and south once, until the amount of inclination of the polar star changes by one degree, and then measured the distance north and south, and this measured distance is one degree from the circumference of the Earth's circle, and it can know the rest of the circumference of the Earth, because the Earth is a ball, and like any ball, rotation around it requires 360 degrees.
The first team of Al-Ma ’ mun astronomers went out to the Sinjar desert, a small city in northwestern Iraq today, and the second team to the Palmyra desert in eastern Syria, and carried out the same experiments in both places. In the Sinjar desert, for example, the height of the polar star was about 35 degrees. south of the wedge site until the measurement dropped by a degree.
According to al-Ma ’ mun ’ s astronomers, the scale of one degree was about 56 parsecs and two-thirds parsecs, which Nalino calculated — according to Edward Kennedy of the American University of Beirut in a paper published in the Encyclopedia of the History of Arab Sciences — to be 111.8 kilometers, a value used by later researchers such as al-Biruni and al-Toussi.
Calculating the circumference of the Earth in this experiment, it turned out to be about 410,248 km, which was close to modern measurements (40075 km) in the most accurate way at the time.
Note that the difference between the two measurements is about 1,100 years, and the reason for the difference is not related to the same method but to the ellipse of the Earth, as the distance between the two latitudes increases slightly as we head north.
Abu Rayhan Al-Biruni
The second attempt was by Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, born in September 973 AD, who used the best and easiest formula to calculate the circumference of the Earth in his time.
The Al-Biruni method is based on triangulation, where the sunset is observed from the top of a high mountain overlooking flat ground to the horizon, the astrolabe measures the angle the sun descends relative to the observer on the top of the mountain, where the line connecting the observer on the top of the mountain and the horizon makes the sunset clock touch the planet Earth.
It is known that the tangent of a circle perpendicular to its diameter, and then we have a right-angled triangle at the horizon, and we can measure the radius of the Earth by knowing the height of the mountain, which is mathematically easy.
Currently, the same calculations can be applied by high school students, for example, in all countries of the Arab world, who have a good amount of trigonometry study.
In a study published in the International Journal of Sciences, an Italian team repeated al-Biruni ’ s experiment and concluded that its results for the radius of the Earth are equal to 3,928.77 English miles, which compares favorably, being 2% different, with the average reference radius at the measurement latitude, which is 3,847.80 miles.
Pakistani physicist Mazhar Mahmood Qureshi, in his book An Introduction to Muslim Contributions to Science and Technology, points out that al-Biruni ’ s experience in what is now Nandana Fort in the mountains of northern Pakistan is a typical example of the use of experimental scientific methods.
The most important book of al-Biruni astronomical is "The Law of Masoudi", in which al-Biruni collected all the astronomical problems of his time, and the way of al-Biruni was to present the origins of the matter and the views of the Indian, Greek and Arab astronomers and then weighted between them.
Modern history of flat earth
But at that point, you might ask yourself: if the sphericity of the Earth was obvious to Muslim scholars and their comrades in other parts of the world in ancient times, why did it come back?
In 1849, the English writer Samuel Rowbotham published a pamphlet entitled "Oil Astronomy" (from the Greek letter zeta, not oil), in which he defended the theory of the flat earth, and followed this with another entitled "The Instability of Modern Astronomy and its opposition to the Bible".
In 1883, Rowbotham founded oil societies in England and New York, shipping thousands of copies of his books to talk about flat earth.
Meanwhile, William Carpenter, a printer and native of Greenwich, England, supported Rowbotham and advocated his theory, learning it from John Jasper and preaching to more people than any cleric of his generation in the southern United States. Once.
From here the myth began to branch again in the United States, and then to Europe, and then to the Arab world and the rest of the world, but in this context it was mixed with conspiracy theories concerning secret groups trying to control the world by deluding people that the earth is round.
The proof of the sphericity of the earth is not new, and has a long history in which Muslim scholars have made an influential contribution, but because the “flat earth ” has been transformed from ignorance of the nature of science into a conspiracy theory it has been imported along with other famous theories into our Arab world.
