Can a "comeback" dust storm in northern China be eradicated for the 10th time this year?
Font Size:
Source: China Newsweek
Author: Peng Dani, Li Jinjin
Liu Song, a 27-year-old Beijing-based resident, said it had been a long time since the dust storm hit Beijing last year.
He described a feeling of “dead memories beginning to strike me. ”
The Central Meteorological Station of China continued to issue a blue sandstorm warning at 1800 hours on April 19. It is expected that from 20: 00 to 20: 00 on April 19, there will be sand or dust storms in central and western Inner Mongolia, southern and eastern Xinjiang, most parts of Gansu, Ningxia, Shanxi, western Hebei and Beijing.
According to the monitoring data of the State Forestry and Grassland Administration, in the past 20 years, China's spring (March-May) dust weather has generally shown a reduction in the number of times, the intensity of weakening trend, has been reduced from the 1960s to the average of 21 times in the past 10 years eight times, and the number of sand and dust days has decreased by an average of 1.63 days every 10 years.
However, the respondents felt that in the past two or three years, the sand and dust weather has "made a comeback."
The north has ushered in the 10th sand and dust weather process so far this year.
This year, the frequency of sand and dust in China is the most frequent in the same period in the past 10 years.
According to the data of the China Meteorological Disaster Yearbook (2020), in the past 20 years, the average number of sand and dust weather in March to April was 7.8 times, and the number of times has exceeded the average.
In 2019, a study released by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) showed that about 1 / 4 of the newly added green areas in the world from 2000 to 2017 came from China, and China's contribution rate ranked first in the world, and part of it originated from the greening of sand areas.
In this context, how to understand the "relapse" of dust storms in recent years?
Or enter a new dust storm active cycle
On April 19, strong wind and dust weather occurred in many parts of Gansu, and yellow warnings of sandstorms were issued in Jiuquan and Silver.
Information released by flight travel service APP shows that on the same day, the visibility of Lanzhou Zhongchuan Airport was 400 meters, and by 12 noon, there were more than 100 return flights and standby flights.
Dust storms are a common meteorological disaster in arid and semi-arid areas.
Strong winds act like “sweeping robots, ” pulling massive amounts of sand and dust from the ground into the atmosphere from dry soil, taking them hundreds to thousands of kilometers away.
The intensity of sand and dust weather is usually distinguished by horizontal visibility, which is divided into five grades of floating dust, sand, dust storm, strong dust storm and super strong dust storm.
The horizontal visibility of the dust or sand weather is between 1 km and 10 km, the horizontal visibility of the dust storm is less than 1 km, the horizontal visibility of the strong dust storm is less than 500 meters, and the ultra-strong dust storm is less than 50 meters, commonly known as "black wind".
According to the literature, the two main sources of global dust storms are the African desert and the Asian region, which is dominated by the Sahara Desert.
There are three main source areas in Asia, namely Mongolia, the Taklamakan Desert and surrounding areas in northwest China, and the source area in western Inner Mongolia with the Badanjilin Desert as the main body.
Zhang Xiaoyan, academician of the Chinese Academy of Engineering and researcher of the Chinese Academy of Meteorological Sciences, told China News Weekly that there are more than 1.7 million square kilometers of desert area in northern China, and more than 300,000 square kilometers of Gobi and desert in southern Mongolia, because of the existence of these sandstorms, China is one of the most affected countries in the world by sandstorm weather.
In a recent paper published in April, scholars from the Chinese Academy of Meteorological Sciences pointed out that there are five main routes for the transmission of sand and dust in China, among which the northwestern route is more complex and covers the most extensive area.
It started outside Mongolia and its sandy land (including the Ulanbu Desert and Kubqi Desert in western Inner Mongolia), and transported sand and dust to the northwest, north China, the Yellow and Huai, and the Jianghuai, as the cold air moved from northwest to southeast.
In addition, the northwest path is also the most important transmission path for sandy weather in China, accounting for 38.5% of the sandy weather in the past 20 years.
At a regular press conference held by the Ministry of Ecology and Environment in March, Liu Bingjiang, director of the Department of Atmospheric Environment of the Ministry of Ecology and Environment, said that since March this year, the domestic dust and dust weather has been high. The soil melts rapidly, and at the same time, the sand source ground is basically no precipitation, and the surface is not covered by snow, resulting in extensive surface exposure.
Second, meteorological conditions are conducive to the transmission of sand and dust.
This year, Mongolia's cyclone intensity is strong and cold air activity is high, and strong winds have provided favorable weather conditions for dust particles to roll up into the sky.
In the past 40 years, the frequency of sand and dust in northern China has shown a slow decline.
However, according to data from the Climate Prediction Room of the National Climate Center, the average total number of sand and dust storms in the North between 2018 and 2022 was higher than the average from 2013 to 2017.
In March 2021, the north suffered from sandstorms in many places, and on March 16 of that year, the Central Meteorological Station characterized it as, "The process reached a strong sandstorm intensity, which is the strongest sandstorm weather process in China in the past 10 years."
According to the Ministry of Ecology and Environment, in the dust storm, the concentration of PM10 in Beijing rose rapidly in a short time, rising four times in an hour to 6450 micrograms / cubic meter; the concentration of PM10 in the six urban areas reached 8108 micrograms / cubic meter.
"In the past few years, everyone felt that the sandstorm was getting less and less, and thought that the sandstorm had disappeared, but from the perspective of the past two or three years, the sandstorm weather has slowly increased in the past two years and is in a shock trend."
An atmospheric scientist in China said in an interview with China Newsweek.
"There is a cyclical change in the climate system, but this cyclical change is not particularly clear now, and it is difficult to judge the trend based on short-term conditions for several years," Wu Chenglai, an associate researcher at the Institute of Atmospheric Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told China News Weekly.
Zhang Xiaoli believes that from the perspective of monsoon activities, we may have entered a new active period of sand and dust.
He further analyzed that the winter wind has a large cycle of 50-70 years.
China in the 1970s this decade, the dust storm disaster is more serious, after the occurrence of dust storms in the downward trend; the large cycle, winter wind and 20-30 years of short cycle, in this process, in 2002 Beijing there was a very large range of sand and dust storms, since then the wind has been in the process of weakening.
If you look at the 50-year cycle, the 2020s are the beginning of a new cycle.
Wu Chenglai also observed this change. Since 2018, the increase in surface wind speed may be a cyclical change to a large extent, but this needs further study.
He said that due to the large scope of the whole dust source area, specific to different areas, but also depends on the local surface conditions, geographical environment, etc., and such differences can sometimes be very large.
Why did Mongolia become a disaster area?
In mid-March 2021, when China suffered the "strongest sandstorm of the decade", disaster weather such as snowstorms and large sandstorms occurred in many provinces in Mongolia, with wind speeds reaching 20 meters per second.
On April 17, the National Meteorological and Environmental Monitoring Bureau of Mongolia issued a new warning of severe sandstorms, which are forming in the western and northwestern parts of the country.
Mongolia is an important source of sandstorm weather in China.
For example, during the strong dust storm from March 19 to 24 this year, according to satellite observations, a clear distribution of sand and dust can be observed in southern Mongolia on the morning of the 21st, and the range of sand and dust has since expanded.
For Wu Cheng, the specific contribution to a certain place, in fact, is not very clear.
Because the situation in the upstream of the dust storm is obtained through satellite observation, it can master some general characteristics, such as the dust content in the atmosphere, etc., but because the dust storm moving process will be accompanied by sand and settlement, so how much of the dust on a certain ground is rolled up such information, more first-hand data is needed.
In the past 10 years, the number of sandstorms in the Gobi region of Mongolia has quadrupled compared to the 1960s. In an interview with Xinhua in 2021, Enkhbat, director of the Climate Change Department of the Ministry of Natural Environment and Tourism of Mongolia, said that Mongolia is one of the countries most affected by global climate change, and the incidence of sandstorms is on the rise.
Most of Mongolia's land is covered by grasslands, mountains in the north and west, and the Gobi Desert in the south.
In the southern region of the country, many provinces bear the word "Gobi" in their names.
On the whole, Zhang Xiaoli pointed out that the main source of sand and dust in Mongolia, the more than 390,000 square kilometers of land in the south, is not mainly due to human activities in recent years, which have destroyed the surface and let the sand become active, in fact, there are few people here, and the desert and the Gobi are there.
Mongolia is located in the middle and high latitudes of the Inner Asian steppe, the whole territory of the inland far away from the sea, belongs to the temperate continental climate zone.
To add insult to injury, natural geographical location, global climate change and other factors have made the natural conditions of the region even worse.
In November 2020, a paper published in the journal Science, “East Asia ’ s Inland Climate Becomes Hot and Dry Beyond the Critical Point, ” mentioned that the past 20 years have witnessed unprecedented“ heatwave – drought ” concurrent phenomena in the interior of East Asia centered in Mongolia, which clearly goes beyond the scope of natural change and forms a vicious circle: soil drying accelerates local high temperatures, which exacerbates soil moisture decline.
Over the past 80 years, the average temperature in Mongolia has risen by about 2.25 degrees Celsius, far higher than the global average temperature rise, and the annual precipitation in Mongolia has decreased by 7% -8% during the same period, especially in the warm seasons such as spring and summer.
Up to now, 76.8 per cent of Mongolia's total land area has suffered from various degrees of desertification and the situation is still deteriorating.
According to official data, the past 10 years have been the hottest decade the country has experienced in nearly 80 years, with drought and heat causing 1,244 large and small rivers and lakes to dry up or stop flowing.
However, on April 14, at the sixth assessment report of the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), IPCC expert Zhai Panmao said that the current research on critical points and irreversible phenomena is far from enough, and to reach conclusions, different researchers and different methods are required to provide multiple evidence from observations, mechanisms, models and other aspects.
Zhai Panmao said that although Mongolia's dry heat conditions have long existed and intensified, which will affect the land vegetation cover, in the context of climate warming, there is still a trend of increasing vegetation and precipitation in many middle and high latitudes.
In 1998, the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography of the Chinese Academy of Sciences was established to provide scientific support for the development of natural resources, ecological restoration and environmental management in international arid zones.
Li Shengyu is a senior engineer of the Institute, and from 2018 to 2020, he led an international scientific and technological cooperation project called “Sino-Mongolian Grassland Desertification Control Technical Cooperation Research and Demonstration ”, and visited Mongolia many times in 2019 to carry out research and experimental research.
He told China News Weekly that the northern part of Mongolia's southern Gobi is a grassland belt, which is greatly affected by global climate change and local economic development activities.
He pointed out that the deterioration of grasslands in these areas is very obvious, and the center of gravity of desertification has shifted northward, adding to the sand and dust sources in Mongolia, which is a new problem.
Mongolia is the second largest landlocked country in the world, after Kazakhstan, but with a population of 3.3 million, it is the least densely populated sovereign country in the world. Livestock production accounts for about 90 per cent of the country's agricultural production, and one in four Mongolians is engaged in animal husbandry, a higher proportion than any other industry in Mongolia.
At the end of 2019, the International Monetary Fund pointed out that Mongolia ’ s livestock industry, once the main engine of the national economy, is now facing the threat of climate change and overgrazing.
Since 1990, the number of livestock has tripled to 70 million, far exceeding the carrying capacity of the land.
The agency ’ s study also noted that overgrazing in Mongolia is linked to soaring global cashmere prices, as well as a lack of appropriate land-use regulations or pasture management standards.
Nomadic herding was originally a kind of human activity with a relatively small burden on grasslands, but Li Shengyu said that driven by the international cashmere trade demand, now the local not only overgrazed, but also preferred to breed goats, goats such animals will eat grass close to the ground, and even the grass roots will be planed out to eat, the damage to the grassland is relatively large.
On the other hand, unlike domestic grazing regulations, Mongolia's rangelands are communal, which leads to a "tragedy of the commons", where everyone wants to make the most of the rangelands, but does not care about their sustainable use.
Mining is another issue.
Mongolia is rich in mineral and coal resources and is known as "the Saudi Arabia of the coal industry".
Relying on mining production and investment from foreign mining companies, Mongolia achieved unprecedented economic growth and entered the ranks of middle-income countries in 2012.
By 2019, mining output value accounted for 23.8% of Mongolia's GDP, and mineral exports accounted for more than 70% of the total, with a trend of increasing year by year.
Li Shengyu said that many of the coal mines are located in Gobi in southern Mongolia and are open pit mines.
Open pit mining needs to peel off the surface of the soil layer, the mining range is very large, and there are not many environmental protection measures, once encountered dry, windy weather, dig out of the dust flying with the wind.
Moreover, mining changes conditions such as groundwater or rivers, exacerbating the deterioration of the grassland growing environment.
Since 2007, the Chinese Academy of Sciences has been cooperating with Mongolia on desertification control. Since 2013, the former State Forestry Administration has organized research institutes such as the Institute of Desertification of the Chinese Academy of Forestry to organize desertification control seminars for Mongolia.
"Due to a variety of factors, the dust storm in Mongolia has entered a new active period, which requires a lot of research in the future."
Huang Ning, a professor at the School of Civil Engineering and Mechanics of Lanzhou University and director of the Key Laboratory of Disaster and Environmental Mechanics of the Ministry of Education in the West, said that Mongolia's lack of field research stations, monitoring equipment and instruments is not conducive to the development of research.
Zhang Xiaoyi, a United Nations expert who went to Mongolia to investigate, said that the China Meteorological Administration and Mongolia have cooperated for a long time to help each other build an observatory, but there is no way to invest people, money and materials, and the observatory is in a very loose state.
Fighting dust storms: What can humans do?
Han Bin, a 32-year-old Beijinger, also noted that in earlier years, Beijing was rarely disturbed by dust storms in spring.
He attributed the good weather to China's achievements in combating desertification.
In the past two or three years, when Beijing and other cities have been hit by dust storms again, some people have asked: Why have the trees planted over the years not been able to stop the dust storms?
In 1978, the Three North Sheltered Forest Project, named the "Great Green Wall", began to be implemented, becoming a landmark project in China to prevent wind and control desertification.
The area covers a total area of 1.49 million square kilometers, accounting for about 85 percent of the country's sandy land.
Since then, China has successively launched key ecological projects such as returning farmland to forests and grasslands, natural forest protection, and management of wind and sand sources in Beijing and Tianjin; at the legal level, the Law of the People's Republic of China on Prevention and Control of Desertification has been promulgated, and policies such as subsidies for sandy land sealing and protection areas, compensation for ecological public welfare forests, and subsidies for grassland ecological protection have been formulated.
"The Chinese government is one of the countries in the world that have been affected by the sandstorms," Li said. "China has invested a lot of money to set up a number of professional management bodies, and a large number of scientists are engaged in scientific research."
Zhang also pointed out that compared with neighboring countries, China's efforts and contributions are the most, which should be affirmed.
In terms of desertification control, China can be called a global benchmark.
However, several experts interviewed pointed out that the extent to which desertification control has slowed down dust storm pollution requires more careful analysis.
In the Taklamakan Desert, the largest desert in China, a study published in 2022 by Huo Wen, a researcher at the Institute of Desert Meteorology of the China Meteorological Administration, found that in the central area of the desert, artificial green space can reduce the near-ground wind speed by about 70%.
In addition, the vegetation root system makes it easier for the soil to retain water, reduce evaporation, and produce a "water lock" function, making the ground sand difficult to pick up.
However, when the cold air from Mongolia swept south with sand and dust to China, he said, the air affected thousands of meters high, and its height was no longer blocked by the Three North Shelters.
Two or three hundred meters high shelterbelts can block part of the surface of the coarse sand, but far from blocking the sand particles that are carried high by the wind.
However, the protective forest system can reduce the "sand and dust relay" on the sand and dust transmission path, which is still of great ecological significance.
In addition to monitoring sandstorm weather, Wu Chenglai also reviewed and analyzed the evolution of sandstorms to understand some of the major sandstorm events, the main drivers, etc. Since 2000, his team has analyzed the reasons for the decline in sandstorm activity in East Asia between 2001 and 2017.
The study, published in Nature Communications in 2022, shows that weakening surface wind speeds contributed 46% of the decline in sand and dust activity during this period, with soil wetting and vegetation greening contributing the remaining 54%.
Among them, the contribution rate of vegetation greening is about 30%, including human tree planting and grass planting projects, but also including naturally growing vegetation.
In this sense, human desertification control projects can play a much smaller role than the impact of changes in meteorological factors.
Some people believe that more fine sand and dust from a large number of dry lakes and desertified land is a more important source of sand and dust, but it has not been given due attention and actively managed.
However, Zhang Xiaoli said that these finer sand and dust sands are relatively large, but their proportion is small compared to the traditional sand and dust source areas of the desert.
Flux refers to the amount of sand that can be released into the atmosphere per unit of time and per unit area.
Unlike the public's optimism, many scholars engaged in desertification control and sandstorm research have emphasized that people are small in the face of sandstorm problems and it is impossible to eradicate sandstorms.
Compared to other air pollution, dust storm weather is a natural dominant force phenomenon, it has existed for millions of years, if not for human likes and dislikes, it is difficult to even be called a "disaster".
As some scholars have pointed out, about 28 million tons of sand and dust from the Sahara desert in Africa cross the sea to South America every year, bringing about 22,000 tons of phosphorus fertilizer to the Amazon rainforest, thus nourishing and compensating for the nutrients lost in the tropical rainforests.
Compared with the vast desert and Gobi area, China's efforts over the past decades have been "green", but only a very small part.
According to an official circular issued by the State Forestry and Grassland Administration in March this year, the area of desertification and desertification in China has been continuously reduced in recent years, and the work of preventing and controlling desertification has achieved good results.
However, China still has 2.5737 million square kilometers of desertified land and 1.6878 million square kilometers of sandy land, especially the large area of desert and the Gobi has always been a huge and permanent source of sand and dust.
“In general, on the edge of the desert, close to the river, we do some governance work, but this is 6% to 7% of the more than 1.7 million square kilometers of desert. ”
"The vast majority of deserts are in extremely arid areas, with average annual rainfall of tens of millimeters or less, and the human impact is very weak," Zhang told China News Weekly.
On the other hand, some unscientific and irrational behaviors in the process of combating desertification have counteracted the ecological environment.
Xue Xian, a researcher at the Northwest Institute of Ecological Environment and Resources of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and director of the Desert and Desertification Research Office, said in an interview with the media that in recent years, protective forests have been degraded and killed because of their single vegetation and high density.
In an interview with China Newsweek, a scholar engaged in desertification control at the grassroots level said that in reality, there are still many problems in the work of desertification control, "we may still overemphasize the new area of desertification control and afforestation, and even turn it into an administrative indicator."
Zhang said that in the scientific community, the research on sandstorms has shifted from scientific understanding to how to prevent and control sandstorms, especially in forecasting and early warning.
In his view, in the future, humans can change relatively limited, and more accurate forecasts and warnings can slow down the damage of dust storms to society and individuals.
"The sandstorm is a large-scale land-surface process, involving climate change and regional anthropogenic activities," said the researchers, who have been engaged in the work for many years, hope that the public will not completely deny China's achievements in combating desertification because of the repeated visits of sandstorms.
Perhaps, when the next sandstorm comes, we will think: How can we better prevent and control sand?
And what ordinary people can do, may just close the doors and windows, reduce the door, wear a good mask.

Geoffrey Hinton: GPT-4 is 100 times more knowledgeable than any human
Author: MIAO Yongqi
Published: Updated:
Computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "godfather of artificial intelligence", announced Monday that he has resigned from Google. He has devoted his life to developing artificial intelligence systems, saying he "regrets his life's work" and is wary of the potential dangers of AI development.
In another recent interview, Hinton further talked about why he is afraid of AI development.
Hinton, 75, left Google a few days after the news broke in an interview with MIT Technology Review senior editor Will Douglas Heaven.
Hinton points out that the new generation of AI language models, especially the GPT-4, which came out in March, made him realize that these machines were moving in a direction that was much smarter than he thought, and he was afraid of these developments.
He is best known for a technique he proposed in the 1980s (with two colleagues) called backpropagation.
In short, the algorithms that allow machines to learn support almost all of today ’ s artificial neural networks, from computer vision systems to large language models.
It wasn ’ t until the 2010s that Hinton and his two recent graduates developed a “neural network ” that demonstrated its power, stronger than any computer ’ s ability to identify objects in images, and trained it to predict the next letter of a sentence, a precursor to today ’ s large-scale language patterns.
One of the students was Ilya Sutskever, the founder of OpenAI, who led the development of ChatGPT.
“We first thought it might be great. ”“ But it ’ s going to take a long time to realize that it needs to be done on a large scale to get good results. ”
In the 1980s, the discussion of “neural networks ” was considered a joke.
But Hinton doesn ’ t think so, and is working on this, software that mimics the abstract human brain and uses code as a connection between neurons. For 40 years, Hinton has viewed artificial neural networks as a clumsy attempt to mimic biological neural networks.
Now he thinks things have changed: he thinks there are better results when trying to mimic the behavior of the biological brain.
“It ’ s scary when you see it with your own eyes, ” he said.“ It ’ s a sudden change. ”
So why did ChatGPT surprise Hinton, too? He explained that the human brain has about 100 trillion connections, and “large language models have up to 500 billion, up to a trillion. ”
However, the knowledge of GPT-4 is a hundred times greater than that of any human.
So maybe it actually has a better learning algorithm than we do. "
He also pointed out that apart from the ability to learn, the ability to communicate is another kind of point.
“If you or I learn a new thing and want to teach it to another person, we can ’ t just send them a copy. ”
But artificial neural networks can do it.
It ’ s like there are 10,000 people here, and when one person learns a new thing, the other 9,999 people all learn it at the same time.
Hinton now believes that there are two types of intelligence: animal brains and artificial neural networks.
“It ’ s a completely different kind of intelligence.
“A new, better intelligence. ” Hinton believes that whether superintelligence is good or bad depends largely on whether you ’ re an optimist or a pessimist, and he says,“ mildly depressed, ” “that ’ s why I ’ m afraid. ”
“Whether these things are going to be smarter than us, I suddenly changed my mind. ”
I think they are very close to us now and they will be much smarter than us in the future, ” he said.
“How do we survive? ” he is particularly worried that people will use the tools he has developed to change the trajectory of human life, including elections and wars.

ChatGPT detonates boom, Africa conference explores AI challenges and opportunities for poor countries
2023 / 5 / 7 19: 38: 03 Source: NetEase Technology Author: Xiaoqian Editor: Ocean
At a time of growing concern about the prospects and dangers of artificial intelligence, more than 2,000 researchers and engineers from around the world gathered in Rwanda this week to debate a different vision for the future of artificial intelligence.
One vision is to build more robust systems like ChatGPT that are designed to go beyond human intelligence to improve worker productivity and boost economic growth.
Another vision is to create smaller, more targeted AI solutions to address global challenges such as climate change, improved health care, and biodiversity conservation.
This is the first major AI research conference held in Africa this year, and one of the highlights of the conference is more ideological exchanges.
The organizers hope that researchers from the United States, China and wealthy companies will become more aware of the various social problems facing Africa, while allowing African researchers to participate in the discussion and express their unique insights.
Joshua Bengio, one of the “godfathers ” of artificial intelligence, is one of the board members of the conference organizers who advocates bringing AI technology to Africa:“ It ’ s clear that in order for everyone to enjoy the potential benefits of AI, we need everyone involved. ”
The launch of ChatGPT, a chatbot that exploded in the months leading up to the conference, added urgency to the discussion about the trajectory of AI and its short- and long-term implications. The launch of ChatGPT sparked a generative artificial intelligence (AIGC) craze around the world, prompting big tech companies like Google and Baidu to launch their own products that generate text and images, raising concerns about job displacement and the spread of misinformation.
At the AI research conference held in Kigali, the capital of Rwanda, although OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, did not show up, it still became the focus of attention.
Accept or resist its direction?
The views of the global artificial intelligence community are polarizing.
Recently, Geoffrey Hinton, another “godfather of artificial intelligence, ” announced his departure from Google to talk more freely about the risks of AI development.
Hinton said in an interview with the media that he is concerned that the technology poses a threat to the long-term survival of humanity.
At the conference, many researchers from Africa and other developing countries said they were instead more concerned about the direct challenge AI poses to their societies.
They worry that current trends in the AIGC model could exacerbate the dominance of the United States and China in AI development, creating two problems: Either Africa is left behind or has to deal with the problems it poses.
The consequences include facing more disinformation in African elections and the gradual disappearance of their native language in digital technology.
There are also concerns among many researchers that there will be a lag in the development of beneficial AI solutions that could help improve the basic quality of life for people around the world.
Girmaw Abebe Tadesse, an Ethiopian researcher at Microsoft ’ s Nairobi office in Kenya, highlighted key data issues, such as filling out wrong medical forms, that hinder AI progress in developing countries and have not yet helped improve maternal health and reduce child mortality.
Tadesse also shared some success stories, such as finding that child mortality rates in southern Nigeria were lower than the national average, using high-quality data and statistical analysis, which allowed researchers to conduct more targeted investigations, identify causes, and design solutions for other places.
Other participants described applications such as using satellite imagery to understand racial disparities in access to parks and health facilities, using sensors and mathematical models to improve grid maintenance, and using computer vision to detect agricultural diseases.
Bengio said he hopes this year ’ s conference will allow researchers to focus more on artificial intelligence for social good applications, rather than simply pursuing profits.
“We ’ ve talked a lot about AI risks, but we haven ’ t talked enough about how to make better use of AI, ” he said.
Organizers said there were 261 participants from Africa, compared with 16 in 2019.
For years, the largest and most prestigious annual AI research conferences have typically been held in the United States or Canada because of its proximity to Silicon Valley.
Because of visa problems, African researchers are often prevented from attending meetings because of difficulties in obtaining visas.
This leads to a lack of an African perspective when it comes to developing one of the most powerful and transformative technologies.
Well-known researchers, including the AI ethicist Timnit Gebru, point out that research tends to focus on a few dominant players in Silicon Valley, with a lack of non-Western or fringe researchers.
Gebu grew up in Ethiopia and came to the United States as a refugee. In 2017, she founded Black in AI, a non-profit organization that aims to bring more diversity to the AI community.
On Friday, Gebru hosted a panel discussion on the limitations of large language models in dealing with African languages.
These models are the underlying technology for building ChatGPT, but African languages are increasingly excluded from the digital world due to the lack of data needed for current AI technologies.
Gebruh said she co-authored a paper criticizing the explosive growth in resource demand and environmental impact of the models that underpin Google ’ s search engine.
Previously, Gebruh had been fired by Google, causing public concern.
Inside Google, Google characterized her departure as a resignation.
In another panel discussion, Vukosi Marivate, a professor of data science at the University of Pretoria in South Africa and chair of the conference program, said that African researchers are battling the threat of losing their mother tongue.
He said after the event that "we are in a race against time" before English dominates and African languages cease to exist.
Although Kigali is thousands of kilometers from Silicon Valley, people still cannot escape the temptation of large language models and AIGC tools such as ChatGPT.
Researchers crowded the lecture hall for related meetings, they sat on the floor, leaning against the wall, and people rushed straight from the airport, sitting on suitcases.
Many researchers said they were surprised by the results of OpenAI ’ s work, prompting them to actively expand their models as well.
One of the participating PhD students said he plans to shift his focus to AIGC to join the most exciting research directions. “This will be the last conference that will not be dominated by large language model research, ” he said.

A group of doctors and medical experts have urged the urgent need for an international treaty on AI regulation.

Source: SBS
Key points:
• A new study says the development of artificial intelligence could lead to the emergence of autonomous weapons capable of killing people “on an industrial scale. ”
The study ’ s authors also warn that the loss of jobs could have an impact on human health as more types of work are automated.
• The authors also warn that powerful AI-powered surveillance systems could be used to oppress people.
A group of doctors and public health experts say the development of artificial intelligence (AI) needs to be put on hold because it poses a risk to public health and safety.
According to a study published in the open journal BMJ Global Health, AI could facilitate the development of autonomous weapons capable of killing people “on an industrial scale ” without human supervision.
The study ’ s authors, David McCoy and Frederik Federspiel, say governments can also use AI to create powerful surveillance systems that can spread misinformation and social divisions, manipulate consumer choices, and even fuel government oppression.
"We do need an international treaty and a global regulatory approach," McCoy, a professor at the United Nations University in Malaysia, a United Nations General Assembly affiliated research institute and author of the study, told SBS News.
"The UN and governments are really critical to any form of effective regulation to prevent the misuse of AI," he said.
More than 75 countries or regions are currently using AI for surveillance.
Given the link between unemployment and “adverse health outcomes and behaviors, ” the study ’ s authors also warn of the health implications of unemployment as AI facilitates the automation of more types of work.
The creators of AI boast about its transformative potential, including in medicine and public health, but doctors are joining calls to stop developing AI until regulation can keep up with its progress.
How does artificial intelligence enable weapons development?
The authors of the study warn that artificial intelligence has enabled the development of lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS) to locate, select and attack human targets, all without human oversight.
"In theory, you could produce a van with hundreds of thousands of small autonomous weapons that could be targeted in a more discriminating way," Professor McCoy said.
The technology for this highly lethal weapon is relatively cheap, he added.
“We don ’ t know exactly who owns this technology or who is developing it.
“But I think it ’ s fair to say that there are governments around the world developing this technology, ” he said.
In 2021, the United Nations held talks on autonomous weapons, which did not start negotiations on an international treaty governing their use, but only agreed to continue discussions.
How does artificial intelligence contribute to the misuse of personal data?
The authors of the study say artificial intelligence has the ability to quickly clean up, organize and analyze massive data sets made up of personal data, including images.
They pointed to the role of AI in subverting democracy in the 2013 and 2017 Kenyan elections, the 2016 US presidential election, and the 2017 French presidential election.
“When combined with a rapidly improving ability to distort or distort reality, AI-powered information systems could further undermine democracy, cause a general breakdown of trust, or drive social divisions and conflict, with consequent public health implications, ” the authors said.
They argue that AI-driven surveillance could also be used by governments to oppress people more directly, such as China ’ s social credit system.
China ’ s social credit system, which combines facial recognition software with analysis of people ’ s financial transactions, activities, police records and social relationships, essentially allows the Chinese government to use a set of incentives and penalties to shape the behavior of its people.
Last week, Geoffrey Hinton, a pioneering computer scientist hailed as the “godfather of artificial intelligence, ” said he had left Google to talk freely about the dangers of the technology after realising that computers could become smarter than people faster than he and other experts expected.
In an interview with The New York Times, Hinton said he was concerned about the ability of AI to create convincing false images and texts, thereby creating a world where people "can no longer know what is real."
"It's hard to see how to prevent bad people from using it to do bad things," he said.

Fifty-one years ago, Geoffrey Hinton, who had not yet been called the “godfather of AI, ” entered the University of Edinburgh in Scotland as a graduate student and began research on artificial neural networks.

This is the foundational technology behind OpenAI ChatGPT and Google Bard.
After Hinton resigned from Google, he did not have to worry about the harm his words would bring to Google, so he was interviewed by different media and said his heart: "AI may lead to the death of mankind." (Photo: University of Toronto official website)

Subsequently, Hinton and two students founded DNNresearch, a startup based on this research project.

In 2018, Hinton, along with University of Montreal professor Yoshua Bengio and Meta chief AI scientist Yann LeCun, won the A.M. Turing Award in recognition of their great contributions to neural networks and deep learning.
As a result, the three later became known as the “godfathers of AI ” or“ godfathers of deep learning. ”

In the 1980s, Hinton was a professor of computer science at Carnegie Mellon University in the United States, but because he was not satisfied that the university's AI research was sponsored by the United States Department of Defense, he decided to leave the United States to teach at the University of Toronto's School of Computer Science.
He pointed out that without some kind of global regulatory agreement or regulatory mechanism, the AI arms race will intensify.
For this reason, Hinton believes that the threat posed by AI to humans may be more urgent than climate change, because the solution to climate change is obvious, as long as carbon emissions are reduced or carbon neutrality is achieved, but the current AI crisis does not know how to start. Although AI may pose an existential threat to humans, he does not agree to suspend AI research, because it can never erase the benefits and application value of AI.
Hinton believes it would be better to step up regulation of AI and make everyone aware of its potential harms.
OpenAI co-founder and CEO Sam Altman also acknowledged that ChatGPT has developed some reasoning capabilities that they can ’ t explain, and that it ’ s not entirely impossible for AI to destroy humans.
However, he said that he has installed a kill switch for ChatGPT, and if the development of ChatGPT exceeds human expectations, he will immediately press the switch to stop working.
OpenAI CEO Altman, known as the “father of ChatGPT, ” recently said he was“ a little scared ” about the potential of his children, and even admitted that there is a real possibility that AI will destroy humanity. (Image: Wikipedia)
Altman admits that ChatGPT ’ s influence in elections and the spread of disinformation is a concern, so the 2024 U.S. presidential election will be a focus for OpenAI.
(Image source: Pexels Gallery website)
The Curtain of Ignorance Makes AI Right Values
However, before we press the switch, we can try to instill the right values in AI, such as helping those most in need, not destroying humans. Google ’ s DeepMind paper published in April 2023 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences suggests that AI can be taught from the perspective of political philosopher John Rawls.
Rawls has proposed a concept called “The Veil of Ignorance ”, which aims to achieve the most equitable distribution of benefits when group decisions are made.
According to his book, The Debate, if a group of people stand behind a curtain, all of them will instantly lose their memory, become ignorant, and forget their identity and status in the real world.
The political philosopher Ross assumes that people are behind the “curtain of ignorance ” (left) and have no idea of their skills, identities, and status.
In this scenario, people tend to choose the most equitable distribution of rights for all. (Image: Wikipedia)
At this time, these people are asked to vote for a working principle for the society.
Because they do not know where they are in this society, they cannot make decisions in an egoistic way, and they can only judge according to the principle of fairness to all people.
The situation is like, at the birthday party, you are responsible for cutting the cake, because you do not know which piece you will get, so you will try to cut each piece to the same size.
Under the curtain of ignorance, fairness and justice that has nothing to do with personal interests will emerge.
For this reason, DeepMind believes that applying the “curtain of ignorance ” to AI training may help promote fairness in the process of“ aligning ” AI with human values.
By “alignment ”, it means aligning AI ’ s wishes with those of humanity.
If AI shares fair values with humans, AI will not have the intention to destroy humanity.
White House convenes tech giants to discuss AI threats
However, even if AI does not intend to destroy humans, it may still have many negative effects on human society.
The Center for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Policy (CAIDP), a U.S. technology ethics organization, has complained to the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) that OpenAI ’ s latest large language model, GPT-4, is biased and deceptive and poses a risk to privacy and public safety.
The CAIDP lists potential threats that may arise from GPT-4, including: helping hackers churn out malicious code to exacerbate cyberattacks; and biased AI training data that may reinforce social stereotypes and make people of all races and genders vulnerable to unfair treatment. The FTC is investigating OpenAI, said FTC Chairman Lina Khan. "They cannot be separated from existing legislation and the Federal Trade Commission will actively enforce them," he said.
In an effort to make GPT-4 more secure, OpenAI hired 50 experts and academics to test GPT-4 against lies, language manipulation, and dangerous scientific common sense.
The OpenAI headquarters is pictured here. (Image: Wikipedia)
In early May 2023, the White House invited Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, OpenAI founder Altman, and artificial intelligence startup Anthropic founder Dario Amodei to attend a conference to discuss the impact of AI on society.
Government officials at the meeting included Vice President Kamala Harris, Biden Chief of Staff Jeff Zients, National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan, National Economic Council Chairman Lael Brainard, and Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo.
U.S. President Joe Biden also attended the meeting.
EU to pass world ’ s first AI regulatory law
Generative AI, while helping to improve lives, can also pose security, privacy and fraud issues, says Ms Ho.
She noted that AI companies have an ethical and legal responsibility to ensure the safety of their AI products, while at the same time working with governments to protect civil rights and privacy.
She stressed that the White House will work to advance potential new legislation and support new legislation to mitigate the potential harms of AI technology.
In contrast, Europe has taken a step ahead in AI legislation.
On 11 May 2023, the European Parliament ’ s Committee on Civil Liberties and Consumer Protection overwhelmingly approved a position paper calling for restrictions on the use of AI in Europe, a crucial first step towards the adoption of the world ’ s first AI regulation bill.
The draft bill will be submitted to the full European Parliament for a vote in June of the same year, after which representatives of the European Parliament, the Council of the European Union and the European Commission will work out the final terms of the bill in tripartite talks.
The European Parliament has adopted a position paper that strengthens restrictions on biometrics, facial recognition, and the use of AI by police in routine duties.
The parliament believes the move could lead to the world ’ s first AI regulation bill. (Image: Wikipedia)
On the other hand, the White House announced that Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, NVIDIA, Stability AI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face have all committed to participating in DEF CON 31, a computer security conference to be held in August 2023, so that their AI models will be tested and evaluated by hackers and AI experts.
Experts will try to identify errors, failures, and vulnerabilities in AI tools so that AI companies can solve existing problems in their models early on.
However, these AI companies simply agree to a one-time test, rather than a commitment to a continuous evaluation when launching or improving their products, and may therefore not be sufficient to meet the regulatory requirements.
Despite this, DEF CON 31 is still seen as the first step for an AI model to be publicly evaluated.
We hope that after each important first step in legislative regulation and public evaluation, we can put generative AI trains on the right track, so that everyone can safely benefit from technological innovation.
DEF CON is one of the largest computer security conferences in the world. In addition to cybersecurity experts and hackers, participants included staff from the FBI, the Department of Defense, and the Postal Inspection Service.
The conference covered areas such as software security, computer architecture, hardware modifications, and other vulnerable areas of information. (Image: DEF CON official website)

Overwork and Deception ｜ Deep in the Age of Overwork, Not Waiting for Standard Hours
Author: Wang Ninghui
Published: Updated:
In the early morning of May 3, a 47-year-old captain of the Star Ferry was found collapsed on the ferry and died after being taken to hospital.
The deceased ’ s younger brother said that because the deceased had been working for 23 consecutive days on the day of his death, the family suspected that he may have “died of overwork ”.
However, Hong Kong has not incorporated “overwork death ” into the law. Although concerned groups from time to time have called on the SAR Government to legislate on“ overwork death ”, the authorities have always refused to protect the rights and interests of workers on the grounds that “death in the workplace ” is not directly related to“ work factors ”.
What is more tragic is that this attitude of many excuses is reflected in other labour protection issues, including regulating standard working hours, raising the minimum wage, and family-friendly policies.
If Hong Kong implements the "four-day work week", will people's lives still be like "walking dead"? (Photo by Lai Wenxin)
Hong Kong law does not recognize "overwork death"
“Working 23 days in a row ” may seem like an extreme case, but overtime work is common across all industries, especially food and beverage, transportation and other industries (see chart below).
The Federation of Hong Kong and Kowloon Labour Unions released the results of the Hong Kong Work Fatigue Survey last year and found that more than 60% of the respondents worked an average of 44 hours per week; more than 35% worked 50 hours or more per week; more than 20% worked 55 hours or more per week; and nearly half worked more than 75 hours per week.
In the past, there were news of sudden deaths in the workplace, but these deaths were not considered as "overwork deaths".
According to the Labour Department, from September 2017 to November 2019, there were a total of 200 deaths from cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases at work in Hong Kong. In 2017, the Labour and Welfare Bureau commissioned the Occupational Safety and Health Council to conduct a study on the death cases to assess the relationship between work conditions and workplace deaths.
However, the study on the relationship between workplace deaths and work conditions published by the OSHC over the past three years concluded that there are many causes of workplace deaths caused by cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases, and none of the cases involved only work-related risk factors.
In fact, in countries and regions that have incorporated “overwork death ” into the law, the“ work factor ” is not regarded as the only factor that causes death.
Taiwan law refers to "overwork death" as "occupational induced acute circulatory system disease", mainly manifested as cerebrovascular disease or heart disease; whether it is caused by occupation, you need to prove that the workload is the cause of the disease, and the criteria are divided into "abnormal events", "short-term (within 1 week) overwork" and "long-term (within 6 months) overwork".
In 1987, Japan also issued the "Standards for Recognition of Cerebrovascular Diseases and Ischemic Heart Disease", which clearly stated that deaths due to work performed at a time and place that can be clearly associated with the onset or death of the disease, or work that is more onerous than in the past, can be considered as death due to work (overwork death).
In fact, overtime work is common in all walks of life, especially in the catering, transportation and other industries. (Hong Kong 01 map)
Regulation of working hours is far away
However, the SAR Government has all along refused to legislate on the grounds that "death in the workplace" is not directly related to "work factors". The previous Secretary for Labour and Welfare, Mr LAW Chi-kwong, even put forth a sentence that "how many people died is not our consideration", which shows the attitude of the principal officials.
The question is, do work factors really have no negative impact on physical health?
Take "overtime work" as an example, there have been many international studies that can explain the problem.
A 2015 study by The Lancet, a medical journal, tracked more than 600,000 workers for an average of 8.5 years and found that workers who worked 49-54 hours a week had a 27% increased risk of stroke compared to workers who worked 36-40 hours; those who worked longer hours, that is, more than 55 hours a week, had a 33% increased risk of stroke.
Coincidentally, the global analysis conducted by the World Health Organization and the International Labour Organization in 2021 similarly highlighted the “55-hour work week ” tipping point, noting that 398,000 people in this group died of stroke and 347,000 died of heart disease.
The negative impact of "overtime work" on physical health is quite obvious, but similar to the definition of "death by overwork", the SAR Government has also shelved the legislation on "standard working hours" on the basis of "inability to achieve a unified view on the regulation of working hours".
In January 2017, the Government submitted a report to the Government on the proposal of replacing "standard working hours" with "contract working hours". In May 2018, the Hong Kong Government decided to shelve the dispute and change to the non-legally binding “11 Industry Hours Guidelines ”, which have not yet been published.
Despite repeated calls from concerned groups to legislate on "overwork death", the authorities have always refused to protect workers' rights and interests on the grounds that "death in the workplace" is not directly related to "work factors". (Photo)
On the issue of legislation governing working hours, the two sides have long had huge differences. In 2016, six labor committee members announced their withdrawal from the committee due to dissatisfaction with the management.
In disputes between employers and employees, the following three common myths are:
Myth 1: Will limiting standard hours hurt the workforce?
One of the reasons for the employers' objection is that once the standard working hours are limited and the per capita working hours are reduced, the overall labor force in Hong Kong will be damaged. In fact, the lack of a series of labor rights protection such as the regulation of working hours is precisely the reason for the loss of labor. Choose to switch.
According to the trade manpower supply and demand questionnaire released by the Federation of Trade Unions in March this year, 51.2% of the respondents believed that the main reason for the shortage of workers was "low labor" and "poor welfare", while 41.5% believed that it was "poor working conditions".
On the contrary, reducing working hours will not only improve the working environment, it will help married people balance the relationship between work and family, but also help married people balance the relationship between work and family.
In recent years, the fertility rate in Hong Kong has continued to decline, one of the important reasons is that women are too stressed and burdened in the workplace to balance the demands of work and family.
If working hours can be reduced and the working environment improved, female labor participation and fertility are also expected to increase.
Reducing working hours will not only improve the working environment, it will help married people balance their work and family relationship, but also help married people balance their work and family relationship. (photo by Alice Lam)
Myth 2: Decline in production efficiency, weakening the competitiveness of SMEs?
Similar to Myth 1, management often believes that reducing the number of working hours is equivalent to reducing production efficiency, which will weaken the competitiveness of SMEs.
But there are two major fallacies to this logic.
First of all, workers are not machines, and high working hours do not mean high output. On the contrary, problems such as work pressure and lack of sleep brought about by high working hours can reduce work efficiency. A study released by Lingnan University in December 2019 pointed out that employees are absent from work for an average of 8.3 days per year, of which 5.1 days are non-sick absence due to stress, “dressing up ” and family factors.
On the contrary, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, Australia and other regions have taken the lead in implementing the "four-day work week", in which the United Kingdom launched a large-scale national pilot, with 73 companies and 3,300 employees participating, and found that employees completed 100% of their normal workload in 80% of the time, and productivity improved.
Second, the purpose of protecting the competitiveness of SMEs is to maintain the vitality of the free market, not to blindly protect it. If the government allows enterprises to rely on cutting labor rights to improve their competitiveness, it will lead to the phenomenon of "bad money driving good money". And...
Myth 3: As long as you reduce your working hours, your income will decrease.
The premise of this argument is that labor income and working hours are directly linked, as long as the longer the work, the higher the income.
But in fact, it is precisely because of the lack of legal protection of "overtime work", coupled with the "minimum wage" for a long time at a low level, most workers even if they work for a long time, their income has not been correspondingly improved; especially in low-skilled industries, their entry barriers are low, poor work conditions, market demand is large, and grass-roots workers lack bargaining power, they can only tolerate overtime.
Long working hours occupations such as bus drivers are not covered by the working hours guidelines of 11 industries.
(Data Image)
No consensus doesn't mean there's nothing to do.
The Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR) is often reluctant to take a step forward for the vast number of labour unions on the grounds that “there is a dispute over standard working hours ”, but as a party exercising public power, even if the authorities and employers still fail to reach a consensus, it should not take“ shelving the dispute ” as the only option. Premises are no different than avoiding problems.
Instead, the authorities should play the role of moderator, stand on the weaker side to balance the discussion, and can find areas of consensus between the two sides in the confrontation, and gradually improve the legislation.
For example, the community may be inconclusive on how many hours a week to work, but it is not difficult to reach a consensus on whether workers should work 23 consecutive days.
Taiwan's "Labor Standards Law" involves a number of different concepts of working hours, including the "catch up" of at least interval time, regular leave arrangement and monthly overtime limit; in contrast, Hong Kong in addition to the regular leave arrangement, there is no law to clarify and stipulate the other two concepts.
Regulating the maximum working hours is not the same as legislating the standard working hours, but it can at least help to reduce the occurrence of tragedies such as the sudden death of the captain of the Star Ferry after 23 consecutive days of work.
Since the Employment Ordinance in Hong Kong does not stipulate any provisions on overtime pay, standard working hours, maximum working hours or rest day wages, the gradual improvement of the policy is a necessary step to improve the status quo and protect the rights and interests of workers.
It is important to know that policy-making is a gradual process in itself, and it would be a self-delusion if the Government simply did not act because it could not solve all the problems in one go.

First of all, workers must first clarify themselves, their weekday work, whether they often encounter what will hinder the work efficiency of the trivial matters? Such as meaningless meetings, gossip chat in the tea room for too long, or lazy Internet browsing, etc., since you want to increase the daily work efficiency, you must first set goals, how to reduce these interference, so that the original five-day work can be completed in four days.
For the employer, if you are willing to give employees an extra day of leave, you must first ensure that the weekly working hours will not increase, and other working days, you can still work on time without overtime.
Otherwise, to work five days a week, eight hours a day, to work four days a week, 10 hours a day, this will also let the workers lose the incentive to this policy.
But even if the employer is willing to take three days off a week, willing to empower the worker to decide their own performance, but the enterprise is still for profit after all, if because the worker takes an extra day off, resulting in a reduction in corporate revenue, or customer complaints increase, such an extra day of leave, it is not feasible.
In addition, workers must also remember that this is the result of coordination between employers and employees, but if the employee finds that the efficiency of the employee has not improved after four days of work per week, at least compared to the efficiency of the employee working for five days, then the employer also has the right to refuse to implement a three-day weekly rest.
Weekly rest three days is the result of each enterprise, labor and capital to communicate with each other, so it is not necessarily a company to be fully implemented within the company, the willingness of both labor and capital is the most important, if the labor is unwilling to cooperate, or the supervisor has doubts, you can also be promoted by some departments first, and weekly rest three days are not mandatory to take three days off at the weekend, otherwise there are fewer rotating staff, which has an impact on the company's operations.
In short, the three-day weekend is a result that can only be achieved after both employers and employees are willing to push each other to come up with a viable alternative.
If implemented smoothly, workers take an extra day off, they can have more time to rest, so that they can be physically and mentally rejuvenated, and they can have more time to spend with their families, which can help increase the marriage rate and fertility rate.
But most workers are still worried that an extra day of leave may reduce their income, and even this day of leave does not know what to do, so it is better to keep working five days a week.
This is also a problem that European and American countries often encounter in the early days of promoting the three-day weekend. Sometimes the workers themselves are unwilling, or can not guarantee that the work efficiency will not be affected by less than one day of work, so that the management will not implement the three-day weekend.
In other words, although in order to live, everyone must work, but work is not the whole of life, with the progress of the times, everyone should pay more attention to their labor rights, the right to decide more rest, the right to value their own health, the right to spend more time on themselves, rather than just work.
Back to the network.
It can be imagined that when there is no consensus between employers and employees, everyone will expect the Government to set the standards.
But different industries are different, how each worker tries to increase their work efficiency, the method is also different, it is difficult for the government to uniformly set standards, and it is impossible to force enterprises to comply with, otherwise it will be punished, after all, the operation of each enterprise is not the same.
Therefore, before discussing "three days off week", it is more important that employees and employees should clearly express their position, why do employees want to take one more day off, how do employers ensure that taking one more day will not harm the interests of the company?

Gediminas Ziemelis, Chairman of Avia Solutions Group: 10 challenges for sustainable passenger aviation over the next three years
DUBLIN, Ireland, May 19, 2023 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Ensuring sustainable operations has become a major driver of the aviation industry in recent years.
Still, this unpredictable industry faces multiple challenges that could hamper airlines ’ efforts to improve profitability.
While the factors contributing to the plight of the aviation industry are diverse, certain key issues can be highlighted as culprits.
Airlines with high leverage and high debt will face higher market rates
In recent years, the airline industry has experienced a significant decline in demand for air travel, resulting in many airlines facing financial losses.
In order to maintain operations during this period, the airline is heavily indebted.
However, this increase in debt has increased the risk faced by lenders, leading to higher market interest rates for airlines.
In addition to the impact of the epidemic on the industry, other factors such as rising fuel costs and increased competition have also led to financial distress for many airlines.
These factors make it increasingly difficult for highly leveraged airlines to make profits and pay down debt, raising concerns about the sustainability of their business models.
A combination of factors has led to heavily indebted airlines now facing higher market interest rates, which could worsen their financial woes.
Insurance costs soar – increased war risk could drive up premiums
As geopolitical risks mount, the airline industry is grappling with rising insurance costs.
This is in large part because about 500 aircraft leased to Russian operators are still trapped in Russia, as the major insurance companies say.
Insurance companies are facing potential liabilities due to the uncertainty caused by the Russian government's refusal to return the plane.
Therefore, according to industry sources, insurance companies are trying to assess the level of risk involved, resulting in a wide range of potential losses estimated at up to $30 billion.
This uncertainty could push up airline premiums, affecting the industry as a whole.
Passengers won't forget to claim flight delay compensation, which will affect airlines' unplanned costs
EU Regulation 261 / 2004 provides for compensation for passengers who suffer delays, cancellations, overbooking or denial.
Depending on the circumstances and specific conditions, affected passengers may be eligible for compensation ranging from €250 to €600 per person.
Prior to Covid-19, the EU ’ s flight delay rate for which compensation conditions were met accounted for 1.5% of all flights, with an average compensation of €375 per delayed flight.
In 2019, EU airlines carried 1.12 billion passengers, of which 1.7 million were delayed, resulting in a total of 6.3 billion euros in compensation.
Currently only 10 per cent of affected passengers complain directly to the airline or through a professional services company such as Skyscanner or Airhelp.
However, the number is expected to climb significantly due to capacity shortages and other challenges faced by the airline industry in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic.
As a result, the number of flights that can be claimed for delay could increase from 1.5% to 5%, which could result in a total compensation of 20 billion euros.
The challenges facing LEAP engines will have a greater impact on grounded aircraft and capacity shortages.
According to our internal research, the aviation industry currently operates 1,397 LEAP-1A-powered A320neo aircraft with a total of 3,080 engines, an average of 2.2 engines per aircraft; and 1,043 LEAP-1B-powered Boeing 737 MAX aircraft with a total of 2,338 engines, an average of 2.2 engines per aircraft.
To maintain these engines, the LEAP-1A and LEAP-1B engines have 21 and 22 repair and maintenance sites worldwide, respectively.
However, 16,000 aircraft (60% of the total fleet) were grounded in 2020-2021, resulting in up to 60% of LEAP engine maintenance delays.
As a result, there are now huge maintenance gaps at 43 sites, resulting in engine maintenance waiting times of up to 9-10 months, which could disrupt airline operations.
Between 2023 and 2025, OEM production and supply chain disruptions will lead to aircraft capacity shortages.
The COVID-19 pandemic has had a profound impact on the aerospace industry.
The production and supply chains of original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) such as Boeing and Airbus have been severely disrupted.
In response to the global economic slowdown and reduced demand for air travel, OEMs have cut production levels by nearly half from pre-pandemic levels.
However, this has led to a shortage of aircraft capacity, hindering the recovery process of the industry.
The cuts affected more than 5,000 suppliers in the supply chain, all of whom had to reduce production during the outbreak.
As a result, the aerospace industry is expected to take 2.5-4 years to return to pre-pandemic production levels.
Such a long-term disruption could have serious consequences for the industry and its stakeholders.
In 2020-2021, the cancellation of the Flight Cadet Program and the planned retirement of existing pilots resulted in a shortage of pilots and a rapid increase in airline costs in 2023-2024.
The airline industry has a constant demand for new pilots, as about 3% of pilots retire each year.
However, Covid-19 caused all pilot programs to be either delayed or cancelled, causing a major setback for the industry.
As a result, there is a serious shortage of pilots today, leading to a rapid increase in costs.
It is estimated that the airline industry will face a shortage of 300,000 pilots within 10 years.
This shortage is expected to pose major challenges, especially in India, where the expected gap for pilots is the largest.
Reservations for maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) sessions after Covid-19 became problematic, and the original maintenance schedule was postponed due to Covid-19
Another major problem caused by COVID-19 is the huge backlog in the global demand for aircraft MRO services.
The unprecedented reduction in demand for air travel and the grounding of many aircraft resulted in the postponement or postponement of scheduled maintenance.
Nevertheless, as air travel demand begins to recover and airlines return to full operations, the challenge of booking MRO slots to perform the necessary maintenance of aircraft has emerged.
Many airlines find that MRO facilities are operating at full capacity, so waiting times are long and may cause disruption to airline operations.
This backlog of maintenance requirements is expected to persist for some time, creating an obstacle to the aviation industry's efforts to recover.
Finding maintenance slots for V2500 and RR engines is also challenging due to maintenance delays
Airlines using V2500 and RR engines also face difficulties in arranging engine maintenance due to high demand and low availability.
Especially for airlines with a large number of such aircraft, this is undoubtedly a tricky situation.
The lack of available maintenance periods has forced airlines to grounded some of their aircraft, resulting in operational disruptions and lost revenue.
In addition to the financial impact, this situation poses safety issues as delayed maintenance can compromise the safety and reliability of the engine and can lead to more serious problems in the future.
Green Aviation ’ s ESG requirements haven ’ t disappeared in the medium term
In October 2022, the 41st General Assembly of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) was held in Montreal, marking an important milestone in the aviation industry ’ s commitment to sustainable development.
The conference ’ s commitment to achieving a “Long Term Vision ” (LTAG) of net-zero carbon dioxide emissions by 2050 puts environmental, social and governance (ESG) issues at the forefront of the aviation industry ’ s sustainable development dialogue.
Achieving the ambitious LTAG is challenging, but it has the potential to encourage airlines to accelerate the development and adoption of more environmentally friendly aircraft fuels and other technological improvements to decarbonize flight.
This will require a major shift in industry-wide thinking, investment in research and development, and collaboration between airlines, manufacturers, and governments to achieve this long-term goal.
After COVID-19, some aircraft will continue to be grounded due to spare parts, MRO services and aircraft lease debt, which will create capacity requirements.
In a challenging situation in the industry, airlines have been forced to raise more debt to fund all aspects of their operations, such as spare parts, MRO services and aircraft leasing.
However, the increase in outstanding debt can have a significant impact on the industry, and some airlines may have difficulty paying their debts and have to suspend some aircraft or reduce routes to minimize costs, which can lead to reduced capacity.
Internal data shows that since 2020, the industry ’ s outstanding debt has jumped more than 20% to more than $300 billion.
To raise funds, global airline bonds and loans have totaled 63 billion U.S. dollars so far this year.

They are also being welcomed by the tourism and hospitality industry, with co-working cafes offering cocktails and swimming pools, while co-op hotels offer high-speed Wi-Fi and group activities.
Canggu is full of signs encouraging tourists to work remotely, and the economic benefits of tourism provide opportunities for the region.
But, as some have questioned on TikTok, is the digital nomadic movement a kind of neo-colonization?
Tourists come and go, but digital nomads can stay in one place for weeks, months or years, potentially exacerbating gentrification and the housing crisis.
Recently, The New York Times reported that Mexico City has become a hub for digital nomads, but the surge has exacerbated the pressure on the already tight housing market, making it unaffordable for locals.
Housing activists accused city leaders of allowing “modern colonization. ”
The rise of digital nomads
Countries around the world are embracing the era of digital nomads, with 50 countries, including Dubai and Iceland, offering specific visas for this new type of traveler.
To work remotely in Mexico, you need to prove that you have $43,000 in your savings account in the past 12 months; to Portugal, you need to have at least $4500 a month in income; to Indonesia, you need to have more than $200,000 in savings but can do “investment and other activities. ”
The requirements mean many digital nomads use tourist visas to leave the country when their visas expire, just to re-enter.
According to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, between January and September last year, 3,000 foreigners entered Indonesia on B211A tourist visas for telecommuting.
One enthusiast of the digital nomad industry predicts that there will be 1 billion digital nomads by 2035, driven by factors such as the rise of high-speed internet and freelancing, as well as declining home ownership and marriage rates.
Are digital nomads taking part in the new colonization?
Some communities are opposed to the influx, and Mexico City residents say they see gentrification and housing drain problems triggered by foreigners seeking cheaper accommodation.
Anthropologist Shaun Busuttil, a PhD candidate at the University of Melbourne who studies digital nomads, believes that digital nomads are undergoing some form of neo-colonization, but it ’ s not all black and white, or good and bad.
In an interview with Erik Muth of YouTube ’ s Rising Nomad channel, Basutil explained: “Historically, colonialism was when a group of people with more power or resources came into a place and effectively took over it and used the space for themselves. ”
“What are we doing as digital nomads? We go into these places, take over them, and enjoy their low cost of living. ”
Shops and businesses will eventually cater to the financial prowess of new visitors, Bousutier believes.
“So the old-fashioned fruit and vegetable shop that has been in town or village for generations now has suddenly turned into a cafe to attract digital nomads.
Is digital nomadism, then, a form of neocolonialism? ” he asked.
"Well, we're coming in and we're effectively taking over," he said.
"Look at Lisbon, or even Mexico City, or Barcelona, where locals are being replaced by foreign teleworkers and digital nomads," he said.
He told Moos that while it was usually those with fewer resources who were most affected by gentrification, those with more resources were able to take advantage of the economic opportunities offered by tourism.
How to avoid causing problems?
Keith thinks deeply about the impact on the communities he visits and how it can have a positive impact.
"As a digital nomad, I feel like we should make sure we contribute to the local economy - eat at local restaurants, stay locally and pay a reasonable fee for that," said the statement.
Both Busutil and Casey believe tourists should pay the full price, not haggle.
“It ’ s important to be aware of the impact you have on the local area, ” says Casey.
"That way you can walk into the local community, eat at the local restaurants, stay in the local area, and give back to the local community," said the statement.
At the moment, Casey likes the pace of life of digital nomads and has no plans for a pause.
“Being able to finish work in the morning and then off work and take an adventure in the afternoon – I experienced paragliding in Laos and was great and went swimming to see the waterfall – I think when you can schedule your own time, you can experience more from life. ”

The billionaire, Bryan Johnson, who is committed to “rejuvenating ”,“ changed blood ” with his 70-year-old father, Richard, and his 17-year-old son, Talmage, at a clinic near Dallas last month.
